children.title: Distributed Optimization Problem
children.top_down_role: Canonical ways to distribute objectives, variables, constraints, and observations.

children.title: Shared-Decision Sum Optimization
children.top_down_role: Agent-local objective components coupled through a common decision.

assumptions_latex: \(m\in\mathbb{N}\) agents share a decision space \(X\subseteq\mathbb{R}^d\).
Each agent owns an extended-real objective \(f_i:X\to(-\infty,+\infty]\).

notation.meaning: Single decision shared by all agents.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Canonical finite-agent shared-variable formulation; convexity is not part of the definition.

source_refs.locator: 11 Distributed and decentralized optimization p. 227
source_refs.source_title: Large-Scale Convex Optimization: Algorithms & Analyses via Monotone Operators

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
A shared-decision sum optimization problem for \(m\) agents is
\[
\operatorname*{minimize}_{x\in X}\;F(x):=\sum_{i=1}^{m} f_i(x).
\]
The same variable \(x\) occurs in every summand, while agent \(i\) owns or evaluates \(f_i\). Feasibility restrictions may be encoded by \(X\) or by assigning value \(+\infty\) outside an agent-local domain. Its solution set is \(\operatorname*{argmin}_{x\in X}F(x)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Agents contribute separate objective terms but optimize one common decision; a solution minimizes their summed objective over the shared feasible set.
knowledge_statements.title: Shared-Decision Sum Optimization

source_witnesses.locator: 11 Distributed and decentralized optimization p. 227
source_witnesses.source_title: Large-Scale Convex Optimization: Algorithms & Analyses via Monotone Operators

children.title: Partitioned-Variable Optimization
children.top_down_role: Distinct variable blocks assigned to different agents.

assumptions_latex: \(m\in\mathbb{N}\) and \(X=X_1\times\cdots\times X_m\), with \(X_i\subseteq\mathbb{R}^{d_i}\).
Agent \(i\) owns block \(x_i\in X_i\), and \(C\subseteq X\) is the joint feasible set.

notation.meaning: Decision block owned by agent i.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Block-distributed model, allowing both separable and coupled objectives or constraints.

source_refs.locator: 3.3.4 The Case of a Product Constraint Set: Parallel Implementations p. 217
source_refs.source_title: Parallel and Distributed Computation: Numerical Methods

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
A partitioned-variable optimization problem assigns distinct blocks \(x_i\in X_i\) to agents and has the form
\[
\operatorname*{minimize}_{x=(x_1,\ldots,x_m)\in C}\;\Phi(x_1,\ldots,x_m),
\]
where \(C\subseteq X_1\times\cdots\times X_m\). The ownership partition concerns variables, not necessarily separability: \(\Phi\) may couple several blocks, and \(C\) need not equal the full product. When \(\Phi(x)=\sum_{i=1}^m f_i(x_i)\), only the constraints can couple agents.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Each agent controls a distinct variable block, while the objective or feasible set may still couple blocks across agents.
knowledge_statements.title: Partitioned-Variable Optimization

source_witnesses.locator: 3.3.4 The Case of a Product Constraint Set: Parallel Implementations p. 217
source_witnesses.source_title: Parallel and Distributed Computation: Numerical Methods

children.title: Distributed Data-Parallel Optimization
children.top_down_role: Shared model variables paired with partitioned observations.

assumptions_latex: \(m\in\mathbb{N}\), and the finite dataset \(D\) is partitioned as \(D=\bigsqcup_{i=1}^m D_i\).
All agents optimize the same parameter \(w\in W\subseteq\mathbb{R}^d\).
The sample loss is \(\ell:W\times D\to(-\infty,+\infty]\), and the optional global regularizer is \(r:W\to(-\infty,+\infty]\).

notation.meaning: Data shard stored by agent i.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-sample empirical-risk form with horizontally partitioned observations.

source_refs.locator: 11 Distributed and decentralized optimization p. 227
source_refs.source_title: Large-Scale Convex Optimization: Algorithms & Analyses via Monotone Operators

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Distributed data-parallel optimization is the shared-model problem
\[
\operatorname*{minimize}_{w\in W}\;r(w)+\sum_{i=1}^{m}L_i(w),
\qquad L_i(w):=\sum_{z\in D_i}\ell(w;z),
\]
where agent \(i\) stores the observation shard \(D_i\), but every local loss is evaluated at the same model parameter \(w\). Dividing the entire objective by the positive constant \(|D|\) does not change its minimizers; other sample-weighting conventions define the corresponding weighted empirical-risk objective.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Observations are partitioned among agents, but every shard contributes loss terms for the same shared model parameters.
knowledge_statements.title: Distributed Data-Parallel Optimization

children.title: Distributed Feasibility Coupling Models
children.top_down_role: Constraints or feasible-set information held locally by agents.

children.title: Local Constraint Ownership
children.top_down_role: Placement of constraint information across agents.

assumptions_latex: \(m\in\mathbb{N}\) agents share a decision space \(X\subseteq\mathbb{R}^d\).
For each \(i\in\{1,\ldots,m\}\), agent \(i\) is assigned a local feasible set \(C_i\subseteq X\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(x\) is globally feasible exactly when \(x\in\bigcap_{i=1}^m C_i\).

notation.meaning: Constraint set whose membership agent i can evaluate.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Set-based ownership of constraints on a shared decision.

source_refs.locator: 11 Distributed and decentralized optimization p. 227
source_refs.source_title: Large-Scale Convex Optimization: Algorithms & Analyses via Monotone Operators

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Local constraint ownership means that agent \(i\) stores, evaluates, or enforces the predicate \(x\in C_i\) for a common candidate \(x\in X\). The distributed constraint system is
\[
x\in C_i\quad(i=1,\ldots,m),
\]
and therefore its global feasible set is \(C:=\bigcap_{i=1}^m C_i\). Ownership specifies information placement; it does not imply that \(C_i\) is private, convex, or independent of the other sets.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Each agent owns a membership constraint on the shared decision; global feasibility requires satisfying every owned constraint.
knowledge_statements.title: Local Constraint Ownership

source_witnesses.locator: 11 Distributed and decentralized optimization p. 227
source_witnesses.source_title: Large-Scale Convex Optimization: Algorithms & Analyses via Monotone Operators

children.title: Intersections of Local Feasible Sets
children.top_down_role: Feasible regions assembled from agent-local sets.

assumptions_latex: \(C_i\subseteq X\subseteq\mathbb{R}^d\) for \(i=1,\ldots,m\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact set representation for conjunctive local constraints.

source_refs.locator: 3.3.4 The Case of a Product Constraint Set: Parallel Implementations p. 217
source_refs.source_title: Parallel and Distributed Computation: Numerical Methods

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For local feasible sets \(C_1,\ldots,C_m\subseteq X\), simultaneous satisfaction is represented by
\[
C:=\bigcap_{i=1}^{m}C_i
 =\{x\in X: x\in C_i\text{ for all }i=1,\ldots,m\}.
\]
Thus a distributed feasibility problem asks for any \(x\in C\), and an optimization problem with local constraints minimizes its objective over \(C\). If every \(C_i\) is convex, then \(C\) is convex; the intersection may nevertheless be empty.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The globally feasible decisions are precisely the intersection of all agent-local feasible sets; convex local sets yield a convex, possibly empty, intersection.
knowledge_statements.title: Intersections of Local Feasible Sets

source_witnesses.locator: 3.3.4 The Case of a Product Constraint Set: Parallel Implementations p. 217
source_witnesses.source_title: Parallel and Distributed Computation: Numerical Methods

children.title: Coupled Feasibility Relations
children.top_down_role: Feasibility requirements spanning multiple local decision blocks.

assumptions_latex: Agent decisions satisfy \(x_i\in X_i\subseteq\mathbb{R}^{d_i}\).
For each relation \(e\), \(R_e\subseteq\prod_{i\in S_e}X_i\) involves the agent subset \(S_e\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(x\in C\iff (x_i)_{i\in S_e}\in R_e\) for every relation \(e\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: General finite relational model encompassing pairwise, hyperedge, and global constraints.

source_refs.locator: 11 Distributed and decentralized optimization p. 227
source_refs.source_title: Large-Scale Convex Optimization: Algorithms & Analyses via Monotone Operators

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
A coupled feasibility system on \(X:=\prod_{i=1}^m X_i\) is specified by relations \(R_e\subseteq\prod_{i\in S_e}X_i\), where each \(S_e\subseteq\{1,\ldots,m\}\). Its joint feasible set is
\[
C:=\left\{x\in X:(x_i)_{i\in S_e}\in R_e\text{ for every }e\right\}.
\]
A relation is genuinely coupling when membership cannot be expressed as independent conditions on each participating block. Pairwise agreement, network balance, and shared-budget constraints are special cases.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Joint feasibility can be defined by relations involving selected groups of agent variables, rather than by independent constraints on single blocks.
knowledge_statements.title: Coupled Feasibility Relations

source_witnesses.locator: 11 Distributed and decentralized optimization p. 227
source_witnesses.source_title: Large-Scale Convex Optimization: Algorithms & Analyses via Monotone Operators

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The relational formulation is mathematically plausible, but the domain over which e ranges is not introduced. More importantly, the cited general chapter opening does not specifically support the hyperedge-style family of relations or the stated characterization of genuine coupling. A source with a precise locator for factor-graph, hypergraph, or multi-block relational constraints is required.

children.title: Feasibility Conflict Boundaries
children.top_down_role: Regimes where local restrictions lack a compatible global solution.

assumptions_latex: \(C_i\subseteq X\) are nonempty closed sets in a normed space \(X\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\rho=0\) exactly when \(\bigcap_{i=1}^m C_i\neq\varnothing\); if the intersection is empty, \(\rho\) quantifies best attainable worst local violation.

notation.meaning: Distance from x to local feasible set i.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Metric boundary between consistent and inconsistent finite local-set systems.

source_refs.locator: 11 Distributed and decentralized optimization p. 227
source_refs.source_title: Large-Scale Convex Optimization: Algorithms & Analyses via Monotone Operators

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Define the feasibility-conflict radius by
\[
\rho:=\inf_{x\in X}\max_{1\le i\le m}d(x,C_i),
\qquad d(x,C_i):=\inf_{y\in C_i}\|x-y\|.
\]
For finitely many nonempty closed sets, \(\rho=0\) whenever their intersection is nonempty. Conversely, if the infimum is attained, then \(\rho=0\) implies \(x\in\bigcap_{i=1}^m C_i\) at a minimizer. Hence \(\rho>0\) certifies a positive incompatibility margin, while nonattainment must be excluded before treating \(\rho=0\) as feasibility.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The minimum worst distance to local sets measures conflict; a positive value certifies infeasibility, while zero certifies feasibility when the infimum is attained.
knowledge_statements.title: Feasibility Conflict Boundaries

source_witnesses.locator: 11 Distributed and decentralized optimization p. 227
source_witnesses.source_title: Large-Scale Convex Optimization: Algorithms & Analyses via Monotone Operators

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The conclusion_latex incorrectly states an unconditional equivalence between rho=0 and nonempty intersection, whereas the statement correctly notes that the reverse implication needs attainment or another sufficient compactness/coercivity condition. The cited distributed-optimization chapter opening does not specifically support this conflict-radius definition or its boundary characterization, so an authoritative source is required before selecting and repairing the precise hypothesis set.

children.title: Coupling Structures
children.top_down_role: Structures that prevent independent solution of agent-local problems.

children.title: Replicated-Decision Agreement Coupling
children.top_down_role: Agreement coupling among replicated decision variables.

children.title: Consensus Coupling
children.top_down_role: Agreement requirements imposed across agent decisions.

assumptions_latex: \(G=(V,E)\) is an undirected graph with \(V=\{1,\ldots,m\}\).
Each agent holds \(x_i\in\mathbb{R}^d\).

notation.meaning: Oriented incidence matrix tensored with the identity.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Undirected connected-graph consensus characterized by incidence constraints.

source_refs.locator: 11.2 Decentralized optimization with graph consensus p. 234
source_refs.source_title: Large-Scale Convex Optimization: Algorithms & Analyses via Monotone Operators

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Choose an orientation of \(E\), let \(\bar B\in\mathbb{R}^{|E|\times m}\) be the incidence matrix, and set \(B:=\bar B\otimes I_d\). Consensus coupling is the condition
\[
Bx=0,
\]
which is equivalent to \(x_i=x_j\) for every edge \(\{i,j\}\in E\). If \(G\) is connected, these edge equalities are equivalent to global agreement \(x_1=\cdots=x_m\); if \(G\) is disconnected, they impose agreement only within each connected component.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Consensus requires neighboring local decisions to agree; on a connected graph this is equivalent to agreement among all agents.
knowledge_statements.title: Consensus Coupling

source_witnesses.locator: 11.2 Decentralized optimization with graph consensus p. 234
source_witnesses.source_title: Large-Scale Convex Optimization: Algorithms & Analyses via Monotone Operators

children.title: Local-Copy Replication
children.top_down_role: Agent-specific copies of shared decision variables.

assumptions_latex: A shared-variable problem has decision \(z\in Z\subseteq\mathbb{R}^d\) and local terms \(f_i(z)\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The replicated formulation is equivalent to the original when \(x_1=\cdots=x_m\), with \(z=x_i\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact lifting of a shared decision into agent-local copies.

source_refs.locator: 11.1 Distributed optimization with centralized consensus p. 227
source_refs.source_title: Large-Scale Convex Optimization: Algorithms & Analyses via Monotone Operators

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Local-copy replication replaces the shared variable \(z\) by one copy \(x_i\in Z\) per agent and rewrites
\[
\operatorname*{minimize}_{z\in Z}\sum_{i=1}^m f_i(z)
\quad\text{as}\quad
\operatorname*{minimize}_{x_1,\ldots,x_m\in Z}\sum_{i=1}^m f_i(x_i)
\quad\text{subject to}\quad x_1=\cdots=x_m.
\]
The mapping \(z\mapsto(z,\ldots,z)\) is a bijection between feasible decisions of the original problem and agreement-feasible replicated decisions, preserving objective values.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A shared decision is lifted to one copy per agent, with equality constraints making the replicated and original formulations equivalent.
knowledge_statements.title: Local-Copy Replication

source_witnesses.locator: 11.1 Distributed optimization with centralized consensus p. 227
source_witnesses.source_title: Large-Scale Convex Optimization: Algorithms & Analyses via Monotone Operators

children.title: Copy-to-Global Coupling
children.top_down_role: Links between replicated variables and a shared reference.

assumptions_latex: Each agent has a local copy \(x_i\in\mathbb{R}^d\).
A global coordination variable satisfies \(z\in\mathbb{R}^d\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Star-form centralized consensus using an explicit global variable.

source_refs.locator: 11.1 Distributed optimization with centralized consensus p. 227
source_refs.source_title: Large-Scale Convex Optimization: Algorithms & Analyses via Monotone Operators

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Copy-to-global coupling introduces \(z\in\mathbb{R}^d\) and imposes
\[
x_i-z=0\quad(i=1,\ldots,m).
\]
Equivalently, for the stacked vector \(x=(x_1,\ldots,x_m)\), the constraint is \(x-\mathbf{1}_m\otimes z=0\). Eliminating \(z\) yields \(x_1=\cdots=x_m\), while any consensual tuple determines the unique value \(z=x_i\). This representation centralizes agreement through a star-shaped coupling variable.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Every local copy is constrained to equal one global variable; eliminating that variable recovers ordinary all-agent consensus.
knowledge_statements.title: Copy-to-Global Coupling

source_witnesses.locator: 11.1 Distributed optimization with centralized consensus p. 227
source_witnesses.source_title: Large-Scale Convex Optimization: Algorithms & Analyses via Monotone Operators

children.title: Agreement-Violation Structure
children.top_down_role: Network disagreement induced by inconsistent local copies.

assumptions_latex: \(G=(V,E)\) is an oriented undirected graph.
The stacked local decision is \(x\in(\mathbb{R}^d)^m\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(r=0\) exactly characterizes edgewise agreement, and \(\|r\|_2^2=x^T(L\otimes I_d)x\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Euclidean residual and Laplacian energy for graph agreement violations.

source_refs.locator: 11.2 Decentralized optimization with graph consensus p. 234
source_refs.source_title: Large-Scale Convex Optimization: Algorithms & Analyses via Monotone Operators

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(\bar B\) be an oriented incidence matrix and define the agreement residual
\[
r:=(\bar B\otimes I_d)x.
\]
The block of \(r\) associated with an oriented edge \((i,j)\) equals \(x_i-x_j\), up to the chosen orientation. Hence \(r=0\) exactly when every edge agrees. Moreover, with \(L:=\bar B^T\bar B\),
\[
\|r\|_2^2=x^T(L\otimes I_d)x=\sum_{\{i,j\}\in E}\|x_i-x_j\|_2^2,
\]
so Laplacian energy is a nonnegative scalar measure of agreement violation.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Edgewise copy differences form a consensus residual, whose squared norm equals the graph-Laplacian disagreement energy.
knowledge_statements.title: Agreement-Violation Structure

source_witnesses.locator: 11.2 Decentralized optimization with graph consensus p. 234
source_witnesses.source_title: Large-Scale Convex Optimization: Algorithms & Analyses via Monotone Operators

children.title: Aggregate Resource Coupling
children.top_down_role: Separable decisions joined by shared budgets or balance relations.

assumptions_latex: Agent \(i\) chooses \(x_i\in X_i\subseteq\mathbb{R}^{d_i}\).
Maps \(A_i:\mathbb{R}^{d_i}\to\mathbb{R}^p\) and a resource vector \(b\in\mathbb{R}^p\) are given.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The decisions are jointly feasible when \(\sum_{i=1}^m A_i x_i\le b\), or when \(\sum_{i=1}^m A_i x_i=b\) in the balance form.

notation.meaning: Agent i's resource-consumption or contribution map.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional linear shared-budget and balance coupling.

source_refs.locator: 11 Distributed and decentralized optimization p. 227
source_refs.source_title: Large-Scale Convex Optimization: Algorithms & Analyses via Monotone Operators

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Aggregate resource coupling joins otherwise separable decisions through a shared relation such as
\[
\sum_{i=1}^{m}A_i x_i\le b
\quad\text{or}\quad
\sum_{i=1}^{m}A_i x_i=b,
\qquad x_i\in X_i.
\]
The inequality is interpreted componentwise and models common capacities; the equality models conservation or balance. Although each contribution \(A_i x_i\) is locally determined, feasibility depends on their aggregate, so the joint feasible set generally is not a Cartesian product of agent-local feasible sets.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Agents make separate decisions, but their summed resource use or contribution must satisfy a common capacity or balance relation.
knowledge_statements.title: Aggregate Resource Coupling

source_witnesses.locator: 11 Distributed and decentralized optimization p. 227
source_witnesses.source_title: Large-Scale Convex Optimization: Algorithms & Analyses via Monotone Operators

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The aggregate-capacity and balance forms fit the leaf, but the assumptions call A_i merely maps while using matrix-style products A_i x_i and claiming a linear finite-dimensional model. The cited chapter opening is too broad to establish this particular resource-coupling formulation. A specific source should determine whether A_i are linear maps or whether the intended definition permits nonlinear contribution maps.

children.title: Network-Flow Coupling Taxonomy
children.top_down_role: Coupling induced by network flows, routing, or edge relations.

children.title: Edge-Relation Coupling
children.top_down_role: Pairwise restrictions attached to communication or physical edges.

knowledge_statements.title: Edge-Relation Coupling
knowledge_statements.scope_note: A graph-local coupling model expressed by relations attached to edges.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(G=(V,E)\) be a graph, let agent \(i\in V\) own \(x_i\in X_i\), and assign each edge \(e=(i,j)\in E\) a relation \(R_e\subseteq X_i\times X_j\). Edge-relation coupling requires \[(x_i,x_j)\in R_{(i,j)}\qquad\text{for every }(i,j)\in E.\] The resulting feasible set is \(\mathcal F=\{x\in\prod_{i\in V}X_i:(x_i,x_j)\in R_{(i,j)}\ \forall(i,j)\in E\}\). Thus each constraint is locally checkable by its incident agents, although all edge relations jointly determine global feasibility.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Each graph edge imposes a relation between its endpoint variables; global feasibility means satisfying every edge relation simultaneously.
assumptions_latex: \(G=(V,E)\) is a fixed finite graph.
Each \(R_e\) is a specified subset of the endpoint product space.

notation.meaning: Feasibility relation associated with edge e.
Joint feasible set induced by all edge relations.

review_flags: A network-optimization source explicitly defining general edge relations is required.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The definition fits the Edge-Relation Coupling leaf and is internally precise, but no inspectable source is supplied for this general relation-based formulation.

children.title: Network-Flow Coupling
children.top_down_role: Shared flow variables distributed across network links.

knowledge_statements.title: Network-Flow Coupling
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Single-commodity capacitated flow coupling in node-edge incidence form.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a directed graph \(G=(V,E)\), choose an orientation and let \(B\in\mathbb R^{|V|\times |E|}\) be its node-edge incidence matrix. A capacitated network-flow coupling consists of edge flows \(f\in\mathbb R^{|E|}\) satisfying \[Bf=b,\qquad \ell\leq f\leq u,\] where \(b\in\mathbb R^{|V|}\) is the vector of node supplies, with positive entries denoting net injection, and \(\ell,u\in\mathbb R^{|E|}\) are edge bounds. Necessarily \(\mathbf 1^{\mathsf T}b=0\) on every connected component containing feasible flow.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Edge flows are coupled through incidence-based node balances and individual edge-capacity bounds.
assumptions_latex: \(G\) is a finite directed graph with a fixed incidence convention.
The bounds satisfy \(\ell_e\leq u_e\) for every edge.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(f\) is feasible exactly when \(Bf=b\) and \(\ell\leq f\leq u\).

notation.meaning: Vector of prescribed net node injections.

review_flags: The supplied inventory contains no network-flow locator supporting this formulation.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The content kind and single-commodity flow formulation fit the leaf, but an authoritative network-flow locator is absent. A supporting source should also fix the incidence-matrix sign convention consistently with positive net injection.

children.title: Node-Conservation Coupling
children.top_down_role: Balance requirements associated with network nodes.

knowledge_statements.title: Node-Conservation Coupling
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Local conservation equations coupling flows incident to each network node.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(G=(V,E)\) be directed and let \(f_e\in\mathbb R\) denote the flow on edge \(e\). Given a prescribed net injection \(b_i\) at each node \(i\), node-conservation coupling is the family of conditions \[\sum_{e\in\delta^+(i)}f_e-\sum_{e\in\delta^-(i)}f_e=b_i\qquad(i\in V),\] where \(\delta^+(i)\) and \(\delta^-(i)\) are the outgoing and incoming edges. With the corresponding incidence matrix \(B\), these local equations are equivalent to the global equality \(Bf=b\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: At every node, outgoing flow minus incoming flow equals the node's prescribed net injection.
assumptions_latex: A fixed orientation is assigned to every edge.
The sign convention treats supply as positive net outflow.

notation.meaning: Outgoing and incoming edge sets of node i.
Prescribed net injection at node i.

review_flags: The supplied inventory contains no network-flow conservation locator.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The condition correctly expresses node conservation under the stated net-outflow convention and fits the terminal container, but it has no inspectable network-flow citation.

children.title: Routing-Capacity Interaction
children.top_down_role: Structural interaction between route selection and link capacity.

knowledge_statements.title: Routing-Capacity Interaction
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Multicommodity routes interact through shared edge-capacity inequalities.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let commodities \(k\in K\) have nonnegative demands \(d_k\), let \(P_k\) be their admissible paths, and let \(z_{kp}\geq0\) be the amount of commodity \(k\) routed on path \(p\in P_k\). Routing and capacity are jointly feasible when \[\sum_{p\in P_k}z_{kp}=d_k\quad(k\in K),\qquad \sum_{k\in K}\sum_{p\in P_k:e\in p}z_{kp}\leq u_e\quad(e\in E).\] The second family couples otherwise independent commodity-routing decisions through each shared edge capacity \(u_e\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Each demand is distributed over admissible paths, while total traffic using any edge cannot exceed that edge's capacity.
assumptions_latex: Every demand and edge capacity is nonnegative.
Each \(P_k\) is a specified set of admissible paths.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(z\) is routing-capacity feasible exactly when the demand equalities and shared-edge inequalities hold.

notation.meaning: Amount of commodity k assigned to path p.

review_flags: A multicommodity-flow source supporting the path-capacity formulation is required.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The path-based multicommodity demand and shared-capacity conditions fit Routing-Capacity Interaction, but no source with a specific multicommodity-flow locator is supplied.

children.title: Distributed Constraint Coupling Family
children.top_down_role: Global linear, cone, or inequality relations across local blocks.

children.title: Global Linear Equality Coupling
children.top_down_role: Cross-agent equality relations over local variable blocks.

knowledge_statements.title: Global Linear Equality Coupling
knowledge_statements.scope_note: A single linear equality aggregates variables owned by multiple agents.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let agent \(i\in\{1,\ldots,m\}\) own \(x_i\in X_i\subseteq\mathbb R^{n_i}\), and let \(A_i\in\mathbb R^{p\times n_i}\). Global linear equality coupling imposes \[\sum_{i=1}^m A_i x_i=b,\] for a prescribed \(b\in\mathbb R^p\). Although each contribution \(A_i x_i\) is locally computable, feasibility is determined only by their aggregate. Equivalently, for \(x=(x_1,\ldots,x_m)\) and \(A=[A_1\ \cdots\ A_m]\), the coupling is \(Ax=b\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Local variable blocks are globally coupled when their linear contributions must sum to a prescribed vector.
assumptions_latex: Each variable block lies in a finite-dimensional real vector space.
All matrices have the common row dimension \(p\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(x\) satisfies the coupling exactly when \(\sum_{i=1}^m A_i x_i=b\).

notation.meaning: Linear map from block i to the shared constraint space.

children.title: Distributed Inequality Coupling
children.top_down_role: Global inequality restrictions assembled from local contributions.

knowledge_statements.title: Distributed Inequality Coupling
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Componentwise inequalities aggregate constraint contributions from multiple agents.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let agent \(i\in\{1,\ldots,m\}\) own \(x_i\in X_i\), and let \(g_i:X_i\to\mathbb R^p\). Distributed inequality coupling imposes the componentwise condition \[\sum_{i=1}^m g_i(x_i)\leq 0.\] Each agent can evaluate its local contribution, but no block alone determines feasibility. In the affine case \(g_i(x_i)=A_i x_i-c_i\), this becomes the global linear inequality \(\sum_i A_i x_i\leq\sum_i c_i\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The sum of agents' local constraint contributions must be nonpositive in every component.
assumptions_latex: All \(g_i\) have the same finite-dimensional codomain \(\mathbb R^p\).
The order is the componentwise order on \(\mathbb R^p\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(x\) is feasible exactly when \(\sum_{i=1}^m g_i(x_i)\in\mathbb R_-^p\).

notation.meaning: Agent i's contribution to the shared inequality.
Nonpositive orthant in the shared constraint space.

children.title: Conic Coupling Across Blocks
children.top_down_role: Cone-structured relations spanning distributed decision blocks.

knowledge_statements.title: Conic Coupling Across Blocks
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Block contributions are coupled by membership of their aggregate in a cone.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(X_i\) be finite-dimensional real vector spaces, let \(A_i:X_i\to Y\) be linear, and let \(K\subseteq Y\) be a closed convex cone. Conic coupling across blocks requires \[\sum_{i=1}^m A_i x_i-b\in -K.\] Equivalently, \(b-\sum_iA_i x_i\in K\). Equality coupling is recovered with \(K=\{0\}\), while componentwise inequality coupling is recovered with \(Y=\mathbb R^p\) and \(K=\mathbb R_+^p\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Linear contributions from all blocks must jointly satisfy one cone-membership constraint.
assumptions_latex: \(K\) is a specified closed convex cone in \(Y\).
Every \(A_i\) maps into the common space \(Y\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(x\) is conically feasible exactly when \(b-\sum_{i=1}^mA_i x_i\in K\).

notation.meaning: Cone defining the shared order or feasibility relation.

review_flags: The supplied inventory contains no conic-optimization locator supporting this definition.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The cone-membership definition and its equality and orthant special cases fit the leaf, but no conic-optimization source with a specific locator is supplied.

children.title: Block-Separability Boundaries
children.top_down_role: Coupling patterns that limit independent local treatment.

assumptions_latex: Both scalar blocks range over \(\mathbb R\).
The equality \(x_1+x_2=0\) is imposed globally.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\mathcal F\neq F_1\times F_2\) for all nonempty \(F_1,F_2\subseteq\mathbb R\).

notation.meaning: Joint feasible set of the coupled problem.

review_flags: The cited distributed-optimization chapter should be inspected in full to confirm its discussion of separability and coupling.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: A cross-block constraint can destroy Cartesian feasibility despite a separable objective.

source_refs.locator: 11 Distributed and decentralized optimization p. 227

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A separable objective does not imply block-separable feasibility. For example, with two scalar blocks and arbitrary functions \(f_1,f_2:\mathbb R\to\mathbb R\), consider \[\min_{x_1,x_2}\ f_1(x_1)+f_2(x_2)\quad\text{subject to}\quad x_1+x_2=0.\] Its feasible set \(\mathcal F=\{(t,-t):t\in\mathbb R\}\) cannot equal \(F_1\times F_2\) for nonempty sets \(F_1,F_2\subseteq\mathbb R\). Thus objective separability alone does not permit independent optimization over Cartesian block-feasible sets when a constraint jointly involves multiple blocks.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A cross-block constraint can make the feasible set non-Cartesian even when the objective is additively separable.

children.title: Consensus Optimization
children.top_down_role: Network optimization with a shared target decision.

knowledge_statements.title: Consensus Optimization
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Graph-based local copies represent one shared decision through neighbor equalities.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(G=(V,E)\) be a connected undirected graph. Agent \(i\in V\) owns a proper function \(f_i:\mathbb R^d\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) and a local copy \(x_i\in\mathbb R^d\). Consensus optimization is \[\min_{(x_i)_{i\in V}}\ \sum_{i\in V}f_i(x_i)\quad\text{subject to}\quad x_i=x_j\quad((i,j)\in E).\] Connectivity makes the edge equalities equivalent to existence of a common \(x\in\mathbb R^d\) with \(x_i=x\) for every agent, reducing the model to \(\min_x\sum_i f_i(x)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Agents minimize the sum of local objectives while graph constraints force all local decision copies to agree.
assumptions_latex: \(G\) is finite, undirected, and connected.
All local copies belong to the same space \(\mathbb R^d\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(x_i=x_j\) on every edge if and only if \(x_i=x\) for some common \(x\) and all \(i\in V\).

notation.meaning: Agent i's local copy of the shared decision.

children.title: Network Resource Allocation Model
children.top_down_role: Allocation under distributed capacities, budgets, or balance requirements.

knowledge_statements.title: Network Resource Allocation Model
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Agents allocate local resources subject to a shared aggregate budget or balance.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let agent \(i\in\{1,\ldots,m\}\) choose \(x_i\in X_i\subseteq\mathbb R^{n_i}\), incur cost \(f_i(x_i)\), and consume \(A_i x_i\in\mathbb R^p\). A network resource-allocation model has the form \[\min_{x_i\in X_i}\ \sum_{i=1}^m f_i(x_i)\quad\text{subject to}\quad \sum_{i=1}^m A_i x_i\leq c,\] with componentwise inequality and shared capacity \(c\in\mathbb R^p\). A balance model replaces the inequality by equality. Local objectives and domains are separable, while the resource constraint couples all allocations.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Agents choose local allocations with separable costs, but their total resource use must respect shared capacities or balances.
assumptions_latex: All resource contributions lie in the common space \(\mathbb R^p\).
The displayed inequality uses the componentwise order.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(x\) is feasible exactly when \(x_i\in X_i\) for every \(i\) and \(\sum_iA_i x_i\leq c\).
review_flags: The supplied inventory lacks a resource-allocation source locator for this canonical formulation.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The shared-capacity model fits the Network Resource Allocation Model leaf and is mathematically coherent, but no resource-allocation source with a specific locator is supplied.

children.title: Distributed Composite Optimization
children.top_down_role: Network problems with smooth and proximable components.

knowledge_statements.title: Distributed Composite Optimization
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Distributed minimization with locally smooth and proximable nonsmooth components.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(G=(V,E)\) be connected. Agent \(i\in V\) owns a differentiable function \(f_i:\mathbb R^d\to\mathbb R\) and a proper lower-semicontinuous function \(g_i:\mathbb R^d\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) whose proximal map is computable. Distributed composite optimization is \[\min_{(x_i)_{i\in V}}\ \sum_{i\in V}\bigl(f_i(x_i)+g_i(x_i)\bigr)\quad\text{subject to}\quad x_i=x_j\quad((i,j)\in E).\] Under consensus this is equivalent to minimizing \(\sum_i(f_i+g_i)\) over one shared decision.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Agents jointly minimize smooth plus proximable local terms while neighbor constraints enforce a common decision.
assumptions_latex: \(G\) is finite, undirected, and connected.
Each \(f_i\) is differentiable and each \(g_i\) is proper and lower semicontinuous.
Each local proximal map \(\operatorname{prox}_{\gamma g_i}\) is available for relevant \(\gamma>0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The consensus model represents \(\min_{x\in\mathbb R^d}\sum_{i\in V}(f_i(x)+g_i(x))\).

notation.meaning: Local proximal map of the nonsmooth term.

children.title: Distributed Saddle Models
children.top_down_role: Saddle-structured problems with variables placed across agents.

knowledge_statements.title: Distributed Saddle Models
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Agents collectively solve a convex-concave saddle problem with coordinated primal and dual variables.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let agent \(i\in V\) own a function \(\Phi_i:X\times Y\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) that is convex in \(x\in X\) and concave in \(y\in Y\). A consensus-form distributed saddle model is \[\min_{(x_i)}\max_{(y_i)}\ \sum_{i\in V}\Phi_i(x_i,y_i)\quad\text{subject to}\quad x_i=x_j,\quad y_i=y_j\quad((i,j)\in E).\] If the undirected graph \(G=(V,E)\) is connected, feasible copies equal common variables \((x,y)\), and the model becomes \(\min_{x\in X}\max_{y\in Y}\sum_i\Phi_i(x,y)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Agents contribute local convex-concave payoffs while network constraints coordinate their primal and dual copies.
assumptions_latex: \(G=(V,E)\) is finite, undirected, and connected.
Every \(\Phi_i\) is convex in its primal argument and concave in its dual argument.
All agents use the common spaces \(X\) and \(Y\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Consensus reduces the distributed model to \(\min_{x\in X}\max_{y\in Y}\sum_{i\in V}\Phi_i(x,y)\).

notation.meaning: Agent i's local dual or adversarial variable.

review_flags: The supplied inventory contains no locator specifically supporting distributed saddle models.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The consensus saddle structure fits the leaf, but no distributed-saddle source is supplied. Moreover, the codomain \((-\infty,+\infty]\) is natural for convex minimization but is not generally suitable for a function asserted to be concave in the maximized variable; a source is needed to determine the intended real-valued or extended-real saddle convention and its hypotheses.

children.title: Distributed Minimax Models
children.top_down_role: Networked optimization with opposing objective roles.

knowledge_statements.title: Distributed Minimax Models
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-agent minimax model with locally held payoff components and shared primal and adversarial variables.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(m\in\mathbb{N}\), let \(X\) and \(Y\) be nonempty convex sets, and let agent \(i\in\{1,\ldots,m\}\) hold a function \(\phi_i:X\times Y\to\mathbb{R}\). Given weights \(w_i>0\) satisfying \(\sum_{i=1}^{m}w_i=1\), a distributed minimax model is
\[\min_{x\in X}\max_{y\in Y}\;\Phi(x,y),\qquad \Phi(x,y)=\sum_{i=1}^{m}w_i\phi_i(x,y).\]
Agent \(i\) can evaluate only its local component or an associated oracle. A distributed representation may introduce copies \((x_i,y_i)\) and impose \(x_i=x_j\) and \(y_i=y_j\) on communication edges.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Agents collectively minimize against an adversary when each agent knows only one weighted, real-valued payoff component; local copies of the shared decisions may be coordinated through network consensus.
assumptions_latex: \(m\in\mathbb{N}\) agents communicate over a prescribed network.
\(X\) and \(Y\) are nonempty convex sets.
Each \(\phi_i\) is convex in \(x\) and concave in \(y\) when a convex–concave model is intended.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\Phi=\sum_{i=1}^{m}w_i\phi_i\) defines a distributed minimax problem with shared primal and adversarial decisions.

notation.meaning: payoff component held by agent i

children.title: Primal–Dual Variable Ownership
children.top_down_role: Placement of primal and dual variables across participants.

knowledge_statements.title: Primal–Dual Variable Ownership
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Ownership representation for distributed saddle formulations using local blocks, replicated shared variables, and consensus constraints.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(P\) and \(Q\) index the primal and dual coordinate blocks of \(x=(x^{(p)})_{p\in P}\) and \(y=(y^{(q)})_{q\in Q}\), and let \(V=\{1,\ldots,m\}\) be the agent set. Ownership maps \(o_x:P\to 2^V\setminus\{\varnothing\}\) and \(o_y:Q\to 2^V\setminus\{\varnothing\}\) assign each block to the agents permitted to update or store it. For a shared block replicated on a set \(R\subseteq V\), stack its copies as \(z_R=(z_i)_{i\in R}\). If the communication subgraph on \(R\) is connected and has oriented node-edge incidence matrix \(B_R\), consistency is
\[(B_R^{\mathsf T}\otimes I)z_R=0.\]
Thus agents update owned blocks from local information, and the replicated copies of a shared block represent one variable exactly when this consensus equation holds.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Ownership maps assign every primal and dual block to one or more agents; copies of a shared block represent one variable exactly when they agree across a connected replica communication graph.
assumptions_latex: \(P\) and \(Q\) are the primal and dual block-index sets, and \(V=\{1,\ldots,m\}\) is the agent set.
Every coordinate block has at least one owner.
The communication subgraph for every replicated shared block is connected.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \((B_R^{\mathsf T}\otimes I)z_R=0\) makes all copies of a shared block on \(R\) equal.

notation.meaning: oriented node-edge incidence matrix of the replica subgraph
stack of copies of a shared block on the replica set R

children.title: Adversarial Coordination Regimes
children.top_down_role: Coordination patterns for distributed opposing-variable problems.

knowledge_statements.title: Adversarial Coordination Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Synchronous, alternating, and delayed regimes for coordinating distributed primal and adversarial updates.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For local states \(z_i^k=(x_i^k,y_i^k)\), an adversarial coordination regime specifies activation sets \(S_k^x,S_k^y\), the information timestamp \(\tau_{ij}(k)\le k\), and the order of primal, adversarial, and mixing operations. The regime is simultaneous when \(S_k^x=S_k^y\) and both updates use round-\(k\) states; alternating when one update uses the other variable's newly computed value; and delayed when some received value is \(z_j^{\tau_{ij}(k)}\) with \(\tau_{ij}(k)<k\). It is bounded-delay when \(0\le k-\tau_{ij}(k)\le D\) uniformly.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A coordination regime records which primal and adversarial agents update, in what order, and whether their neighbor information is current or delayed.
assumptions_latex: Iterations are indexed by \(k\in\mathbb{N}\).
Each active agent uses only locally available or received states.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \((S_k^x,S_k^y,\tau(k))\) distinguishes simultaneous, alternating, and bounded-delay adversarial coordination.

notation.meaning: active primal and adversarial agent sets at round k
timestamp of agent j's state used by agent i

children.title: Distributed Variational Inequalities
children.top_down_role: Variational-inequality structure distributed across network participants.

knowledge_statements.title: Distributed Variational Inequalities
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional variational inequality whose operator or feasible-set information is distributed among networked agents.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(m,d\in\mathbb{N}\), let \(K\subseteq\mathbb{R}^d\) be nonempty, closed, and convex, and let agent \(i\in\{1,\ldots,m\}\) hold a map \(F_i:K\to\mathbb{R}^d\). Given weights \(w_i>0\) satisfying \(\sum_{i=1}^{m}w_i=1\), define \(F=\sum_{i=1}^{m}w_iF_i\). The distributed variational inequality is to find \(x^\star\in K\) such that
\[\left\langle F(x^\star),z-x^\star\right\rangle\ge0\quad\text{for every }z\in K.\]
The model is distributed when agent \(i\) accesses only \(F_i\) or its oracle and the agents coordinate to obtain the common solution \(x^\star\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A finite set of agents holding separate operator components seek one feasible point whose aggregate operator has a nonnegative inner product with every feasible displacement.
assumptions_latex: \(m,d\in\mathbb{N}\).
\(K\subseteq\mathbb{R}^d\) is nonempty, closed, and convex.

notation.meaning: operator component held by agent i

children.title: Distributed Monotone Inclusions

knowledge_statements.title: Distributed Monotone Inclusions
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Common-zero monotone inclusion assembled from agent-local operators and an optional shared constraint.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(m\in\mathbb{N}\), let \(\mathcal H\) be a real Hilbert space, let agent \(i\in\{1,\ldots,m\}\) hold a set-valued monotone operator \(A_i:\mathcal H\rightrightarrows\mathcal H\), and let \(C\subseteq\mathcal H\) be nonempty, closed, and convex. A distributed monotone inclusion seeks
\[x^\star\in\mathcal H\quad\text{such that}\quad 0\in\sum_{i=1}^{m}A_i(x^\star)+N_C(x^\star).\]
Each agent accesses only its own operator or an available local resolvent. With local copies \(x_i\), consensus imposes the common-variable requirement, while \(N_C\) incorporates the shared feasibility constraint.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A finite set of agents holding monotone operators seek a shared point where the sum of their operator values and the normal cone enforcing common feasibility contains zero.
assumptions_latex: \(m\in\mathbb{N}\).
Each \(A_i\) is monotone; maximal monotonicity may additionally be imposed by a splitting method.
\(C\) is nonempty, closed, and convex.

normal-cone operator of the shared feasible set
zero set of a set-valued operator

children.title: Network Equilibrium Problems

knowledge_statements.title: Network Equilibrium Problems
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Generalized Nash equilibrium with agent objectives and feasibility sets coupled through a network.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For agents \(i=1,\ldots,m\), let \(x_i\in X_i\subseteq\mathbb{R}^{d_i}\), let \(J_i(x_i,x_{-i})\) be agent \(i\)'s cost, and let \(K_i(x_{-i})\subseteq X_i\) be its feasible-response set. A network equilibrium is a profile \(x^\star\) satisfying
\[x_i^\star\in K_i(x_{-i}^\star),\qquad J_i(x_i^\star,x_{-i}^\star)\le J_i(u_i,x_{-i}^\star)\quad\text{for every }u_i\in K_i(x_{-i}^\star),\]
for every agent \(i\). Network structure restricts each cost, constraint, and information exchange to specified neighbors, except for explicitly shared coupling constraints.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A network equilibrium is a feasible strategy profile at which no agent can lower its cost by a feasible unilateral deviation.
assumptions_latex: Each strategy set \(X_i\) is nonempty.
Each feasible-response set \(K_i(x_{-i})\) is specified by local, neighbor, or shared constraints.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(x^\star\) is a generalized Nash equilibrium of the network-coupled game.

notation.meaning: strategies of all agents other than i

children.title: Equilibrium Coupling Structures
children.top_down_role: Cross-agent dependencies shaping equilibrium conditions.

knowledge_statements.title: Equilibrium Coupling Structures
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Representation of local, edgewise, and aggregate coupling in network equilibrium models with a shared joint constraint set.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(G=(V,E)\) be an interaction graph, let \(x=(x_i)_{i\in V}\), and let \(X_i\subseteq\mathbb{R}^{d_i}\). For every \((i,j)\in E\), let \(c_{ij}:\mathbb{R}^{d_i}\times\mathbb{R}^{d_j}\to\mathbb{R}^{p_{ij}}\); let \(A_i:\mathbb{R}^{d_i}\to\mathbb{R}^{p}\) be linear; and let \(b\in\mathbb{R}^{p}\). A shared joint constraint set may be represented as
\[K=\left\{x:\ x_i\in X_i\ (i\in V),\quad c_{ij}(x_i,x_j)\le0\ ((i,j)\in E),\quad \sum_{i\in V}A_ix_i\le b\right\}.\]
The three displayed classes are agent-local, edgewise, and aggregate constraints, respectively. Removing either coupling class yields a corresponding local-only or reduced-coupling structure.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A shared equilibrium constraint set can combine agent-local restrictions, pairwise edge constraints, and an aggregate resource constraint, with each class imposing a different coordination requirement.

\(X_i\subseteq\mathbb{R}^{d_i}\), \(c_{ij}\) takes values in \(\mathbb{R}^{p_{ij}}\), and every \(A_i\) takes values in a common space \(\mathbb{R}^{p}\).
All vector inequalities are interpreted componentwise.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(K\) separates local, edgewise, and aggregate coupling in a shared equilibrium constraint set.

knowledge_statements.title: Central-Coordinator Architectures
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Round-based distributed architecture in which one persistent coordinator aggregates all worker messages and broadcasts the next shared state.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
A central-coordinator architecture consists of workers \(1,\ldots,m\), a coordinator state \(x^k\), worker message maps \(M_i^k\), and a coordinator aggregation map \(A^k\). At round \(k\),
\[u_i^k=M_i^k(x^k;\mathcal D_i),\qquad x^{k+1}=A^k(x^k,u_1^k,\ldots,u_m^k),\]
after which the coordinator broadcasts \(x^{k+1}\) or designated blocks to the workers. Workers need not communicate directly; every contribution to the shared iterate passes logically through the persistent coordinator.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Workers compute local messages from the shared state, while a persistent coordinator aggregates every contribution and broadcasts the next state.
assumptions_latex: Worker \(i\) has local information \(\mathcal D_i\).
The coordinator is the unique logical aggregation point for the shared iterate.

notation.meaning: coordinator's shared state at round k

children.title: Parameter-Server Architectures

knowledge_statements.title: Parameter-Server Architectures
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Server–worker architecture whose central service stores parameter blocks and applies worker-generated updates.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
A parameter-server architecture maintains server-resident parameter blocks \(x_{(1)},\ldots,x_{(q)}\). Worker \(i\) pulls a version \(x^{\tau_i(k)}\), computes \(u_i^k=U_i(x^{\tau_i(k)};\mathcal D_i)\), and pushes the update to the responsible server blocks. A server may apply one received update as
\[x^{k+1}=S^k(x^k,u_i^k)\]
or aggregate a batch of concurrently received updates. Execution is synchronous when workers use the designated round-\(k\) version and update application is separated by a round barrier; it is stale-read asynchronous when updates computed from \(\tau_i(k)<k\) may be accepted without such a global barrier.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Servers own parameter blocks; workers pull parameter versions, compute local-data updates, and push them for barrier-synchronized batch application or asynchronous application that may accept stale reads.
assumptions_latex: Every parameter block has a designated server owner.
Worker \(i\) computes from local data \(\mathcal D_i\) and a pulled parameter version.
Synchronous execution uses a round barrier in addition to current-version reads.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \((x^{\tau_i(k)},u_i^k,S^k)\), together with the update-application schedule, specifies the pull-compute-push parameter-server cycle.

notation.meaning: version timestamp read by worker i

children.title: Worker–Aggregator Topologies

knowledge_statements.title: Worker–Aggregator Topologies
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Bipartite graph representation of which workers send optimization messages to which aggregators.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(W\) be a set of workers and \(A\) a set of aggregators. A worker–aggregator topology is the bipartite graph \(G=(W\cup A,E)\), where \((i,a)\in E\) exactly when worker \(i\) may send a local message to aggregator \(a\). For messages \(u_i^k\), aggregator \(a\) computes
\[v_a^k=\mathcal A_a^k\bigl((u_i^k)_{i\in N(a)}\bigr).\]
A single-star topology has \(|A|=1\) and \(N(a)=W\); multiple aggregators partition or overlap worker neighborhoods and require an additional rule to reconcile \((v_a^k)_{a\in A}\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A bipartite graph specifies worker-to-aggregator communication; one aggregator gives a star, while multiple aggregators require reconciliation of their outputs.
assumptions_latex: Messages travel only along edges in \(E\).
Every participating worker has at least one adjacent aggregator.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(G=(W\cup A,E)\) determines the admissible aggregation neighborhoods \(N(a)\).

notation.meaning: output of aggregator a at round k

children.title: Central-Service Bottlenecks
children.top_down_role: Scalability, availability, and congestion limits at distinguished services.

knowledge_statements.title: Central-Service Bottlenecks
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Per-round communication and service-time lower bounds caused by routing all worker traffic through one central service.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Suppose \(m\) workers each send and receive \(s\) bits through one central service during every synchronous round. The service must process at least \(2ms\) incident bits per round. If its aggregate ingress-plus-egress rate is at most \(B\) bits per unit time and it processes at most \(P\) worker messages per unit time, then the round duration satisfies
\[T_{\mathrm{round}}\ge\max\left\{\frac{2ms}{B},\frac{2m}{P}\right\}.\]
Consequently, with fixed \(B\), \(P\), and \(s\), central-service communication time grows at least linearly with the worker count.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Because every worker message crosses one service, fixed service bandwidth and processing capacity force synchronous round time to grow at least linearly with workers.
assumptions_latex: Every synchronous round requires one upload and one download of \(s>0\) bits per worker.
The central service has total traffic rate \(B>0\) and message-processing rate \(P>0\).

children.title: Peer-to-Peer Decentralized Architectures
children.top_down_role: Optimization supported by neighbor exchanges without a permanent coordinator.

knowledge_statements.title: Peer-to-Peer Decentralized Architectures
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Neighbor-exchange architecture with local states and no permanent node responsible for global aggregation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(G=(V,E)\) be a communication graph and let iterations be indexed by \(k\in\mathbb{N}\). A peer-to-peer decentralized architecture assigns a state \(x_i^k\) and local information \(\mathcal D_i\) to each node \(i\in V\), with updates of the form
\[x_i^{k+1}=U_i^k\bigl(x_i^k,(x_j^{\tau_{ij}(k)})_{j\in N_i};\mathcal D_i\bigr),\qquad 0\le\tau_{ij}(k)\le k.\]
Nodes exchange states only along edges of \(G\), and no distinguished permanent service has exclusive responsibility for aggregating all contributions or determining a global iterate. In linear mixing,
\[x_i^{k+1}=\sum_{j\in V}w_{ij}x_j^k,\qquad w_{ij}=0\quad\text{whenever }j\notin N_i\cup\{i\}.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Each peer stores and updates a local state using local information and neighbor messages, while no distinguished permanent service exclusively performs global aggregation.
assumptions_latex: \(G=(V,E)\) specifies admissible peer-to-peer communication.
\(k\in\mathbb{N}\) and \(0\le\tau_{ij}(k)\le k\) for every received neighbor state.
Each update uses only the node's local information and received neighbor states.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The architecture has no distinguished permanent aggregation service, and communication is local to \(G\).

notation.meaning: local state of node i at round k
mixing weight from peer j to peer i

children.title: Clustered Coordination Hierarchies
children.top_down_role: Coordination organized through nested agent clusters.

assumptions_latex: \(V\) is a finite set of agents partitioned as \(V=V_1\mathbin{\dot\cup}\cdots\mathbin{\dot\cup}V_K\).
Each agent stores a local objective \(f_i:\mathbb{R}^d\to\mathbb{R}\cup\{+\infty\}\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\mathcal H=(V,\{c_k\}_{k=1}^K,c_0)\) is a clustered coordination hierarchy.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite, two-level coordinator model with cluster-mediated inter-agent communication.

source_refs.locator: 1.1 Parallel and Distributed Architectures p. 2
source_refs.source_title: Parallel and Distributed Computation: Numerical Methods

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A clustered coordination hierarchy is a communication architecture \(\mathcal H=(V,\{c_k\}_{k=1}^K,c_0)\) in which every agent \(i\in V_k\) exchanges optimization messages only within \(V_k\) or with its cluster coordinator \(c_k\), while each \(c_k\) exchanges aggregate messages with the top-level coordinator \(c_0\). Intercluster information used by an agent in \(V_k\) must therefore traverse a path through \(c_k\), \(c_0\), and the destination cluster coordinator. The associated global problem is \(\min_x\sum_{k=1}^K\sum_{i\in V_k}f_i(x)\), with local computations performed at agents and aggregation performed at the two coordinator tiers.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Agents are partitioned into clusters; cluster coordinators aggregate locally and communicate through a top-level coordinator to solve a shared optimization problem.

children.title: Edge–Cloud Coordination
children.top_down_role: Optimization responsibilities divided across edge and cloud tiers.

assumptions_latex: \(E\) is a finite set of edge devices and \(F_i:\mathbb{R}^d\to\mathbb{R}\cup\{+\infty\}\) is device \(i\)'s local objective.
A cloud coordinator can broadcast model states and receive finite-dimensional device messages.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The communication boundary is \(x^t\mapsto\{m_i^t:i\in S_t\}\mapsto x^{t+1}\), while each \(F_i\) remains local.

notation.meaning: Participating edge devices at round t
Message returned by edge device i

source_refs.locator: 11.1 Distributed optimization with centralized consensus p. 227

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Edge-cloud coordination for \(\min_x\sum_{i\in E}F_i(x)\) is represented roundwise by a cloud broadcast \(x^t\), local edge computations \(m_i^t=\Phi_i(x^t;F_i,\xi_i^t)\) for participating devices \(i\in S_t\), and a cloud update \(x^{t+1}=\Psi_t(x^t,\{m_i^t:i\in S_t\})\). The maps \(\Phi_i\) may encode gradients, proximal points, or model increments. The defining architectural boundary is that the cloud accesses each local objective \(F_i\) only through \(m_i^t\); objective data and local state need not be transferred to the cloud.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The cloud broadcasts a model, selected edge devices compute local messages, and the cloud aggregates them without directly accessing local objectives or data.

children.title: Regional Aggregator Architectures
children.top_down_role: Intermediate aggregation services serving geographic or logical regions.

assumptions_latex: \(V\) is partitioned into nonempty regions \(V_1,\ldots,V_R\).
Each region has an aggregator \(a_r\), and aggregators communicate over a graph \(G_A\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The architecture factors coordination into regional maps \(A_r\) and an interregional map \(B\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite regional decomposition with explicit intra-region aggregation and inter-region coordination.

source_refs.locator: 1.1 Parallel and Distributed Architectures p. 2

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A regional aggregator architecture for \(\min_x\sum_{r=1}^R\sum_{i\in V_r}f_i(x)\) assigns each region \(V_r\) an aggregator \(a_r\). At iteration \(t\), agents in \(V_r\) send local messages \(m_i^t\) to \(a_r\), which forms \(z_r^t=A_r^t(\{m_i^t:i\in V_r\})\). The aggregators then exchange messages only along edges of \(G_A\) and compute \((y_1^t,\ldots,y_R^t)=B^t(z_1^t,\ldots,z_R^t;G_A)\). Regional feedback to agent \(i\in V_r\) depends on \(y_r^t\), so all interregional influence is mediated by regional aggregators.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Each region aggregates its agents' messages locally; regional aggregators then coordinate over a separate network and return region-specific feedback.

children.title: Cross-Tier Information Flow
children.top_down_role: Movement of optimization information across hierarchy levels.

assumptions_latex: The coordination system has tiers \(0,1,\ldots,L\), with tier \(0\) lowest.
Messages passed between adjacent tiers belong to specified finite-dimensional spaces.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A valid cross-tier flow factors as \(U=U_{L-1}\circ\cdots\circ U_0\) upward and \(D=D_0\circ\cdots\circ D_{L-1}\) downward.

notation.meaning: Upward aggregation from tier l to tier l+1
Downward disaggregation from tier l+1 to tier l

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Adjacent-tier factorization condition for hierarchical optimization messages.

source_refs.locator: 1.1 Parallel and Distributed Architectures p. 2
source_refs.source_title: Parallel and Distributed Computation: Numerical Methods

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Cross-tier information flow is admissible when optimization information moves only through adjacent-tier maps. For upward messages, \(s_{l+1}^t=U_l^t(s_l^t)\) for \(l=0,\ldots,L-1\); for downward messages, \(q_l^t=D_l^t(q_{l+1}^t,s_l^t)\). Thus the upward dependence factors through \(U_{L-1}^t\circ\cdots\circ U_0^t\), and downward feedback factors through \(D_0^t\circ\cdots\circ D_{L-1}^t\). No state at tier \(l\) may directly influence a nonadjacent tier except through these compositions. This condition distinguishes genuine hierarchical flow from a nominal hierarchy containing bypass communication links.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Hierarchical information flow is cross-tier when every upward aggregate and downward feedback message factors through adjacent tiers, with no nonadjacent bypass.
knowledge_statements.title: Cross-Tier Information Flow

source_witnesses.locator: 1.1 Parallel and Distributed Architectures p. 2

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: A condition is the correct role for this leaf, but the downward maps D_l^t take both q_{l+1}^t and s_l^t, so the displayed unqualified composition D_0^t circ ... circ D_{L-1}^t is not well-typed without fixing or augmenting the side-state arguments. The broad architecture citation does not resolve the intended formalization; a hierarchy-specific source is needed.

children.title: Federated Coordination Boundary
children.top_down_role: Coordinator-mediated optimization with persistent data locality and heterogeneous participation.

assumptions_latex: Client \(i\) holds a local objective \(F_i(x)=\mathbb{E}_{\zeta\sim P_i}[\ell(x;\zeta)]\).
At round \(t\), only clients in \(S_t\) participate.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The coordinator observes \(\{M_i^t:i\in S_t\}\), but neither \(P_i\) nor the underlying samples.

notation.meaning: Client participation set at round t

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: standard coordinator-mediated federated optimization model
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Coordinator-mediated finite-client model with persistent data locality and partial participation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The federated coordination boundary for \(\min_x F(x)=\sum_{i=1}^n p_iF_i(x)\), where \(p_i\geq0\) and \(\sum_i p_i=1\), is the interface under which a coordinator broadcasts \(x^t\) and participating client \(i\in S_t\) returns \(M_i^t=\Phi_i(x^t;P_i,\xi_i^t)\). The coordinator updates \(x^{t+1}=\Psi_t(x^t,\{M_i^t:i\in S_t\})\). Persistent data locality means that samples from \(P_i\) remain at client \(i\); heterogeneous participation permits \(S_t\) and the local maps \(\Phi_i\) to vary across clients and rounds.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A coordinator optimizes a weighted client objective using messages from varying participant subsets, while each client's samples remain local.
knowledge_statements.title: Federated Coordination Boundary

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The definition matches the federated-coordination leaf and distinguishes local data from disclosed messages, but no citation is supplied for the weighted client objective, partial participation, persistent data locality, or heterogeneous local maps. children.title: Static Undirected Networks
children.top_down_role: Fixed reciprocal communication structures.

assumptions_latex: \(V=\{1,\ldots,n\}\) is fixed and finite.
Communication is reciprocal and does not change with iteration.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(G=(V,E)\) is a static undirected communication network.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Fixed finite reciprocal communication graph and its compatible mixing matrices.

source_refs.locator: 11.2 Decentralized optimization with graph consensus p. 234
source_refs.source_title: Large-Scale Convex Optimization: Algorithms & Analyses via Monotone Operators

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
A static undirected network is a fixed graph \(G=(V,E)\) with \(E\subseteq\{\{i,j\}:i,j\in V,\ i
eq j\}\). Agents \(i\) and \(j\) can exchange messages exactly when \(\{i,j\}\in E\), so the neighbor relation is reciprocal: \(j\in N_i\) if and only if \(i\in N_j\). A compatible mixing matrix \(W\in\mathbb{R}^{n	imes n}\) satisfies \(W_{ij}=0\) whenever \(i
eq j\) and \(\{i,j\}
otin E\). When consensus over all agents is required, connectivity of \(G\) is the standard structural condition.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A static undirected network has fixed reciprocal links; compatible mixing matrices use only self-weights and weights on those links.

children.title: Static Directed Networks
children.top_down_role: Fixed asymmetric communication structures.

assumptions_latex: \(V=\{1,\ldots,n\}\) is fixed and finite.
Directed communication links do not change with iteration.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(G=(V,A)\) is a static directed communication network.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Fixed finite asymmetric communication graph with sender-to-receiver arc convention.

source_refs.locator: 11.2 Decentralized optimization with graph consensus p. 234
source_refs.source_title: Large-Scale Convex Optimization: Algorithms & Analyses via Monotone Operators

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A static directed network is a fixed digraph \(G=(V,A)\), where \((j,i)\in A\) means that agent \(j\) can send information to agent \(i\). Accordingly, \(N_i^-=\{j:(j,i)\in A\}\) and \(N_i^+=\{j:(i,j)\in A\}\), and these sets need not coincide. A compatible update matrix \(W\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times n}\) satisfies \(W_{ij}=0\) for \(j\neq i\) whenever \((j,i)\notin A\). For information from every agent to influence every other agent, the fixed digraph must be strongly connected, unless a weaker rooted objective is explicitly intended.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A static directed network has fixed asymmetric arcs; an agent's update may use only its own state and messages from its in-neighbors.

children.title: Time-Varying Graph Sequences
children.top_down_role: Communication topologies that evolve across optimization rounds.

assumptions_latex: \(V=\{1,\ldots,n\}\) is fixed while communication may vary over discrete times \(t\in\mathbb{N}\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\mathcal G=(G_t)_{t\geq0}\) is a time-varying graph sequence on common vertex set \(V\).

notation.meaning: Communication graph active at time t

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Discrete-time graph sequence with fixed agents and changing communication edges.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A time-varying graph sequence is \(\mathcal G=(G_t)_{t\geq0}\), where every \(G_t=(V,E_t)\) has the same finite vertex set \(V\), while the edge or arc set \(E_t\) may change with \(t\). Communication performed at time \(t\) must respect \(E_t\): a compatible mixing matrix \(W_t\) has \((W_t)_{ij}=0\) whenever \(j\neq i\) and the link from \(j\) to \(i\) is absent from \(E_t\). The sequence may be deterministic, stochastic, or generated by a switching signal; those regimes require additional assumptions beyond this definition.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A time-varying network keeps the agent set fixed while its communication links, and hence its compatible mixing matrix, may change each iteration.
knowledge_statements.title: Time-Varying Graph Sequences

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The definition is mathematically coherent and correctly keeps deterministic, stochastic, and switching assumptions outside the basic graph-sequence definition. However, no inspectable source is supplied for the dynamic-network formulation or its time-indexed mixing-matrix support condition.

children.title: Topology-Switching Regimes
children.top_down_role: Networks selected from recurring or constrained topology families.

assumptions_latex: \(\{G^{(1)},\ldots,G^{(M)}\}\) is a finite family of graphs on the same vertex set \(V\).
\(\sigma:\mathbb{N}\to\{1,ldots,M\}\) is a switching signal.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The active topology satisfies \(G_t=G^{(\sigma(t))}\) for every \(t\geq0\).

notation.meaning: Mixing matrix assigned to mode m

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-mode discrete-time switching representation; dwell-time restrictions are optional additions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A topology-switching regime is represented by a finite graph family \(\{G^{(1)},\ldots,G^{(M)}\}\) and a switching signal \(\sigma:\mathbb{N}\to\{1,\ldots,M\}\), with active graph \(G_t=G^{(\sigma(t))}\). If each mode has a compatible mixing matrix \(W^{(m)}\), then the communication update uses \(W_t=W^{(\sigma(t))}\). The admissible switching class is a specified set \(\Sigma\) of signals; it may impose dwell time, transition constraints, or connectivity conditions. Arbitrary switching is the special case in which \(\Sigma\) contains every signal with values in \(\{1,\ldots,M\}\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A switching regime selects each active communication graph from a finite family using a signal that may obey dwell-time or transition restrictions.
knowledge_statements.title: Topology-Switching Regimes

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: Representation is the appropriate role and the statement itself gives a coherent finite-mode switching model. Nevertheless, no source supports the formulation, and the second assumption contains malformed LaTeX, using 1,ldots,M instead of 1,\ldots,M. A sourced corrected record is required.

children.title: Joint-Connectivity Windows
children.top_down_role: Time windows over which graph sequences accumulate connectivity.

assumptions_latex: \((G_t)_{t\geq0}\) is a sequence of graphs on a fixed finite vertex set \(V\).
\(B\geq1\) is an integer window length.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: For every \(t\), the union graph \(\bigl(V,\bigcup_{s=t}^{t+B-1}E_s\bigr)\) is connected, or strongly connected in the directed version.

notation.meaning: Union graph over the window starting at t
Edge or arc set active at time s

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Uniform sliding-window connectivity for undirected or strongly connected directed graph sequences.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The graph sequence \((G_t)_{t\geq0}\), with \(G_t=(V,E_t)\), is uniformly jointly connected with window \(B\) when, for every \(t\geq0\), the union graph \(G_{[t,t+B-1]}=\bigl(V,\bigcup_{s=t}^{t+B-1}E_s\bigr)\) is connected. For directed graphs, the corresponding uniform joint strong-connectivity condition requires every such union digraph to be strongly connected. Individual graphs \(G_t\) may be disconnected; the condition requires paths to be available collectively within every window of the same finite length \(B\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Every block of a fixed number of consecutive topologies must have a connected union, although individual graphs may be disconnected.
knowledge_statements.title: Joint-Connectivity Windows

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: A condition is the correct content kind, and the record clearly distinguishes connected undirected union graphs from strongly connected directed union digraphs. No source is supplied for the uniform sliding-window condition, so standard-field rationale alone is insufficient.

children.title: Topology-Change Boundaries
children.top_down_role: Variation patterns that prevent sustained information propagation.

assumptions_latex: \(V=V_1\mathbin{\dot\cup}V_2\) with nonempty \(V_1\) and \(V_2\).
Every mixing matrix \(W_t\) is supported only within the two groups and preserves constants.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Global consensus cannot be guaranteed when topology changes never create a jointly connected window.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Concrete impossibility boundary caused by persistent separation despite arbitrary within-group topology changes.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let every \(G_t\) contain edges only within \(V_1\) and within \(V_2\), although those internal edges may change arbitrarily with \(t\). Initialize \(x_i^0=0\) for \(i\in V_1\) and \(x_i^0=1\) for \(i\in V_2\), and apply \(x^{t+1}=W_tx^t\), where each \(W_t\) is row-stochastic and supported on \(G_t\). Then \(x_i^t=0\) on \(V_1\) and \(x_i^t=1\) on \(V_2\) for all \(t\). Hence topology variation alone cannot ensure global consensus when no finite window joins the persistent components.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: If all changing topologies preserve the same separation into two groups, distinct group constants remain distinct and global consensus is impossible.
knowledge_statements.title: Topology-Change Boundaries

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: Failure boundary is the correct role, and the persistent two-component construction is a valid obstruction. However, the conclusion generalizes this to every sequence lacking a uniformly jointly connected finite window; that broader absence alone does not imply consensus impossibility because connectivity windows may grow with time. No source is supplied to justify either a corrected narrow boundary or additional hypotheses.

children.title: Randomized Activation Network Family
children.top_down_role: Random edge, node, or subgraph activation regimes.

children.title: Random Graph Activation
children.top_down_role: Communication graphs selected through random activation.

assumptions_latex: \(V=\{1,\ldots,n\}\) is fixed and \((\Omega,\mathcal F,\mathbb P)\) is a probability space.
Communication occurs at discrete times \(t\in\mathbb N\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \((G_t)_{t\geq0}\) is a random graph activation process, and each update must be supported on the realized \(G_t\).

notation.meaning: Random active graph at time t

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Discrete-time random edge activation without imposing independence or identical distributions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A random graph activation process is a sequence of graph-valued random variables \(G_t=(V,E_t)\). Equivalently, for each admissible link \(e\), the indicator \(A_e^t=\mathbf 1\{e\in E_t\}\) is a random variable measurable with respect to the round history \(\mathcal F_t\). A communication or mixing matrix \(W_t\) is admissible only if \((W_t)_{ij}=0\) whenever the corresponding link from \(j\) to \(i\) is inactive at time \(t\). Independence across links or times, identical activation probabilities, and positive lower probability bounds are additional regime assumptions, not parts of the basic definition.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: At each round the active communication graph is random, and the realized update may use only links activated in that round.
knowledge_statements.title: Random Graph Activation

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The definition fits random graph activation and appropriately leaves independence and probability bounds as additional assumptions. No source is supplied, and the meaning of the history sigma-field F_t must specify whether it includes the round-t realization before asserting that A_e^t is F_t-measurable.

children.title: Pairwise Gossip Networks
children.top_down_role: Randomized exchanges involving selected agent pairs.

knowledge_statements.title: Pairwise Gossip Networks
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Canonical randomized edge-activated averaging on a fixed undirected graph.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(G=(V,E)\) be an undirected graph with \(V=\{1,\ldots,n\}\), and let each node hold \(x_i^k\in\mathbb R^d\). At iteration \(k\), sample an edge \(e_k=\{i,j\}\) with probability \(p_{ij}>0\). Its endpoints update by \(x_i^{k+1}=x_j^{k+1}=(x_i^k+x_j^k)/2\), while \(x_\ell^{k+1}=x_\ell^k\) for \(\ell\notin\{i,j\}\). Equivalently, with stacked state \(x^k\), \[x^{k+1}=\left(W_{ij}\otimes I_d\right)x^k,\qquad W_{ij}=I_n-\tfrac12(e_i-e_j)(e_i-e_j)^\top.\] The running convention outputs \(x^k\); a finite implementation may stop when a prescribed disagreement measure is below tolerance.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A sampled edge averages its two endpoint states while every other node retains its state.
assumptions_latex: \(G\) is fixed and undirected.
\(p_{ij}>0\) for every \(\{i,j\}\in E\).

notation.meaning: the ith standard basis vector of \(\mathbb R^n\)
