knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let there be \(n\geq1\) agents. For each \(i\in\{1,\ldots,n\}\), let \(X_i\subseteq\mathbb R^{d_i}\), \(f_i:X_i\to\mathbb R\), \(A_i:\mathbb R^{d_i}\to\mathbb R^m\), and \(b_i\in\mathbb R^m\), with \(\sum_{i=1}^n b_i=b\). Let \(\Lambda\subseteq\mathbb R^m\) be a nonempty closed convex multiplier set, and initialize \(\lambda_i^0\in\Lambda\). At iteration \(k\), agent \(i\) computes \[x_i^k\in\operatorname*{argmin}_{x_i\in X_i}\bigl(f_i(x_i)+(\lambda_i^k)^\top(A_ix_i-b_i)\bigr),\] exchanges multiplier copies with its neighbors, and updates \[\lambda_i^{k+1}=\Pi_\Lambda\!\left(\sum_{j=1}^n w_{ij}^k\lambda_j^k+\alpha_k(A_ix_i^k-b_i)\right).\] Stop when neighboring multiplier copies agree within a prescribed tolerance and the aggregate residual \(\left\lVert\sum_{i=1}^n(A_ix_i^k-b_i)\right\rVert\) is small. Return the common price estimate together with an ergodically recovered primal allocation.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Each agent maintains a local price, solves its own Lagrangian subproblem, then mixes prices with neighbors while adding its local coupling residual.

knowledge_statements.title: Distributed Primal Recovery
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Ergodic primal recovery and computable feasibility–duality-gap certification.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For dual-decomposition iterates \(x_i^t\) and positive weights \(\alpha_t\), define \(S_k=\sum_{t=0}^k\alpha_t\) and \[\bar x_i^k=S_k^{-1}\sum_{t=0}^k\alpha_tx_i^t.\] Agents can average their local residuals to evaluate \(r^k=\sum_iA_i\bar x_i^k-b\). Given any dual-feasible \(\lambda^k\) with dual value \(q(\lambda^k)\), the pair is an \((\varepsilon_f,\varepsilon_g)\)-certificate when \[\lVert r^k\rVert\leq\varepsilon_f,\qquad \sum_if_i(\bar x_i^k)-q(\lambda^k)\leq\varepsilon_g.\] The first inequality certifies approximate coupling feasibility; weak duality makes the second a verifiable upper bound on primal suboptimality whenever \(\bar x^k\) is feasible.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Weighted averages of local primal responses provide a recoverable decision; its coupling residual and primal–dual gap certify feasibility and, when feasible, suboptimality.
assumptions_latex: The primal problem is convex and each averaged local point remains in its convex set \(X_i\).
\(q(\lambda^k)\) is a valid dual lower bound.
Agents can aggregate the local residuals and objective values.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The displayed residual and gap constitute a distributedly aggregable certificate for the recovered primal point.

children.title: Dual-Decomposition Applicability Boundaries
children.top_down_role: Limitations involving dual regularity, primal recovery, and coupling structure.

knowledge_statements.title: Dual-Decomposition Applicability Boundaries
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Loss of strict convexity can make the dual nonsmooth and primal recovery nonunique.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Consider \[\min\ 0\quad\text{subject to}\quad x_1+x_2=0,\qquad x_1,x_2\in\{-1,1\}.\] Its Lagrangian dual function is \[q(\lambda)=\inf_{x_1,x_2\in\{-1,1\}}\lambda(x_1+x_2)=-2|\lambda|.\] The dual optimum is attained at \(\lambda^\star=0\), but every pair in \(\{-1,1\}^2\) minimizes the local Lagrangian at that multiplier. Independent agents may therefore return \((1,1)\) or \((-1,-1)\), both violating the coupling constraint. Thus dual optimality alone does not recover a feasible primal point when local responses are nonunique; averaging or an additional coordinated selection rule is necessary.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A dual-optimal price may leave local minimizers nonunique, allowing independently chosen primal responses to violate coupling feasibility even though the dual optimum is exact.
assumptions_latex: Local decision sets are discrete and hence nonconvex.
Agents select local Lagrangian minimizers independently.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Dual convergence does not imply feasibility of the unaveraged primal responses without uniqueness or coordinated recovery.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The counterexample correctly shows that independently selected local minimizers at a dual-optimal multiplier can violate coupling feasibility. However, ordinary averaging is not necessarily a valid remedy here because averages can leave the discrete local sets \(\{-1,1\}\). No source is supplied for the exact boundary claim or remedy.

knowledge_statements.title: Dual-Price Coordination
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Distributed price consensus for equality-constrained separable resource allocation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Consider \(\min_{x_i\in X_i}\sum_i f_i(x_i)\) subject to \(\sum_ix_i=d\), and choose shares \(d_i\) satisfying \(\sum_id_i=d\). Initialize local prices \(\lambda_i^0\in\mathbb R^p\). Each agent computes \[x_i^k\in\operatorname*{argmin}_{x_i\in X_i}\bigl(f_i(x_i)+(\lambda_i^k)^\top x_i\bigr),\] then updates \[\lambda_i^{k+1}=\sum_jw_{ij}^k\lambda_j^k+\alpha_k(x_i^k-d_i).\] Stop when neighboring prices agree and \(\lVert\sum_ix_i^k-d\rVert\) is small. Output the local allocations and their common limiting price, using ergodic primal recovery if instantaneous allocations oscillate.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Agents respond to local price estimates and adjust those prices by mixing with neighbors plus their individual supply–demand imbalance.
assumptions_latex: Every local price-response problem attains a solution.
The mixing matrices are doubly stochastic and uniformly connected.
A diminishing nonsummable, square-summable stepsize sequence is used.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The innovation \(x_i^k-d_i\) is a local supergradient of the decomposed dual objective.

children.title: Primal Feasibility-Preserving Allocation
children.top_down_role: Resource balancing directly in primal variables.

knowledge_statements.title: Primal Feasibility-Preserving Allocation
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Laplacian-gradient allocation preserving an equality resource balance at every iteration.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For scalar allocations, solve \(\min_x\sum_i f_i(x_i)\) subject to \(\mathbf1^\top x=d\). Choose a feasible initialization \(x^0\) with \(\mathbf1^\top x^0=d\), and let \(L_G\) be the Laplacian of a connected undirected communication graph. Iterate \[x^{k+1}=x^k-\alpha_kL_G\nabla f(x^k).\] Equivalently, each agent exchanges marginal costs and applies \(x_i^{k+1}=x_i^k-\alpha_k\sum_ja_{ij}(f_i'(x_i^k)-f_j'(x_j^k))\). Stop when neighboring marginal costs agree within tolerance; output \(x^k\). Since \(\mathbf1^\top L_G=0\), every iterate satisfies the resource balance exactly.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Starting from a balanced allocation, agents exchange marginal costs and move resources along graph edges; the Laplacian update preserves total resource exactly.
assumptions_latex: Each \(f_i:\mathbb R\to\mathbb R\) is differentiable.
The communication graph is connected, undirected, and has nonnegative symmetric edge weights.
The initial allocation satisfies \(\mathbf1^\top x^0=d\).

children.title: Primal-Dual Resource Allocation
children.top_down_role: Joint network evolution of allocation and price information.

knowledge_statements.title: Primal-Dual Resource Allocation
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Projected primal descent coupled to distributed price consensus and balance innovations.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(\min_{x_i\in X_i}\sum_if_i(x_i)\) subject to \(\sum_ix_i=d\), select shares \(d_i\) with \(\sum_id_i=d\), initialize \(x_i^0\in X_i\) and local prices \(\lambda_i^0\). With a mixing matrix \(W=(w_{ij})\), perform \[x_i^{k+1}=P_{X_i}\!\left(x_i^k-\alpha_k(\nabla f_i(x_i^k)+\lambda_i^k)\right),\] \[\lambda_i^{k+1}=\sum_jw_{ij}\lambda_j^k+\beta_k(x_i^{k+1}-d_i).\] Stop when primal changes, price disagreement, and the aggregate balance residual are below tolerances. Output \((x_i^k,\lambda_i^k)\); at a fixed point, allocations satisfy local stationarity and prices agree.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Allocations descend on local Lagrangians while price copies mix and integrate local imbalance, jointly seeking stationarity, price consensus, and resource balance.
assumptions_latex: Each \(X_i\) is nonempty, closed, and convex, and each \(f_i\) is convex and differentiable.
The communication graph is connected and \(W\) is doubly stochastic.
Stepsizes are chosen to satisfy the stability conditions of the selected primal-dual discretization.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Any converged fixed point with zero aggregate residual satisfies the KKT conditions for the convex resource-allocation problem.

children.title: Resource-Allocation Dual Convergence Conditions
children.top_down_role: Convergence families for prices, allocations, and balance residuals.

knowledge_statements.title: Resource-Allocation Dual Convergence Conditions
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Convergence of distributed dual subgradient prices and ergodically recovered allocations.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Consider the convex allocation problem \(\min_{x_i\in X_i}\sum_if_i(x_i)\) subject to \(\sum_ix_i=d\), and the consensus-based dual-price iteration with local residuals \(x_i^k-d_i\). Suppose strong duality holds, the dual solution set is nonempty, residuals are uniformly bounded, the doubly stochastic graph sequence is uniformly connected, and \(\alpha_k>0\), \(\sum_k\alpha_k=\infty\), \(\sum_k\alpha_k^2<\infty\). Then every local price copy converges to a common dual-optimal multiplier. Moreover, weighted ergodic primal averages have coupling residual converging to zero and objective values converging to the primal optimum. If the primal optimizer is unique, the recovered allocations converge to it.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Under strong duality, network connectivity, bounded residuals, and standard diminishing stepsizes, local prices agree at a dual optimum and ergodic allocations become optimal and balanced.
assumptions_latex: The local objectives and constraint sets define a convex problem satisfying strong duality with attained primal and dual optima.
Dual supergradients are uniformly bounded along the iterates, and the mixing sequence is doubly stochastic and uniformly connected.
\(\alpha_k>0\), \(\sum_k\alpha_k=\infty\), and \(\sum_k\alpha_k^2<\infty\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\lambda_i^k\to\lambda^\star\) for all \(i\), while \(\lVert\sum_i\bar x_i^k-d\rVert\to0\) and \(\sum_if_i(\bar x_i^k)\to p^\star\).

children.title: Primal-Dual Consensus Methods
children.top_down_role: Consensus mechanisms applied to primal and multiplier variables.

assumptions_latex: The communication graph is connected and has oriented incidence matrix \(B\).
Each \(f_i:\mathbb{R}^d\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) is proper, closed, and convex.
Step sizes satisfy \(\tau\sigma\lVert B\rVert^2<1\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Every fixed point satisfies \(Bx^\star=0\) and \(0\in\partial f(x^\star)+B^\top y^\star\), hence its primal components agree and solve the consensus problem.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Synchronous incidence-based primal-dual consensus with proximal primal updates.

source_refs.locator: 3 Primal-dual splitting methods p. 69; 11.2 Decentralized optimization with graph consensus p. 234
source_refs.source_title: Large-Scale Convex Optimization: Algorithms & Analyses via Monotone Operators

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For the replicated consensus problem \(\min_x f(x)\) subject to \(Bx=0\), initialize \(x^0,x^{-1}\) and \(y^0\). For \(k=0,1,\ldots\), agents and edges perform
\[
y^{k+1}=y^k+\sigma B\bar x^k,\qquad x^{k+1}=\operatorname{prox}_{\tau f}\!\left(x^k-\tau B^\top y^{k+1}\right),\qquad \bar x^{k+1}=2x^{k+1}-x^k.
\]
The proximal map separates across agents, while multiplication by \(B\) and \(B^\top\) uses only incident-edge messages. Stop when both \(\lVert Bx^k\rVert\) and \(\operatorname{dist}(0,\partial f(x^k)+B^\top y^k)\) meet prescribed tolerances; otherwise output the latest primal-dual pair.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Update edge multipliers from disagreement, update each primal variable proximally using neighboring multipliers, and stop when consensus and stationarity residuals are small.
knowledge_statements.title: Primal-Dual Consensus Methods

children.title: Distributed Saddle-Point Dynamics
children.top_down_role: Continuous- and discrete-time network saddle dynamics.

assumptions_latex: The graph incidence matrix is \(B\), and \(f\) is convex and continuously differentiable.
A saddle point of \(L(x,y)=f(x)+\langle y,Bx\rangle\) exists.
For the displayed Euler discretization, a step size \(h>0\) is chosen for the desired stability regime.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Equilibria of the flow, and fixed points of its Euler discretization, are precisely primal-dual solutions satisfying \(Bx=0\) and \(\nabla f(x)+B^\top y=0\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Unconstrained smooth convex consensus saddle flow and its forward-Euler discretization.

source_refs.locator: 3 Primal-dual splitting methods p. 69; 11.2 Decentralized optimization with graph consensus p. 234
source_refs.source_title: Large-Scale Convex Optimization: Algorithms & Analyses via Monotone Operators

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The continuous-time network saddle dynamics for \(L\) are
\[
\dot x(t)=-\nabla_xL(x(t),y(t))=-\nabla f(x(t))-B^\top y(t),\qquad \dot y(t)=\nabla_yL(x(t),y(t))=Bx(t).
\]
Given \((x^0,y^0)\), the forward-Euler realization is
\[
x^{k+1}=x^k-h\bigl(\nabla f(x^k)+B^\top y^k\bigr),\qquad y^{k+1}=y^k+hBx^k.
\]
Each derivative or update uses local gradients and incident-edge communication. A continuous trajectory is reported at a prescribed horizon; the discrete method stops at a horizon or when its consensus and stationarity residuals satisfy selected tolerances.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Primal variables descend the network Lagrangian while edge multipliers ascend it; Euler discretization yields a local-message primal-dual iteration.
knowledge_statements.title: Distributed Saddle-Point Dynamics

children.top_down_role: Predictive and corrective methods for network saddle problems.

children.title: Distributed Extragradient Methods
children.top_down_role: Network methods using an auxiliary predictive evaluation.

assumptions_latex: The closed convex set \(K=K_1\times\cdots\times K_n\) is nonempty.
The block operator \(F:K\to\mathbb{R}^{nd}\) is monotone and Lipschitz.
The mixing matrix \(W\) respects a connected graph and is doubly stochastic.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Any fixed point lying in consensus solves the variational inequality \(\langle F(z^\star),z-z^\star\rangle\ge0\) for every consensus-feasible \(z\in K\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Synchronous projected extragradient with one mixing operation at each evaluation stage.

source_refs.locator: 3 Primal-dual splitting methods p. 69; 11.2 Decentralized optimization with graph consensus p. 234
source_refs.source_title: Large-Scale Convex Optimization: Algorithms & Analyses via Monotone Operators

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Initialize \(z^0\in K\) and choose \(\alpha>0\). At iteration \(k\), compute the distributed predictor and corrector
\[
u^k=\Pi_K\!\left(\mathcal Wz^k-\alpha F(z^k)\right),\qquad z^{k+1}=\Pi_K\!\left(\mathcal Wz^k-\alpha F(u^k)\right).
\]
Each block of \(\mathcal Wz\) is obtained from neighbor messages, and each block of \(F\) is evaluated locally. The second evaluation at \(u^k\) corrects the first-order step without an implicit solve. Stop when a prescribed network variational-inequality residual and the disagreement \(\lVert (I-\mathcal W)z^k\rVert\) are below tolerance; output \(z^k\) or an ergodic average.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Mix neighboring iterates, predict with one operator evaluation, and correct from the same mixed base using an evaluation at the predictor.
knowledge_statements.title: Distributed Extragradient Methods

children.title: Distributed Optimistic Methods
children.top_down_role: Network methods using prediction from recent operator information.

assumptions_latex: The closed convex set \(K\) is a Cartesian product across agents.
The operator \(F\) is monotone and Lipschitz on \(K\).
The matrix \(W\) is graph-compatible and doubly stochastic.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A consensual fixed point satisfies the network variational inequality, while the correction \(2F(z^k)-F(z^{k-1})\) uses one new operator evaluation per iteration after initialization.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Projected one-call optimistic method with synchronous graph mixing.

source_refs.locator: 3 Primal-dual splitting methods p. 69; 11.2 Decentralized optimization with graph consensus p. 234
source_refs.source_title: Large-Scale Convex Optimization: Algorithms & Analyses via Monotone Operators

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Choose \(z^{-1}=z^0\in K\) and \(\alpha>0\). For \(k=0,1,\ldots\), each agent exchanges its current block, evaluates its local operator block, and performs
\[
q^k=2F(z^k)-F(z^{k-1}),\qquad z^{k+1}=\Pi_K\!\left(\mathcal Wz^k-\alpha q^k\right).
\]
The stored value \(F(z^{k-1})\) makes the iteration a one-new-evaluation predictive correction. Stop when both \(\lVert z^{k+1}-z^k\rVert\) and \(\lVert(I-\mathcal W)z^k\rVert\) meet prescribed tolerances, or after a fixed horizon; output the final or averaged iterate according to the convergence guarantee being used.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An optimistic method predicts the next operator value by extrapolating the two latest evaluations, then combines this correction with neighbor mixing and projection.
knowledge_statements.title: Distributed Optimistic Methods

children.title: Predictive–Corrective Relations
children.top_down_role: Structural links between prediction and correction mechanisms.

assumptions_latex: The operator \(F\) is twice continuously differentiable near \(z^k\), with locally bounded second derivative.
The recent displacement satisfies \(z^k-z^{k-1}=-\alpha F(z^k)+O(\alpha^2)\).
Projection and network-mixing errors are absent or themselves \(O(\alpha^2)\) in the local comparison.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Extragradient and optimistic corrections evaluate the same first-order prediction of the future operator, differing by \(O(\alpha^2)\) under the stated local trajectory relation.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Local first-order relation; it does not assert exact trajectory equivalence.

source_refs.locator: 3 Primal-dual splitting methods p. 69
source_refs.source_title: Large-Scale Convex Optimization: Algorithms & Analyses via Monotone Operators

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Taylor expansion at \(z^k\) gives the extragradient evaluation
\[
F(u^k)=F(z^k)-\alpha JF(z^k)F(z^k)+O(\alpha^2).
\]
The displacement assumption gives
\[
F(z^{k-1})=F(z^k)+\alpha JF(z^k)F(z^k)+O(\alpha^2),
\]
and therefore
\[
2F(z^k)-F(z^{k-1})=F(z^k)-\alpha JF(z^k)F(z^k)+O(\alpha^2)=F(u^k)+O(\alpha^2).
\]
Thus the extragradient evaluation at a predicted point and the optimistic extrapolation from stored evaluations implement locally matching predictive-corrective information through first order.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Along a consistent small-step trajectory, extragradient evaluation and optimistic extrapolation approximate the same future operator value to first order.
knowledge_statements.title: Predictive–Corrective Relations

children.title: Network Saddle Regimes
children.top_down_role: Distributed saddle structures suited to predictive correction.

assumptions_latex: The matrix \(W\) is nonnegative, graph-compatible, and doubly stochastic.
The fixed-point space satisfies \(\ker(I-W)=\operatorname{span}\{\mathbf 1\}\).
Each local saddle operator is monotone and \(L\)-Lipschitz on the common domain.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The pair \((L,\delta)\) separates operator difficulty from network difficulty; predictive-corrective step restrictions and rates may depend on both quantities.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Static connected-network regime for monotone Lipschitz saddle operators.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
A static network saddle regime is admissible when
\[
W\mathbf 1=\mathbf 1,\qquad \mathbf 1^\top W=\mathbf 1^\top,\qquad W_{ij}=0\ \text{for nonedges},\qquad \rho=\lVert W-J\rVert_2<1,
\]
and the stacked saddle operator \(F\) satisfies, for all domain points \(z,z'\),
\[
\langle F(z)-F(z'),z-z'\rangle\ge0,\qquad \lVert F(z)-F(z')\rVert\le L\lVert z-z'\rVert.
\]
Here \(\rho<1\) makes disagreement contract under mixing, while monotonicity and Lipschitz continuity specify the operator regime addressed by distributed extragradient or optimistic corrections.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A standard network saddle regime combines connected doubly stochastic mixing, a positive consensus gap, and a monotone Lipschitz saddle operator.
knowledge_statements.title: Network Saddle Regimes

children.title: Distributed Saddle-Residual Convergence
children.top_down_role: Gap, residual, ergodic, and last-iterate convergence families.

knowledge_statements.title: Distributed Saddle-Residual Convergence
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Abstract ergodic gap bound exposing accumulated distributed error.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(K\ge 1\), let \(\bar z^K=K^{-1}\sum_{k=0}^{K-1}z^k\), and define \(G_Z(w)=\sup_{z\in Z}\langle F(z),w-z\rangle\). If, for every \(z\in Z\), \(\sum_{k=0}^{K-1}\langle F(z^k),z^k-z\rangle\le C+\sum_{k=0}^{K-1}\varepsilon_k\), then
\[
G_Z(\bar z^K)\le \frac{C+\sum_{k=0}^{K-1}\varepsilon_k}{K}.
\]
If \(\sum_{k=0}^{\infty}\varepsilon_k<\infty\), then \(G_Z(\bar z^K)=O(K^{-1})\). If only \(K^{-1}\sum_{k=0}^{K-1}\varepsilon_k\to0\), then \(G_Z(\bar z^K)\to0\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The ergodic saddle gap is bounded by the centralized cumulative constant plus accumulated network errors, divided by the iteration count. Summable errors preserve an order-one-over-K rate.
assumptions_latex: The set \(Z\subseteq\mathbb{R}^m\) is nonempty, compact, and convex, and contains a solution.
The operator \(F:Z\to\mathbb{R}^m\) is monotone, and \(z^k\in Z\) for every \(k\).
The constant satisfies \(C\ge0\), the errors satisfy \(\varepsilon_k\ge0\), and the displayed cumulative inequality holds for every integer \(K\ge1\) and every \(z\in Z\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: For every \(K\ge1\), \(G_Z(\bar z^K)\le\bigl(C+\sum_{k=0}^{K-1}\varepsilon_k\bigr)/K\); summable errors yield \(G_Z(\bar z^K)=O(K^{-1})\).

children.title: Consensus ADMM

knowledge_statements.title: Consensus ADMM
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Scaled two-block ADMM for a centralized replicated-variable consensus model.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Rewrite \(\min_z\sum_{i=1}^n f_i(z)\) as \(\min_{x,z}\sum_i f_i(x_i)\) subject to \(x_i=z\). Initialize \(z^0\) and \(u_i^0\). Scaled ADMM performs, in parallel,
\[
x_i^{k+1}=\operatorname{prox}_{f_i/\rho}(z^k-u_i^k),
\]
followed by
\[
z^{k+1}=\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^n(x_i^{k+1}+u_i^k),\qquad u_i^{k+1}=u_i^k+x_i^{k+1}-z^{k+1}.
\]
Stop when the primal residuals \(x_i^k-z^k\) and dual residual \(\rho(z^k-z^{k-1})\) satisfy prescribed tolerances; output \(z^k\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Consensus ADMM alternates parallel local proximal solves, averaging into a shared variable, and scaled-dual updates enforcing agreement.
assumptions_latex: Each \(f_i:\mathbb{R}^d\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) is proper, closed, and convex.
The consensus problem has a primal-dual solution.
The penalty parameter satisfies \(\rho>0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Every fixed point satisfies \(x_i^\star=z^\star\) for all \(i\) and the optimality conditions for \(\min_z\sum_i f_i(z)\).

notation.meaning: Agent replicas and shared consensus variable

children.title: Edge-Based ADMM

knowledge_statements.title: Edge-Based ADMM
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Scaled ADMM on node-edge incidence constraints for an undirected graph.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Represent consensus by \(x_i=z_e\) for every incidence \(i\in e\). Given \((z^0,u^0)\), scaled ADMM performs
\[
x_i^{k+1}=\arg\min_x\left\{f_i(x)+\frac\rho2\sum_{e\in E_i}\lVert x-z_e^k+u_{ie}^k\rVert^2\right\},
\]
then, for each edge \(e=\{i,j\}\),
\[
z_e^{k+1}=\frac{x_i^{k+1}+u_{ie}^k+x_j^{k+1}+u_{je}^k}{2},\qquad u_{ie}^{k+1}=u_{ie}^k+x_i^{k+1}-z_e^{k+1}.
\]
The analogous multiplier update is made for \((j,e)\). Stop when all incidence primal and dual residuals meet tolerance; output the node variables.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Edge-based ADMM gives each edge a coupling variable, alternates local node solves with edge averaging, and updates one multiplier per incidence.
assumptions_latex: The undirected communication graph is connected.
Every local objective \(f_i\) is proper, closed, and convex.
The edge penalty satisfies \(\rho>0\), and a primal-dual solution exists.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: At a fixed point, every incidence constraint holds; graph connectivity then implies \(x_1=\cdots=x_n\), and the common value minimizes \(\sum_i f_i\).

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Initialize \((x^0,z^0,u^0)\). Linearize the quadratic penalty in the \(x\)-block and iterate
\[
x^{k+1}=\operatorname{prox}_{\tau f}\!\left(x^k-\tau\rho A^\top r^k\right),
\]
\[
z^{k+1}=\arg\min_z\left\{g(z)+\frac\rho2\lVert Ax^{k+1}+Bz-c+u^k\rVert^2\right\},
\]
\[
u^{k+1}=u^k+Ax^{k+1}+Bz^{k+1}-c.
\]
In a distributed model, separability of \(f\), \(g\), and the incidence structure makes these updates local after neighbor communication. Stop using standard primal and dual residual tolerances; output \((x^k,z^k)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Linearized distributed ADMM replaces one quadratic augmented-Lagrangian subproblem by a proximal gradient step, reducing local solve cost.

assumptions_latex: The linearly constrained convex problem has a primal-dual solution.
The functions \(f\) and \(g\) are proper, closed, and convex, and \(\rho>0\).
The regularization matrices satisfy \(P\succeq0\) and \(Q\succeq0\).

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For \(\min_{x,z}f(x)+g(z)\) subject to \(Ax+Bz=c\), initialize \((x^0,z^0,u^0)\) and iterate
\[
x^{k+1}=\arg\min_x\left\{f(x)+\frac\rho2\lVert Ax+Bz^k-c+u^k\rVert^2+\frac12\lVert x-x^k\rVert_P^2\right\},
\]
\[
z^{k+1}=\arg\min_z\left\{g(z)+\frac\rho2\lVert Ax^{k+1}+Bz-c+u^k\rVert^2+\frac12\lVert z-z^k\rVert_Q^2\right\},
\]
\[
u^{k+1}=u^k+Ax^{k+1}+Bz^{k+1}-c.
\]
Distributed implementation uses block-diagonal \(P,Q\) and graph-sparse constraints. Stop at prescribed primal and dual residual tolerances.

assumptions_latex: The objective is \(h(x)+f(x)+g(z)\), where \(h\) is convex with \(L_h\)-Lipschitz gradient and \(f,g\) are proper closed convex.
The constraint is \(Ax+Bz=c\), and a primal-dual solution exists.
The metric satisfies \(P- L_h I/2\succeq0\), with \(Q\succeq0\) and \(\rho>0\).

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Initialize \((x^0,z^0,u^0)\). A hybrid regularized ADMM step is
\[
x^{k+1}=\arg\min_x\left\{f(x)+\langle\nabla h(x^k),x-x^k\rangle+\frac12\lVert x-x^k\rVert_P^2+\frac\rho2\lVert Ax+Bz^k-c+u^k\rVert^2\right\},
\]
\[
z^{k+1}=\arg\min_z\left\{g(z)+\frac\rho2\lVert Ax^{k+1}+Bz-c+u^k\rVert^2+\frac12\lVert z-z^k\rVert_Q^2\right\},
\]
\[
u^{k+1}=u^k+Ax^{k+1}+Bz^{k+1}-c.
\]
Choose graph-compatible block metrics for distributed local solves. Stop when primal and dual residuals meet tolerance; output the latest primal blocks.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Hybrid regularized ADMM linearizes a smooth objective component while retaining proximal metrics and exact augmented coupling in distributed subproblems.

children.title: Local-Subproblem Tradeoffs

knowledge_statements.title: Local-Subproblem Tradeoffs
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Compares exact, proximal, and linearized local solves within two-block distributed ADMM.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Consider the convex problem \(\min_{x,z} f(x)+g(z)\) subject to \(Ax+Bz=c\). A regularized ADMM local step has the form \[x^{k+1}\in\mathop{\rm argmin}_x\left\{f(x)+\langle y^k,Ax+Bz^k-c\rangle+\frac{\rho}{2}\lVert Ax+Bz^k-c\rVert^2+\frac12\lVert x-x^k\rVert_P^2\right\},\] where \(P\succeq0\). Choosing \(P=0\) retains the exact augmented-Lagrangian subproblem; a positive block-diagonal \(P\) can make local solves separable or strongly convex; choosing \(P\) to majorize and cancel difficult quadratic curvature yields a linearized step. These choices change per-iteration computation and admissible stepsizes, but any converged fixed point satisfying the unchanged dual and constraint updates obeys the original KKT system.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Exact local solves cost more per round; proximal or linearized solves reduce local work but impose regularization or stepsize restrictions. Their converged fixed points still satisfy the unregularized problem’s KKT conditions.
assumptions_latex: \(f\) and \(g\) are proper, closed, and convex.
\(\rho>0\) and \(P\succeq0\).

children.top_down_role: Augmented-Lagrangian coordination under irregular activation.

knowledge_statements.title: Asynchronous Distributed ADMM
knowledge_statements.scope_note: A bounded-delay, irregular-activation consensus-ADMM template with worker-local primal updates.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(\min_{x_1,\ldots,x_m,z}\sum_{i=1}^m f_i(x_i)\) subject to \(x_i=z\), initialize \(x_i^0,z^0,u_i^0\) and choose \(\rho>0\). At event \(k\), activate a nonempty worker set \(S_k\). Each \(i\in S_k\) reads a delayed master value \(z^{\tau_i(k)}\) and computes \[x_i^{k+1}\in\mathop{\rm argmin}_{x_i}\left\{f_i(x_i)+\frac{\rho}{2}\lVert x_i-z^{\tau_i(k)}+u_i^k\rVert^2\right\};\] inactive workers retain their values. After receiving the selected updates, the coordinator sets \(z^{k+1}=m^{-1}\sum_i(x_i^{k+1}+u_i^k)\), and each activated worker sets \(u_i^{k+1}=u_i^k+x_i^{k+1}-z^{k+1}\); inactive dual variables are retained. Stop when primal and dual residual tolerances hold.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Workers solve local ADMM subproblems using possibly delayed consensus values. A coordinator aggregates available states, while only activated workers update their dual variables.
assumptions_latex: Every worker is activated infinitely often and \(0\le k-\tau_i(k)\le D<\infty\).
Each \(f_i\) is proper, closed, and convex, and a primal-dual solution exists.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The algorithm outputs the latest \((x_1^k,\ldots,x_m^k,z^k,u_1^k,\ldots,u_m^k)\) when its prescribed residual test is met.

notation.meaning: Iteration index of the consensus value read by worker i.

children.title: Distributed Augmented-Lagrangian Frameworks
children.top_down_role: Distributed decomposition organized around augmented dual penalties.

knowledge_statements.title: Distributed Augmented-Lagrangian Frameworks
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Product-space augmented-Lagrangian representation of separable objectives with network coupling.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\mathcal X_1,\ldots,\mathcal X_m\) and \(\mathcal Y\) be real Hilbert spaces, let \(x=(x_1,\ldots,x_m)\in\mathcal X_1\times\cdots\times\mathcal X_m\), and define \(F(x)=\sum_{i=1}^m f_i(x_i)\). Let \(K:\mathcal X_1\times\cdots\times\mathcal X_m\to\mathcal Y\) be a bounded linear network-coupling operator and let \(b\in\mathcal Y\). For \(y\in\mathcal Y\) and \(\rho>0\), the augmented Lagrangian is \[\mathcal L_\rho(x,y)=\sum_{i=1}^m f_i(x_i)+\langle y,Kx-b\rangle_{\mathcal Y}+\frac{\rho}{2}\lVert Kx-b\rVert_{\mathcal Y}^2.\] A distributed augmented-Lagrangian framework performs an exact or specified inexact minimization of \(\mathcal L_\rho(\cdot,y^k)\), using the sparsity of \(K\), and updates \[y^{k+1}=y^k+\rho(Kx^{k+1}-b).\] When \(K\) is induced by a graph incidence operator, each component of \(Kx\) can be evaluated using endpoint or neighbor exchanges.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A separable network problem can be represented by an augmented Lagrangian whose sparse coupling operator permits local and neighbor computations, followed by multiplier ascent on the coupling residual.
assumptions_latex: \(\mathcal X_1,\ldots,\mathcal X_m\) and \(\mathcal Y\) are real Hilbert spaces.
Each \(f_i:\mathcal X_i\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) is proper, closed, and convex.
\(K:\prod_{i=1}^m\mathcal X_i\to\mathcal Y\) is bounded and linear, and \(\{x:Kx=b\}\ne\varnothing\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\mathcal L_\rho\) combines separable agent objectives with sparse network coupling, and \(y^{k+1}-y^k=\rho(Kx^{k+1}-b)\) accumulates the coupling residual.

notation.meaning: Multiplier in the coupling-space Hilbert space.

children.title: Augmentation–Splitting Relations
children.top_down_role: Structural connections between augmented penalties and distributed splitting formats.

knowledge_statements.title: Augmentation–Splitting Relations
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Consensus ADMM viewed as Douglas–Rachford splitting of the associated dual inclusion.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For proper closed convex \(f,g\) and the split problem \(\min_{x,z} f(x)+g(z)\) subject to \(x=z\), the Fenchel dual optimality condition can be written \[0\in \partial f^*(-y)-\partial g^*(y).\] Applying Douglas–Rachford splitting to the two maximal monotone operators \(A:y\mapsto-\partial f^*(-y)\) and \(B=\partial g^*\), with resolvent parameter \(\rho>0\), is equivalent, after the standard affine identification of the splitting and scaled-multiplier variables, to ADMM applied to the primal equality split. Thus quadratic augmentation produces the proximal resolvents, while operator splitting permits alternating evaluation of the two component subproblems.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For an equality-split convex problem, primal ADMM and Douglas–Rachford splitting of the dual optimality inclusion generate equivalent iterates after a standard variable identification.
assumptions_latex: \(f\) and \(g\) are proper, closed, and convex.
Strong duality holds and the primal-dual solution set is nonempty.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The ADMM multiplier sequence is an affine shadow of the Douglas–Rachford sequence for \(0\in A(y)+B(y)\).

notation.meaning: Fenchel conjugates of the primal objective terms.
Dual maximal monotone operators used by Douglas–Rachford splitting.

knowledge_statements.title: Distributed Forward-Backward Splitting
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Product-space forward-backward iteration with local resolvents and a communication-realizable forward operator.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\mathcal H=\prod_{i=1}^m\mathcal H_i\) and seek \(x^\star\) satisfying \(0\in A x^\star+B x^\star\), where \(A=\prod_i A_i\) is maximally monotone and \(B\) is \(\beta\)-cocoercive. Choose \(0<\gamma<2\beta\), initialize \(x^0\in\mathcal H\), and iterate \[x^{k+1}=J_{\gamma A}(x^k-\gamma Bx^k),\qquad J_{\gamma A}=(I+\gamma A)^{-1}.\] Agent \(i\) computes \((Bx^k)_i\) from its local state and prescribed neighbor messages, then applies the local resolvent \(J_{\gamma A_i}\). Stop when a fixed-point residual such as \(\lVert x^k-J_{\gamma A}(x^k-\gamma Bx^k)\rVert\) meets tolerance, and output \(x^k\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Each agent communicates to evaluate a cocoercive coupling step, then independently applies its local resolvent. A stepsize below twice the cocoercivity constant makes the map averaged.
assumptions_latex: \(A_i\) is maximally monotone for every agent \(i\).
\(B\) is \(\beta\)-cocoercive and network-realizable.
\(\operatorname{zer}(A+B)\ne\varnothing\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: For \(0<\gamma<2\beta\), the update operator \(J_{\gamma A}(I-\gamma B)\) is averaged and its fixed points equal \(\operatorname{zer}(A+B)\).

notation.meaning: Resolvent of the block-separable monotone operator.
Cocoercivity constant of the forward operator.

knowledge_statements.title: Distributed Forward-Backward-Forward Splitting
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Tseng-type product-space splitting for monotone Lipschitz network coupling.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: On \(\mathcal H=\prod_{i=1}^m\mathcal H_i\), seek \(x^\star\) satisfying \(0\in Ax^\star+Bx^\star\), where \(A=\prod_{i=1}^m A_i\) is maximally monotone and \(B\) is monotone and \(L\)-Lipschitz. Choose \(0<\gamma<1/L\), initialize \(x^0\in\mathcal H\), and iterate \[y^k=J_{\gamma A}(x^k-\gamma Bx^k),\qquad x^{k+1}=y^k-\gamma(By^k-Bx^k).\] Each component of each evaluation of \(B\) is computed by the corresponding agent using the required neighbor exchanges, while \(J_{\gamma A}=\prod_{i=1}^mJ_{\gamma A_i}\) is block-local. Stop when \(\lVert x^k-y^k\rVert\) meets tolerance and output \(y^k\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The method uses one local backward step and two communicated forward evaluations, handling monotone Lipschitz couplings that need not be cocoercive.
assumptions_latex: \(A_i\) is maximally monotone for every \(i\in\{1,\ldots,m\}\).
\(B\) is monotone, \(L\)-Lipschitz, and network-realizable.
\(\operatorname{zer}(A+B)\ne\varnothing\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Every fixed point satisfies \(x^\star=y^\star\) and \(0\in Ax^\star+Bx^\star\).

notation.meaning: Lipschitz constant of the forward coupling operator.

knowledge_statements.title: Distributed Fixed-Point Splitting
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Represents a network primal-dual method as an averaged fixed-point iteration on product space.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\mathcal H=\prod_{i=1}^m\mathcal H_i\), let \(w=(w_1,\ldots,w_m)\in\mathcal H\), and let \(T:\mathcal H\to\mathcal H\) be an operator whose component \((Tw)_i\) depends only on agent \(i\)'s state and prescribed messages from its neighbors. A distributed splitting method has the relaxed fixed-point representation \[w^{k+1}=w^k+\lambda_k(Tw^k-w^k),\] where \(T\) is \(\alpha\)-averaged, \(\operatorname{Fix}(T)\ne\varnothing\), and \(0<\lambda_k<1/\alpha\). If a decoding map \(D\) maps \(\operatorname{Fix}(T)\) onto the primal-dual solution set, then \[r^k=w^k-Tw^k\] is a computable fixed-point residual, and every zero of this residual decodes to a network primal-dual solution.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A distributed primal-dual method can be represented as a relaxed averaged-map iteration whose components use prescribed neighbor messages; its fixed points decode to primal-dual solutions.
assumptions_latex: \(T:\mathcal H\to\mathcal H\) is \(\alpha\)-averaged for some \(0<\alpha<1\).
\(\operatorname{Fix}(T)\ne\varnothing\).
\(0<\inf_k\lambda_k\le\sup_k\lambda_k<1/\alpha\).
\(D(\operatorname{Fix}(T))\) is the primal-dual solution set.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(r^k=0\) if and only if \(w^k\in\operatorname{Fix}(T)\), in which case \(D(w^k)\) is a primal-dual solution.

notation.meaning: Map decoding fixed points into primal-dual variables.

knowledge_statements.title: Multi-Block Distributed Splitting
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Preconditioned product-space splitting across local operator and variable blocks.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\mathcal H=\prod_{i=1}^m\mathcal H_i\) and solve \(0\in Ax+Bx\), where \(A=\prod_{i=1}^m A_i\) and \(B\) contains sparse cross-block coupling. Choose a self-adjoint strongly positive block-diagonal preconditioner \(M=\operatorname{diag}(M_1,\ldots,M_m)\), initialize \(x^0\in\mathcal H\), and iterate \[x^{k+1}=J_{M^{-1}A}\bigl(x^k-M^{-1}Bx^k\bigr).\] Agent \(i\) obtains the neighbor blocks needed for \((Bx^k)_i\) and computes \[x_i^{k+1}=J_{M_i^{-1}A_i}\bigl(x_i^k-M_i^{-1}(Bx^k)_i\bigr).\] Stop when the product-space fixed-point residual meets tolerance and output all local blocks.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A block-diagonal metric separates the backward step across agents, while sparse cross-block terms are evaluated through neighbor communication.
assumptions_latex: Each \(A_i:\mathcal H_i\rightrightarrows\mathcal H_i\) is maximally monotone.
\(M\) is self-adjoint, strongly positive, and block-diagonal.
\(M^{-1}B\) is \(\beta\)-cocoercive in the \(M\)-induced inner product for some \(\beta>1/2\).
\(\operatorname{zer}(A+B)\ne\varnothing\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The global resolvent decomposes as \(J_{M^{-1}A}=\prod_{i=1}^mJ_{M_i^{-1}A_i}\), so the backward computation is block-local.

notation.meaning: Maximally monotone operator for local block i.

children.title: Primal-Dual Convergence under Graph Connectivity
children.top_down_role: Convergence regimes coupling network propagation and saddle stability.

knowledge_statements.title: Primal-Dual Convergence under Graph Connectivity
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional convergence of an averaged network primal-dual map on a connected graph.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(G=(V,E)\) be a finite connected undirected graph, let \(\mathcal X\) be a finite-dimensional real Hilbert space, and let \(K\) be an oriented incidence operator lifted to \(\mathcal X^{|V|}\), so that \[\ker K=\{(x_1,\ldots,x_{|V|}):x_1=\cdots=x_{|V|}\}.\] Suppose a distributed primal-dual splitting on a finite-dimensional product space \(\mathcal H\) is represented by \[w^{k+1}=Tw^k,\] where \(T:\mathcal H\to\mathcal H\) is averaged in an inner product induced by a positive-definite operator and \(\operatorname{Fix}(T)\ne\varnothing\). Suppose a decoding map \(D\) maps the fixed-point equations exactly to the KKT system of the network saddle problem, including \(Kx=0\). Then, for every \(w^0\in\mathcal H\), the sequence \((w^k)\) converges to some \(w^\star\in\operatorname{Fix}(T)\); the decoded primal component reaches agreement, and \(D(w^\star)\) satisfies the network saddle conditions.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: On a connected graph, incidence-based agreement is exact. If a finite-dimensional distributed primal-dual update is averaged and its fixed points are exactly KKT points, every iterate sequence converges to a consensual primal-dual solution.
assumptions_latex: \(G\) is finite, connected, and undirected.
\(\mathcal H\) is finite-dimensional.
\(T:\mathcal H\to\mathcal H\) is averaged in a positive-definite metric and \(\operatorname{Fix}(T)\ne\varnothing\).
The decoding map \(D\) identifies the fixed-point system of \(T\) with the network KKT system.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(w^k\to w^\star\in\operatorname{Fix}(T)\), the decoded primal component satisfies \(Kx^\star=0\), and \(D(w^\star)\) is a primal-dual solution.

notation.meaning: Oriented graph-incidence operator lifted to the decision space.
Map decoding a fixed point into network primal-dual variables.

children.title: Distributed Primal-Dual Stepsize Conditions
children.top_down_role: Stability regions shaped by operator and network geometry.

knowledge_statements.title: Distributed Primal-Dual Stepsize Conditions
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Diagonal primal-dual stability condition coupling local stepsizes to the network operator norm.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\mathcal X\) and \(\mathcal Y\) be finite-dimensional real Hilbert spaces and consider the convex saddle problem \[\min_{x\in\mathcal X}\max_{y\in\mathcal Y}\; f(x)+\langle Kx,y\rangle-g^*(y),\] where \(K:\mathcal X\to\mathcal Y\) is linear. Let the primal and dual stepsize operators be \(T=\operatorname{diag}(\tau_i I)\succ0\) and \(\Sigma=\operatorname{diag}(\sigma_e I)\succ0\). A sufficient preconditioned primal-dual stability condition is \[\bigl\lVert\Sigma^{1/2}KT^{1/2}\bigr\rVert<1.\] This condition is equivalent to \[T^{-1}-K^*\Sigma K\succ0.\] When \(K\) is a graph-incidence or other sparse coupling operator, the condition couples the local primal stepsizes \(\tau_i\) and dual stepsizes \(\sigma_e\) to the graph and coupling weights.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Positive local primal and dual stepsizes satisfy the stated stability condition when the norm of the diagonally scaled network-coupling operator is strictly below one.
assumptions_latex: \(\mathcal X\) and \(\mathcal Y\) are finite-dimensional real Hilbert spaces.
\(f\) and \(g^*\) are proper, closed, and convex.
\(K:\mathcal X\to\mathcal Y\) is linear.
\(T\) and \(\Sigma\) are block-diagonal and strongly positive.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\lVert\Sigma^{1/2}KT^{1/2}\rVert<1\) if and only if \(T^{-1}-K^*\Sigma K\succ0\), yielding a positive primal-dual metric for the splitting.

notation.meaning: Sparse network or saddle coupling operator.

children.title: Primal–Dual Feasibility Certificates
children.top_down_role: Residual families assessing distributed coupling feasibility.

knowledge_statements.title: Primal–Dual Feasibility Certificates
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact KKT residual certificate for a convex linearly constrained distributed problem.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\mathcal X\), \(\mathcal Z\), and \(\mathcal Y\) be real Hilbert spaces, let \(A:\mathcal X\to\mathcal Y\) and \(B:\mathcal Z\to\mathcal Y\) be bounded linear operators, and consider \[\min_{x\in\mathcal X,\,z\in\mathcal Z} f(x)+g(z)\quad\text{subject to}\quad Ax+Bz=c.\] A tuple \((x,z,y,s_x,s_z)\) is an exact primal-dual feasibility certificate when \[s_x\in\partial f(x),\qquad s_z\in\partial g(z),\qquad Ax+Bz-c=0,\] and \[s_x+A^*y=0,\qquad s_z+B^*y=0.\] These relations are the KKT conditions. Under the stated convexity and strong-duality assumptions, they certify that \((x,z)\) is primal optimal and \(y\) is dual optimal.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A feasible primal pair, a multiplier, and matching local subgradients certify optimality when the primal and stationarity residuals all vanish.
assumptions_latex: \(\mathcal X\), \(\mathcal Z\), and \(\mathcal Y\) are real Hilbert spaces.
\(f:\mathcal X\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) and \(g:\mathcal Z\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) are proper, closed, and convex.
\(A:\mathcal X\to\mathcal Y\) and \(B:\mathcal Z\to\mathcal Y\) are bounded and linear.
Strong duality holds for the linear constraint.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The displayed zero residuals certify primal feasibility, dual optimality, primal optimality, and equality of the primal and dual optimal values.

notation.meaning: Objective subgradients at the candidate primal variables.

children.title: Consensus Certificates
children.top_down_role: Residual families assessing agreement across agent variables.

knowledge_statements.title: Consensus Certificates
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Incidence-residual certificate for exact agreement on a connected undirected graph.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(G=(V,E)\) be a finite connected undirected graph with an arbitrary orientation, let \(D\in\mathbb R^{|E|\times|V|}\) be its oriented edge-node incidence matrix, and let \(x=(x_i)_{i\in V}\in(\mathbb R^d)^{|V|}\) be the stacked local decisions. Define the consensus residual \[r_{\mathrm{con}}=(D\otimes I_d)x.\] Each edge can compute its oriented endpoint difference, and the assembled residual vanishes exactly when all adjacent decisions agree. Connectivity gives \[\ker(D\otimes I_d)=\{\mathbf 1\otimes v:v\in\mathbb R^d\},\] so \(r_{\mathrm{con}}=0\) certifies global agreement.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Edgewise endpoint differences form a directly verifiable residual. On a connected graph, its vanishing is equivalent to every agent holding the same decision.
assumptions_latex: \(G=(V,E)\) is finite, connected, and undirected.
\(D\in\mathbb R^{|E|\times|V|}\) is an oriented edge-node incidence matrix of \(G\).
Every local decision belongs to \(\mathbb R^d\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(r_{\mathrm{con}}=0\) if and only if there exists \(v\in\mathbb R^d\) such that \(x=\mathbf 1\otimes v\).

notation.meaning: Stacked vector with common value v at every node.

children.title: Joint Feasibility–Agreement Residuals
children.top_down_role: Combined reporting of coupling feasibility and network agreement.

knowledge_statements.title: Joint Feasibility–Agreement Residuals
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Residual for affine local feasibility and graph-consensus constraints.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(m,d,p\in\mathbb N\), let \(G=(V,E)\) be an undirected communication graph with \(V=\{1,\ldots,m\}\), and let \(B\in\mathbb R^{|E|\times m}\) be an oriented incidence matrix of \(G\). For \(x=(x_1,\ldots,x_m)\in\mathbb R^{md}\), where \(x_i\in\mathbb R^d\), let \(A\in\mathbb R^{p\times md}\), \(b\in\mathbb R^p\), and \(C=B\otimes I_d\). Define \[r_{\mathrm{joint}}(x):=\bigl(\|Ax-b\|_2^2+\|Cx\|_2^2\bigr)^{1/2}.\] Then \(r_{\mathrm{joint}}(x)\ge0\), and \(r_{\mathrm{joint}}(x)=0\) if and only if \(Ax=b\) and \(x_i=x_j\) for every pair \(i,j\) in the same connected component of \(G\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The joint residual combines affine-feasibility violation and network disagreement, and it vanishes exactly when the affine constraints and componentwise consensus both hold.
assumptions_latex: \(m,d,p\in\mathbb N\).
\(G=(V,E)\) is undirected and \(B\) is an oriented incidence matrix of \(G\).
\(A\in\mathbb R^{p\times md}\) and \(b\in\mathbb R^p\).

children.title: Incompatibility Detection
children.top_down_role: Certificate behavior indicating conflicting feasibility or agreement requirements.

knowledge_statements.title: Incompatibility Detection
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional alternative certificate for affine feasibility plus consensus.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(m,d,p,r\in\mathbb N\), \(A\in\mathbb R^{p\times md}\), \(C\in\mathbb R^{r\times md}\), and \(b\in\mathbb R^p\). For the joint system \(Ax=b\), \(Cx=0\) over \(x\in\mathbb R^{md}\), any \(y\in\mathbb R^p\) and \(z\in\mathbb R^r\) satisfying \[A^{\mathsf T}y+C^{\mathsf T}z=0,\qquad b^{\mathsf T}y=1\] form an incompatibility certificate, and no jointly feasible \(x\) exists. Conversely, if the joint affine system is inconsistent, finite-dimensional linear alternatives provide \(y\in\mathbb R^p\) and \(z\in\mathbb R^r\) satisfying the displayed normalization.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Multipliers that annihilate the two constraint operators and pair to one with the affine right-hand side certify incompatibility; conversely, every inconsistent finite-dimensional joint affine system admits such normalized multipliers.
assumptions_latex: \(m,d,p,r\in\mathbb N\).
\(A\in\mathbb R^{p\times md}\), \(C\in\mathbb R^{r\times md}\), and \(b\in\mathbb R^p\).
The consensus constraints have zero right-hand side.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\{x\in\mathbb R^{md}:Ax=b,\ Cx=0\}=\varnothing\iff\exists(y,z)\in\mathbb R^p\times\mathbb R^r:\ A^{\mathsf T}y+C^{\mathsf T}z=0,\ b^{\mathsf T}y=1\).

children.top_down_role: Communication-round, message, and bit-cost families.

knowledge_statements.title: Distributed Primal-Dual Communication Complexity
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Synchronous neighbor-exchange accounting with fixed-precision vector messages.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(G=(V,E)\) be a fixed undirected graph and let \(T,d,q\in\mathbb N\). Consider a synchronous distributed primal-dual execution lasting \(T\) communication rounds. Suppose that in every round each endpoint of every edge sends one \(d\)-coordinate vector to the other endpoint, with each coordinate encoded using at most \(q\) bits. Then the execution uses exactly \(T\) rounds and exactly \(2|E|T\) directed messages, and it transmits at most \(2|E|Tdq\) payload bits. If accuracy \(\varepsilon>0\) is guaranteed after \(T(\varepsilon)\) rounds, these counts hold with \(T=T(\varepsilon)\). Headers, synchronization traffic, and retransmissions are excluded.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Under this synchronous protocol, every edge contributes two directed vector messages per round, giving exactly two messages and at most twice the encoded vector payload per edge-round.
assumptions_latex: \(G=(V,E)\) is a fixed undirected communication graph.
\(T,d,q\in\mathbb N\).
Every coordinate uses at most \(q\) bits.
Protocol overhead and retransmissions are excluded.

children.title: General Convex Regime
children.top_down_role: Distributed convergence without strong curvature.

knowledge_statements.title: General Convex Regime
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Convex distributed objectives without assumed positive curvature.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(m,d\in\mathbb N\). For \(i=1,\ldots,m\), let \(f_i:\mathbb R^d\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) be proper, closed, and convex, define \(F=\sum_{i=1}^m f_i\), and assume \(X^*:=\operatorname*{argmin}_{x\in\mathbb R^d}F(x)\ne\varnothing\). Write \(F^*:=\min_{x\in\mathbb R^d}F(x)\), without assuming any positive strong-convexity modulus. For a sequence \(x^k=(x_1^k,\ldots,x_m^k)\in\mathbb R^{md}\), define \(\bar x^k=m^{-1}\sum_{i=1}^m x_i^k\) and \(D(x^k)=\bigl(\sum_{i=1}^m\|x_i^k-\bar x^k\|^2\bigr)^{1/2}\). Distributed convergence in this regime requires \(F(\bar x^k)-F^*\to0\) and \(D(x^k)\to0\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The general convex regime assumes proper closed convex local objectives and an attained aggregate optimum, but no uniform curvature; distributed convergence requires both vanishing aggregate objective error and vanishing disagreement.
assumptions_latex: \(m,d\in\mathbb N\).
Each \(f_i:\mathbb R^d\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) is proper, closed, and convex.
\(X^*=\operatorname*{argmin}F\ne\varnothing\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(F(\bar x^k)-F^*\to0\) and \(D(x^k)\to0\) constitute distributed convergence in this regime.

notation.meaning: Euclidean consensus disagreement at index k.

children.title: Strongly Convex Regime
children.top_down_role: Distributed convergence under uniform curvature.

knowledge_statements.title: Strongly Convex Regime
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Distributed objectives possessing uniform quadratic curvature.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(m,d\in\mathbb N\), let \(f_i:\mathbb R^d\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) for \(i=1,\ldots,m\), and define \(F=\sum_{i=1}^m f_i\). Let \(X\subseteq\mathbb R^d\) be convex and suppose \(F\) is proper and subdifferentiable at every point of \(X\). The problem is in the strongly convex regime with modulus \(\mu>0\) when, for every \(x,y\in X\) and every \(g\in\partial F(x)\), \[F(y)\ge F(x)+\langle g,y-x\rangle+\frac{\mu}{2}\|y-x\|^2.\] If \(F\) attains its minimum over \(X\) at \(x^*\), then this minimizer is unique and \(F(x)-F(x^*)\ge(\mu/2)\|x-x^*\|^2\) for every \(x\in X\). Distributed convergence additionally requires all local copies to agree with \(x^*\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Uniform quadratic curvature of the aggregate objective makes its constrained minimizer unique and bounds squared distance to that minimizer by objective error, while distributed convergence also requires consensus.
assumptions_latex: \(m,d\in\mathbb N\) and \(X\subseteq\mathbb R^d\) is convex.
\(F=\sum_{i=1}^m f_i\) is proper and subdifferentiable at every point of \(X\).
A minimizer \(x^*\in X\) exists.

children.title: Error-Bound Regimes
children.top_down_role: Distributed objective geometries characterized by error-bound behavior.

knowledge_statements.title: Error-Bound Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Residual-to-solution-distance bounds for convex aggregate objectives.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(F:\mathbb R^d\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) be proper, closed, and convex with nonempty minimizer set \(X^*\). An error-bound regime holds on a set \(U\subseteq\operatorname{dom}F\) if there exists \(\kappa>0\) such that \[\operatorname{dist}(x,X^*)\le \kappa\operatorname{dist}(0,\partial F(x))\qquad\text{for every }x\in U.\] The bound is local when \(U\) is a neighborhood of \(X^*\), and global when \(U=\operatorname{dom}F\). For distributed iterates, this condition controls optimization distance but does not replace a separate agreement residual.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An error bound converts a computable first-order residual into distance from the aggregate solution set; distributed methods must still control disagreement separately.
assumptions_latex: \(F\) is proper, closed, and convex.
\(X^*=\operatorname*{argmin}F\ne\varnothing\).

notation.meaning: Region on which the error bound holds.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The condition is a recognizable convex subdifferential error bound and fits the leaf, but no inspectable source is supplied. The plain statement should also avoid calling the residual computable without additional assumptions.

children.title: Gradient-Dominance Regimes
children.top_down_role: Distributed objective geometries characterized by gradient dominance.

knowledge_statements.title: Gradient-Dominance Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Polyak–Łojasiewicz gradient dominance for smooth aggregate objectives.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(F:\mathbb R^d\to\mathbb R\) be differentiable with finite attained minimum \(F^*\). The objective satisfies gradient dominance with constant \(\mu>0\) on \(U\subseteq\mathbb R^d\) when \[\frac12\|\nabla F(x)\|^2\ge \mu\bigl(F(x)-F^*\bigr)\qquad\text{for every }x\in U.\] This condition does not require convexity. It ensures that a small gradient norm certifies small objective suboptimality on \(U\). In a distributed method, the gradient condition concerns the aggregate objective, while consensus error remains an additional quantity to control.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Gradient dominance bounds aggregate objective error by squared gradient norm without requiring convexity; network disagreement remains a separate distributed residual.
assumptions_latex: \(F\) is differentiable on \(U\).
The finite value \(F^*\) is attained.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The normalization and nonconvex interpretation of the Polyak–Łojasiewicz condition are mathematically standard, but the record has no source with a section, theorem, definition, or page locator.

children.title: Growth-Condition Hierarchies
children.top_down_role: Comparative placement of weaker and stronger growth conditions.

knowledge_statements.title: Growth-Condition Hierarchies
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Ordering of Hölderian objective-growth exponents near the solution set.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(F\) have nonempty minimizer set \(X^*\), and suppose \(U\subseteq\operatorname{dom}F\) satisfies \(\operatorname{dist}(x,X^*)\le1\) for every \(x\in U\). For \(p>0\), define order-\(p\) growth on \(U\) by \[F(x)-F^*\ge c\operatorname{dist}(x,X^*)^p\qquad(x\in U)\] for some \(c>0\). If this inequality holds with exponent \(p\), then it also holds with every exponent \(q\ge p\) on \(U\), using the same constant. Thus, on a normalized neighborhood, smaller exponents impose stronger growth.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Near the solution set, order-p growth implies every weaker order-q growth condition with q at least p; smaller exponents are stronger.
assumptions_latex: \(X^*=\operatorname*{argmin}F\ne\varnothing\).
\(\operatorname{dist}(x,X^*)\le1\) throughout \(U\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(p\le q\) and order-\(p\) growth on \(U\) imply order-\(q\) growth on \(U\).
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: direct ordering of powers on the unit neighborhood

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The exponent ordering on a unit neighborhood is correct and the property kind fits the hierarchy leaf, but no inspectable authoritative source is supplied.

children.title: Local-versus-Global Growth
children.top_down_role: Distinction between neighborhood-limited and global growth behavior.

knowledge_statements.title: Local-versus-Global Growth
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Local growth need not extend uniformly over the full domain.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A growth inequality is local if it holds only when \(\operatorname{dist}(x,X^*)\le\delta\) for some \(\delta>0\), and global if it holds for every point in the domain. Every global inequality is local, but the converse fails. For example, the convex Huber function \[F(x)=\begin{cases}x^2/2,&|x|\le1,\\ |x|-1/2,&|x|>1\end{cases}\] has \(X^*=\{0\}\) and satisfies local quadratic growth with constant \(1/2\). No constant \(c>0\) makes \(F(x)\ge c|x|^2\) hold globally, because its growth is only linear as \(|x|\to\infty\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Global growth implies local growth, but the convex Huber function shows that local quadratic growth can coexist with merely linear behavior at infinity.
assumptions_latex: Growth is measured relative to the nonempty minimizer set \(X^*\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Local quadratic growth does not imply global quadratic growth, even for a finite convex function on \(\mathbb R\).

notation.meaning: Radius of the local growth neighborhood.

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: explicit Huber counterexample is directly checkable

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The Huber example correctly separates local from global quadratic growth and the failure-boundary kind fits the leaf, but the counterexample and terminology lack an inspectable source.

children.title: Smooth Nonconvex Stationarity
children.top_down_role: Network convergence to first-order stationary behavior.

knowledge_statements.title: Smooth Nonconvex Stationarity
knowledge_statements.scope_note: First-order aggregate stationarity combined with network agreement.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(f_i:\mathbb R^d\to\mathbb R\) be continuously differentiable and define \(F=m^{-1}\sum_{i=1}^m f_i\). For local vectors \(x=(x_1,\ldots,x_m)\), set \(\bar x=m^{-1}\sum_i x_i\). The vector collection is an \(\varepsilon\)-stationarity certificate when \[\|\nabla F(\bar x)\|^2+\frac1m\sum_{i=1}^m\|x_i-\bar x\|^2\le\varepsilon.\] The first term certifies approximate first-order stationarity of the aggregate smooth objective; the second certifies approximate agreement. A sequence reaches distributed stationary behavior when this combined quantity converges to zero.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Smooth distributed stationarity requires both a small aggregate gradient at the network average and small mean-square disagreement among agents.
assumptions_latex: Each \(f_i\) is continuously differentiable.
All local vectors lie in \(\mathbb R^d\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\|\nabla F(\bar x)\|^2+m^{-1}\sum_i\|x_i-\bar x\|^2\le\varepsilon\) certifies joint stationarity and agreement.

children.title: Composite Nonconvex Regimes

knowledge_statements.title: Composite Nonconvex Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Proximal-gradient stationarity for smooth-plus-convex composite objectives.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(F=f+g\), where \(f:\mathbb R^d\to\mathbb R\) is continuously differentiable and may be nonconvex, while \(g:\mathbb R^d\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) is proper, closed, and convex. For \(\eta>0\), define \[G_\eta(x):=\eta^{-1}\bigl(x-\operatorname{prox}_{\eta g}(x-\eta\nabla f(x))\bigr).\] The composite nonconvex regime uses \(\|G_\eta(x)\|\) as its stationarity residual. Exactly, \(G_\eta(x)=0\) if and only if \(0\in\nabla f(x)+\partial g(x)\). Distributed certification additionally requires agreement among local copies.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a smooth nonconvex term plus a convex regularizer, the proximal-gradient mapping provides the first-order stationarity residual, supplemented by consensus error.
assumptions_latex: \(f\) is continuously differentiable.
\(g\) is proper, closed, and convex.

children.title: Nonsmooth Nonconvex Regimes
children.top_down_role: Distributed objectives lacking smoothness and convexity.

knowledge_statements.title: Nonsmooth Nonconvex Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Limiting-subdifferential stationarity with an explicit consensus residual.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(F:\mathbb R^d\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) be proper and lower semicontinuous, possibly nonsmooth and nonconvex, and let \(\partial F\) denote its limiting subdifferential. A point \(u\in\operatorname{dom}F\) is \(\varepsilon\)-stationary when \[\operatorname{dist}(0,\partial F(u))\le\varepsilon.\] For distributed local vectors \(x_i\) and a representative \(u\), joint approximate stationarity and agreement require \[\operatorname{dist}(0,\partial F(u))^2+\frac1m\sum_{i=1}^m\|x_i-u\|^2\le\varepsilon^2.\] The chosen subdifferential must be fixed explicitly because alternative nonsmooth stationarity notions need not coincide in nonconvex problems.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Nonsmooth nonconvex stationarity uses distance to the limiting subdifferential, while distributed stationarity also requires local variables to agree with the representative point.
assumptions_latex: \(F\) is proper and lower semicontinuous.
\(\partial F\) is the limiting subdifferential.
\(u\in\operatorname{dom}F\).

notation.meaning: Limiting subdifferential of the aggregate objective.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The limiting-subdifferential choice is appropriate for a nonsmooth nonconvex regime, but no authoritative locator supports it or the proposed joint normalization. A sourced revision should also state the domains of m, the local vectors, and the nonnegative tolerance explicitly.

children.title: Composite Stationarity Certificates
children.top_down_role: Stationarity measures suited to distributed composite objectives.

knowledge_statements.title: Composite Stationarity Certificates
knowledge_statements.scope_note: First-order certificate for a smooth-plus-nonsmooth, possibly nonconvex composite objective.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(F=f+r\) on \(\mathbb{R}^d\), where \(f\) is continuously differentiable and \(r\) is proper and lower semicontinuous. At any \(x\in\operatorname{dom}r\), a composite \(\varepsilon\)-stationarity certificate is a vector \(u\in\partial r(x)\) satisfying \[\|\nabla f(x)+u\|\leq\varepsilon.\] Equivalently, its optimal residual is \[\mathcal R_F(x):=\operatorname{dist}\!\left(0,\nabla f(x)+\partial r(x)\right)\leq\varepsilon.\] Here \(\partial r\) is the limiting subdifferential; thus the certificate remains meaningful when \(r\) is nonconvex.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A subgradient of the nonsmooth term certifies approximate stationarity when it nearly cancels the smooth gradient; the smallest such residual is the composite stationarity measure.
assumptions_latex: \(f:\mathbb{R}^d\to\mathbb{R}\) is continuously differentiable.
\(r:\mathbb{R}^d\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) is proper and lower semicontinuous.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The pair \((x,u)\) certifies \(\mathcal R_F(x)\leq\varepsilon\); for \(\varepsilon=0\), it certifies \(0\in\nabla f(x)+\partial r(x)\).

notation.meaning: Limiting subdifferential of r at x.

children.title: Nonsmooth-Regularization Boundaries
children.top_down_role: Regularity limits affecting distributed stationarity guarantees.

knowledge_statements.title: Nonsmooth-Regularization Boundaries
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Uniform smoothing accuracy does not preserve finite-parameter nonsmooth stationarity.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Fix \(a\in(0,1)\). The nonsmooth objective \(F(x)=|x|-ax\) has \(0\in\partial F(0)\). Its smooth approximation \(F_\mu(x)=\sqrt{x^2+\mu^2}-ax\), with \(\mu>0\), satisfies \(\sup_x|F_\mu(x)-F(x)|\leq\mu\). Nevertheless, \(F_\mu\) has the stationary point \[x_\mu=\frac{a\mu}{\sqrt{1-a^2}}>0,\] while the original nonsmooth residual there is \[\operatorname{dist}(0,\partial F(x_\mu))=1-a.\] Hence uniform value approximation and exact stationarity of the regularized problem do not imply vanishing stationarity residual for the original problem at finite \(\mu\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Even uniformly accurate smooth approximations can have stationary points whose original nonsmooth stationarity residual stays bounded away from zero for every positive smoothing parameter.

notation.meaning: Smooth regularization of the nonsmooth objective.
Exact stationary point of the regularized objective.

children.title: Distributed Information-Oracle Taxonomy
children.top_down_role: Local information-access models governing distributed guarantees.

children.title: Deterministic Local Oracles
children.top_down_role: Exact local derivative or proximal information.

knowledge_statements.title: Deterministic Local Oracles
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact first-order or proximal information available privately at each agent.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For agents \(i\in\{1,\ldots,n\}\), let \(f_i:\mathbb R^d\to\mathbb R\) be a local loss and let \(r_i:\mathbb R^d\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) be proper, lower semicontinuous, and convex. A deterministic local oracle \(\mathcal O_i\) returns a response determined solely by its query and agent \(i\)'s local data. At \(x\in\mathbb R^d\), declared query types may return \(f_i(x)\), \(\nabla f_i(x)\) when \(f_i\) is differentiable, a deterministically selected \(g_i(x)\in\partial f_i(x)\) when that subdifferential is nonempty, or the unique proximal point \[\operatorname{prox}_{\gamma r_i}(x):=\arg\min_{y\in\mathbb R^d}\left\{r_i(y)+\frac{\|y-x\|^2}{2\gamma}\right\},\qquad \gamma>0.\] No sampling randomness or data from another agent is used to form the response.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Each agent returns an exact value, derivative, deterministically selected subgradient, or unique proximal point using only its local objective and the query.
assumptions_latex: \(f_i:\mathbb R^d\to\mathbb R\) is finite-valued, with differentiability or a nonempty subdifferential required by the selected query type.
\(r_i:\mathbb R^d\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) is proper, lower semicontinuous, and convex.
\(\gamma>0\) for a proximal query.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Conditioned on the query and local data, \(\mathcal O_i\) returns the same exact response on every invocation.

notation.meaning: Deterministic oracle held by agent i.

children.title: Stochastic Local Oracles
children.top_down_role: Noisy or sampled information with agent-local distributions.

knowledge_statements.title: Stochastic Local Oracles
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Agent-local sampled first-order information with conditional moment controls.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For each agent \(i\), let \(\xi_i\sim P_i\) and \(f_i(x)=\mathbb E_{\xi_i}[\ell_i(x;\xi_i)]\). A stochastic local first-order oracle queried at \(x\in\mathbb R^d\) returns \(G_i(x,\xi_i)\) using a fresh local sample and satisfies \[\mathbb E[G_i(x,\xi_i)\mid x]=\nabla f_i(x),\qquad \mathbb E[\|G_i(x,\xi_i)-\nabla f_i(x)\|^2\mid x]\leq\sigma_i^2.\] Samples may follow different distributions across agents, but each response depends only on the query, the agent's local distribution, and its sampling randomness.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Each agent samples an unbiased local gradient estimate with controlled conditional variance; local sampling distributions may differ across the network.
assumptions_latex: \(f_i(x)=\mathbb E_{\xi_i\sim P_i}[\ell_i(x;\xi_i)]\) is differentiable.
Fresh oracle randomness is conditionally independent of the past given the query.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The oracle error is conditionally mean zero and has conditional second moment at most \(\sigma_i^2\).

children.title: Local Finite-Sum Oracles
children.top_down_role: Agent-local finite sums supporting variance reduction.

knowledge_statements.title: Local Finite-Sum Oracles
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite component decomposition and indexed derivative access at each agent.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Agent \(i\)'s differentiable local objective admits the finite-sum representation \[f_i(x)= rac{1}{m_i}\sum_{j=1}^{m_i}f_{ij}(x).\] A local finite-sum oracle accepts \((x,j)\), where \(x\in\mathbb R^d\) and \(j\in\{1,\ldots,m_i\}\), and returns \(f_{ij}(x)\), \(
abla f_{ij}(x)\), or both. Full local information is recovered by averaging: \[
abla f_i(x)= rac{1}{m_i}\sum_{j=1}^{m_i}
abla f_{ij}(x).\] Retaining component indices permits algorithms to store or refresh component information and construct variance-reduced estimators.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Each local objective is an average of finitely many components, and the oracle exposes component values or gradients by index, enabling variance reduction.
assumptions_latex: \(m_i\) is a positive integer.
Each \(f_{ij}:\mathbb R^d\to\mathbb R\) is differentiable.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Averaging all \(m_i\) component gradients yields the exact local gradient \(\nabla f_i(x)\).

notation.meaning: Number of components stored by agent i.
Component objective j at agent i.

children.title: Distributed Zeroth-Order Oracles
children.top_down_role: Network optimization using local function-value information.

knowledge_statements.title: Distributed Zeroth-Order Oracles
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Local objective information obtained without derivative queries.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For agents \(i\in\{1,\ldots,n\}\), a distributed zeroth-order oracle permits agent \(i\) to query only local function values. Given \(x\in\mathbb R^d\), it returns either \(f_i(x)\) or a random value \(Y_i(x,\xi_i)\) satisfying \[\mathbb E[Y_i(x,\xi_i)\mid x]=f_i(x),\qquad \mathbb E[|Y_i(x,\xi_i)-f_i(x)|^2\mid x]\leq\nu_i^2.\] The oracle returns no gradient, subgradient, or proximal point. Agents may combine value queries at perturbed points with network messages to construct derivative-free estimates.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Each agent observes only exact or unbiased noisy values of its local objective, then combines perturbed queries and communication to estimate useful directions.
assumptions_latex: Each \(f_i:\mathbb R^d\to\mathbb R\) is evaluable at admissible query points.
In the noisy model, the local value noise has bounded conditional variance.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Every local optimization direction must be inferred from function values and communicated information rather than obtained through derivative access.

children.title: Distributed Rate Theory
children.top_down_role: Rate families separating objective, network, stochastic, and transient effects.

children.title: Sublinear Distributed Rate Families
children.top_down_role: Rates for general convex, nonsmooth, and nonconvex regimes.

knowledge_statements.title: Sublinear Distributed Rate Families
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Polynomially decaying guarantees for distributed optimization error or stationarity measures.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(E_t\geq0\) denote a specified expected optimality, feasibility, consensus, or stationarity error after \(t\) distributed iterations. A method has a sublinear distributed rate of order \(p>0\) when constants \(C>0\) and \(t_0\geq0\) exist such that \[E_t\leq \frac{C}{(t+1)^p}\qquad\text{for all }t\geq t_0.\] Consequently, the iteration count sufficient for \(E_t\leq\varepsilon\) is \[t=O\!\left((C/\varepsilon)^{1/p}\right).\] The constant may depend on network connectivity, initialization, noise, and problem geometry; the exponent identifies the rate family.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A distributed error belongs to a sublinear family when it decays polynomially; order p yields iteration complexity proportional to epsilon raised to minus 1/p.
assumptions_latex: \(E_t\) is a nonnegative, explicitly specified performance measure.
The bound holds uniformly for all \(t\geq t_0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The accuracy requirement \(E_t\leq\varepsilon\) is attained within \(O((C/\varepsilon)^{1/p})\) distributed iterations.

notation.meaning: Chosen distributed performance error after iteration t.

children.title: Linear Distributed Rate Families
children.top_down_role: Fast rates under curvature, regularity, and stable mixing.

knowledge_statements.title: Linear Distributed Rate Families
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Geometric convergence under curvature, regularity, and contractive network mixing.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(E_t\geq0\) be a specified distributed optimality-consensus error indexed by \(t\in\mathbb N_0\). A method has a linear distributed rate when constants \(C>0\), \(t_0\in\mathbb N_0\), and \(\rho\in(0,1)\) exist such that \[E_t\leq C\rho^{t-t_0}\qquad\text{for every }t\geq t_0.\] For any \(\varepsilon\in(0,C)\), the condition \[t\geq t_0+\left\lceil\frac{\log(C/\varepsilon)}{-\log\rho}\right\rceil\] is sufficient for \(E_t\leq\varepsilon\). In distributed methods, \(\rho\) may reflect both objective curvature or an error-bound constant and contraction of the communication operator.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A distributed method has a linear rate when its declared error contracts geometrically; reaching an accuracy below the initial bound requires logarithmically many additional iterations.
assumptions_latex: \(E_t\) includes every error component required by the guarantee.
The target satisfies \(\varepsilon\in(0,C)\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The iteration complexity sufficient for \(E_t\leq\varepsilon\) is \(t_0+O\!\left(\log(C/\varepsilon)/(-\log\rho)\right)\).

children.title: Network-Independent Asymptotic Rates
children.top_down_role: Regimes whose leading asymptotic behavior matches centralized methods.

knowledge_statements.title: Network-Independent Asymptotic Rates
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Leading-order distributed behavior matches the corresponding centralized performance law.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(E_t^{\mathrm{dist}}\) and \(E_t^{\mathrm{cent}}\) measure the same nonnegative error for a distributed method and its centralized reference, and let \(\phi(t)>0\) eventually with \(\phi(t)\to0\). The distributed guarantee is network-independent asymptotically when there is a constant \(C>0\), independent of the communication graph, such that \[E_t^{\mathrm{cent}}=C\phi(t)+o(\phi(t)),\qquad E_t^{\mathrm{dist}}=C\phi(t)+o(\phi(t)).\] Graph-dependent terms may occur at finite times but are lower order than \(\phi(t)\). Under these expansions, \[\frac{E_t^{\mathrm{dist}}}{E_t^{\mathrm{cent}}}\longrightarrow1.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The distributed method is asymptotically network-independent when its leading decay scale and positive leading constant match the centralized reference, while graph-dependent effects are lower order.
assumptions_latex: Both errors use the same objective normalization and accuracy criterion.
\(\phi(t)>0\) eventually and \(\phi(t)\to0\).
The common leading constant \(C>0\) is independent of the communication graph.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The communication graph does not affect the leading asymptotic term, and \(E_t^{\mathrm{dist}}/E_t^{\mathrm{cent}}\to1\).
