children.title: Network-Dependent Transient Theory
children.top_down_role: Pre-asymptotic effects of topology, population size, and initialization.

knowledge_statements.title: Network-Dependent Transient Theory
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Error decomposition separating centralized decay from pre-asymptotic network effects.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(t\in\mathbb N_0\). A network-dependent transient bound has the form \[E_t\leq A\phi(t)+B(\mathcal G,n,x^0)\psi(t),\] where \(A\phi(t)\) is a centralized-scale term, \(A>0\), and the finite coefficient \(B(\mathcal G,n,x^0)\geq0\) records the communication graph \(\mathcal G\), the number of agents \(n\), and the initialization \(x^0\). Suppose \(\phi(t)>0\) eventually and \(\psi(t)=o(\phi(t))\). Define \[T_{\mathrm{tr}}:=\inf\left\{T\in\mathbb N_0: B(\mathcal G,n,x^0)\psi(t)\leq A\phi(t)\ \text{for every }t\geq T\right\}.\] This horizon is finite. For every \(t\geq T_{\mathrm{tr}}\), the network-dependent term is no larger than the centralized-scale term. Poor connectivity or larger initial disagreement may increase \(T_{\mathrm{tr}}\) without changing the leading asymptotic scale.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A distributed error bound separates centralized and network-dependent terms, and the transient horizon is the first time after which the network term remains no larger than the centralized term.
assumptions_latex: \(E_t\geq0\), \(\phi(t)>0\) eventually, and \(\psi(t)\geq0\).
\(A>0\) and \(B(\mathcal G,n,x^0)\) is finite and nonnegative.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The horizon \(T_{\mathrm{tr}}\) is finite, and \(B(\mathcal G,n,x^0)\psi(t)\leq A\phi(t)\) for every \(t\geq T_{\mathrm{tr}}\).

children.title: Distributed Complexity Measures
children.top_down_role: Cost models distinguishing computation, communication, synchronization, and total work.

children.title: Local Oracle Complexity
children.top_down_role: Local derivative, subgradient, proximal, or function-value costs.

knowledge_statements.title: Local Oracle Complexity
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Per-agent and aggregate counts of local information requests needed for accuracy.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Fix a distributed algorithm execution, an oracle class, and an accuracy criterion \(E(x)\leq\varepsilon\). Let \(q_i(t)\in\mathbb N_0\) be the number of declared local oracle calls made by agent \(i\in\{1,n\}\) through iteration \(t\). Define the execution-level worst-agent and aggregate local oracle costs by \[Q_{\max}(\varepsilon):=\inf_{t:E(x^t)\leq\varepsilon}\max_{1\leq i\leq n}q_i(t),\qquad Q_{\Sigma}(\varepsilon):=\inf_{t:E(x^t)\leq\varepsilon}\sum_{i=1}^n q_i(t).\] If no qualifying iterate exists, the corresponding value is \(+\infty\). The first quantity measures worst-agent local work, and the second measures total network-wide oracle work. Query types with materially different costs are counted separately or combined through an explicit cost model.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a fixed distributed execution, local oracle complexity records either the largest per-agent query count or the total query count needed to reach the declared accuracy.
assumptions_latex: The algorithm execution, error criterion \(E\), outputs \(x^t\), and target \(\varepsilon\) are specified.
The permitted oracle responses and their counting convention are fixed.
\(q_i(t)\in\mathbb N_0\) counts agent \(i\)'s oracle calls through iteration \(t\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(Q_{\max}(\varepsilon)\) and \(Q_{\Sigma}(\varepsilon)\) quantify worst-agent and aggregate execution-level local oracle costs, respectively.

notation.meaning: Number of local oracle calls made by agent i through iteration t.

children.title: Distributed Communication-Round Complexity
children.top_down_role: Sequential network exchanges required to reach an accuracy target.

knowledge_statements.title: Distributed Communication-Round Complexity
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Sequential network-exchange rounds required to attain a declared accuracy.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Fix a synchronous graph model and an accuracy predicate \(\mathcal A_\varepsilon(x)\) that incorporates the selected deterministic, expected, or high-probability success convention. One communication round permits every agent to send messages to its current neighbors and receive the corresponding messages before the next adaptive exchange. If \(x^R\) is the distributed output after \(R\in\mathbb N_0\) rounds, define \[R(\varepsilon):=\inf\left\{R\in\mathbb N_0:\mathcal A_\varepsilon(x^R)\text{ holds}\right\}.\] If the set is empty, \(R(\varepsilon):=+\infty\). Local computations between two exchanges do not increase this count, whereas \(k\) sequential consensus or gossip exchanges count as \(k\) rounds.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Communication-round complexity is the minimum number of sequential neighbor-exchange stages needed to satisfy a declared accuracy and success criterion, regardless of intervening local computation.
assumptions_latex: Communication is organized into synchronous neighbor-exchange rounds.
The graph model and accuracy predicate \(\mathcal A_\varepsilon\) are fixed.
The predicate includes the selected deterministic, expected, or high-probability success convention.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(R(\varepsilon)\) is the minimum number of sequential communication rounds after which \(\mathcal A_\varepsilon(x^R)\) holds, or \(+\infty\) if no such round exists.

notation.meaning: Distributed output after R communication rounds.
Accuracy predicate including the chosen success convention.

children.title: Message-Bit Communication Complexity Taxonomy
children.top_down_role: Communication volume measured by messages, coordinates, or encoded bits.

children.title: Message-Count Complexity
children.top_down_role: Communication cost measured through transmitted message events.

assumptions_latex: \(A\) has a specified termination rule and accuracy predicate \(P_\varepsilon\).
\(\mathcal I\) is the declared instance class, and \(\Omega_A(I)\) is the declared class of admissible executions on \(I\).

notation.meaning: Admissible execution transcript of algorithm A on instance I under execution choice omega.
Number of completed edgewise message transmissions in transcript tau.
Declared set of admissible executions of A on instance I.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Counts completed point-to-point message transmissions needed to reach a prescribed accuracy.

source_refs.locator: 1.3 Communication Aspects of Parallel and Distributed Systems p. 27
source_refs.source_title: Parallel and Distributed Computation: Numerical Methods

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For an admissible execution transcript \(\tau\), define \[M(\tau)=\sum_{e\in\tau}\mathbf{1}\{e\text{ is a completed message transmission}\}.\] For a distributed algorithm \(A\), instance class \(\mathcal I\), accuracy predicate \(P_\varepsilon(x;I)\), and admissible-execution set \(\Omega_A(I)\), define \[M_A(\varepsilon;\mathcal I)=\sup_{I\in\mathcal I,\,\omega\in\Omega_A(I)}M(\tau_A(I,\varepsilon;\omega)).\] Here \(\tau_A(I,\varepsilon;\omega)\) ends when an output satisfying \(P_\varepsilon\) is first produced. Its message count is \(+\infty\) if no such output is produced. Each multicast is counted once per receiving edge, and retransmissions are counted separately.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Message-count complexity is the worst-case number of completed edgewise message transmissions over all declared instances and admissible executions before an accuracy-qualified output is produced; an unsuccessful execution has infinite count.

children.title: Bit-Communication Complexity
children.top_down_role: Communication cost measured through encoded bit volume.

assumptions_latex: \(\ell(e)\) is fixed by a declared binary encoding and accounting convention.
\(\mathcal I\) and each admissible-execution set \(\Omega_A(I)\) are specified.

notation.meaning: Charged encoded length of communication event e in bits.
Declared set of admissible executions of A on instance I.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Counts encoded payload and protocol bits transmitted before attaining accuracy.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\ell(e)\in\mathbb N_0\) be the complete encoded length, in bits, of communication event \(e\), including every header charged by the declared model. For a transcript \(\tau\), define \[B(\tau)=\sum_{e\in\tau}\ell(e).\] For algorithm \(A\), instance class \(\mathcal I\), and admissible-execution set \(\Omega_A(I)\), define \[B_A(\varepsilon;\mathcal I)=\sup_{I\in\mathcal I,\,\omega\in\Omega_A(I)}B(\tau_A(I,\varepsilon;\omega)).\] The transcript ends when an output satisfying the declared \(\varepsilon\)-accuracy predicate is first produced, and an execution that produces no such output has value \(+\infty\). Preshared random seeds cost zero only when the declared model makes them free; otherwise their communicated descriptions contribute to \(B\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Bit-communication complexity is the worst-case total charged binary length over all declared instances and admissible executions before an accuracy-qualified output is produced; an unsuccessful execution has infinite cost.

children.title: Coordinate-Transmission Volume
children.top_down_role: Communication cost measured through transmitted scalar coordinates.

knowledge_statements.title: Coordinate-Transmission Volume
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Counts transmitted scalar coordinates independently of their bit precision.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Suppose each communication event \(e\) carries an encoded vector whose decoded payload exposes a set \(S_e\subseteq\{1,\ldots,d_e\}\) of transmitted scalar coordinates. Define the coordinate-transmission volume of transcript \(\tau\) by \[V_{\mathrm{coord}}(\tau)=\sum_{e\in\tau}|S_e|.\] The worst-case volume for algorithm \(A\) is \[V_A(\varepsilon;\mathcal I)=\sup_{I\in\mathcal I}V_{\mathrm{coord}}(\tau_A(I,\varepsilon)).\] A coordinate sent to several neighbors is charged once per receiving edge; metadata and coordinate precision are excluded and must instead be charged by a bit measure.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Coordinate volume is the worst-case total number of scalar entries carried across receiving edges, irrespective of their encoding precision.

knowledge_statements.title: Encoding-Precision Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Classifies communication models by how message precision may depend on target accuracy.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a family of encoders \(Q_\varepsilon\), let \(b(\varepsilon)=\sup_z\ell(Q_\varepsilon(z))\) over admissible payloads \(z\). The family has fixed precision if \(\sup_{0<\varepsilon\leq\varepsilon_0}b(\varepsilon)<\infty\); it has accuracy-dependent finite precision if every \(b(\varepsilon)<\infty\) but \(\sup_{0<\varepsilon\leq\varepsilon_0}b(\varepsilon)=\infty\); and it is an exact-real regime if payloads are ideal real words whose charged length is not represented by finite \(b(\varepsilon)\). Bit-complexity comparisons are meaningful only within the same regime and encoding convention.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Precision is fixed, accuracy-dependent finite, or ideal exact-real according to whether the maximum encoded payload length stays bounded as accuracy tightens.

children.title: Parallel-Time Complexity
children.top_down_role: Critical-path cost under concurrent local computation.

knowledge_statements.title: Parallel-Time Complexity
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Measures critical-path depth in an idealized parallel execution DAG.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Represent an execution by a directed acyclic graph \(D_\tau=(V_\tau,E_\tau)\), where vertices are primitive computation or communication operations, edges encode causal precedence, and \(w(v)\geq0\) is the charged duration of operation \(v\). Its parallel time is the weighted span \[T_\infty(\tau)=\max_{P\in\mathcal P(D_\tau)}\sum_{v\in P}w(v).\] For algorithm \(A\), define \[T_A^\infty(\varepsilon;\mathcal I)=\sup_{I\in\mathcal I}T_\infty(\tau_A(I,\varepsilon)).\] With unit operation weights this equals the maximum number of causally sequential operations, not total work.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Parallel-time complexity is the worst-case weighted critical-path length of the execution, assuming causally independent operations can run concurrently.
assumptions_latex: \(D_\tau\) is acyclic and contains every charged operation preceding the output.
Each operation has a nonnegative model weight \(w(v)\).

children.title: Communication-Latency Bottlenecks

assumptions_latex: Every causal path leading to a valid output contains at least one chain \(C\in\mathcal C_\varepsilon\).

Lower bound on the elapsed duration of communication operation v.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(D_\tau\) be the causal graph of a timed execution \(\tau\), and let \(\lambda(v)\geq0\) be a lower bound on the actual elapsed duration of each communication operation \(v\). Let \(\mathcal C_\varepsilon\) be a family of directed communication chains such that every causal path producing an \(\varepsilon\)-valid output contains at least one \(C\in\mathcal C_\varepsilon\). Because causally ordered operations cannot overlap, \[T_{\mathrm{wall}}(\tau)\geq\min_{C\in\mathcal C_\varepsilon}\sum_{v\in C}\lambda(v).\] In particular, if every such chain contains at least \(R_\varepsilon\) causally sequential communication operations and \(\lambda(v)\geq\lambda_{\min}\) for each of them, then \[T_{\mathrm{wall}}(\tau)\geq R_\varepsilon\lambda_{\min}.\] Concurrent local computation cannot reduce this causal latency term.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: When every valid-output causal path contains an unavoidable communication chain, elapsed time is at least the smallest accumulated duration lower bound among those chains; in particular, R sequential communications of latency at least lambda_min require at least R times lambda_min.
knowledge_statements.title: Communication-Latency Bottlenecks

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Consider barriers \(k=1,\ldots,K\) with finite participant sets \(W_k\). Let \(a_{ik}\) be worker \(i\)'s arrival time, let \(r_k\geq\max_{i\in W_k}a_{ik}\) be the release time, and let \(s_k\geq0\) be a separately charged service cost not already included in the waiting intervals. Define aggregate worker-time synchronization overhead by \[H_{\mathrm{sync}}^{\mathrm{agg}}(\tau)=\sum_{k=1}^{K}\left(\sum_{i\in W_k}(r_k-a_{ik})+s_k\right).\] A distinct per-barrier maximum-wait measure is \[H_{\mathrm{sync}}^{\max}(\tau)=\sum_{k=1}^{K}\left(\max_{i\in W_k}(r_k-a_{ik})+s_k\right).\] Neither quantity is, without additional execution-path assumptions, identical to the synchronization contribution on the global critical path. The selected convention must accompany every reported value.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Synchronization overhead may be measured either as total worker waiting plus separately charged barrier service or as the sum of maximum individual waiting at each barrier; neither convention alone determines global critical-path overhead.

children.title: Joint Oracle–Network Lower Bounds

knowledge_statements.title: Joint Oracle–Network Lower Bounds
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Abstract joint lower bound for local oracle calls and sequential network rounds.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(q_A(I)\) be the maximum number of local oracle calls made by any processor and \(R_A(I)\) the number of sequential communication rounds. Suppose a common hard family \(\mathcal H\) satisfies: every algorithm producing an \(\varepsilon\)-valid output on all \(I\in\mathcal H\) has some instance \(I_q\) with \(q_A(I_q)\geq Q_\varepsilon\), and some possibly different instance \(I_R\) with \(R_A(I_R)\geq R_\varepsilon\). Then its worst-case resource vector obeys \[\left(\sup_{I\in\mathcal H}q_A(I),\sup_{I\in\mathcal H}R_A(I)\right)\succeq(Q_\varepsilon,R_\varepsilon).\] A scalar time lower bound additionally requires explicit oracle and network timing rules.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: On a common hard family, worst-case local-oracle work and communication depth must simultaneously dominate their respective lower bounds.
assumptions_latex: \(\mathcal H\) is a common hard instance family for both resource arguments.
Every admissible algorithm must return an \(\varepsilon\)-valid output on every \(I\in\mathcal H\).

notation.meaning: Maximum local-oracle calls at any processor on instance I.
Sequential communication rounds on instance I.

Moreover, the displayed vector inequality merely combines two marginal worst-case bounds that may be witnessed by different instances; it does not establish a per-instance oracle-network tradeoff or a genuinely joint lower bound. A source and a precise joint lower-bound formulation are required.

children.title: Communication-Round Lower Bounds
children.top_down_role: Minimum sequential communication depth for distributed accuracy.

knowledge_statements.title: Communication-Round Lower Bounds
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Locality-based lower bound on sequential synchronous communication depth.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: In a synchronous graph \(G=(V,E)\), after \(R\) neighbor-to-neighbor communication rounds, the state of node \(v\) depends only on initial data and oracle responses within the closed radius-\(R\) neighborhood \(N_R[v]\). Hence, if two admissible instances \(I_0,I_1\) agree on \(N_R[v]\) but their sets of \(\varepsilon\)-valid outputs at \(v\), denoted \(S_\varepsilon(I_0,v)\) and \(S_\varepsilon(I_1,v)\), are disjoint, no deterministic algorithm terminating at \(v\) within \(R\) rounds is correct on both. Consequently its worst-case round complexity exceeds \(R\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: If radius-R information cannot distinguish two instances requiring incompatible outputs, every correct deterministic algorithm needs more than R communication rounds.
assumptions_latex: Communication in each synchronous round traverses at most one edge.
\(I_0\) and \(I_1\) induce identical observations within \(N_R[v]\).
\(S_\varepsilon(I_0,v)\cap S_\varepsilon(I_1,v)=\varnothing\).

notation.meaning: Closed graph neighborhood of radius R around node v.
Set of epsilon-valid outputs permitted at node v for instance I.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The deterministic synchronous locality argument is mathematically plausible and its complexity-bound role fits the container, but no source with a theorem, section, or page locator is supplied. A formal distributed-locality or communication-round lower-bound reference is required before accepting the claim.

children.title: Bit-Communication Lower Bounds
children.top_down_role: Information limits under finite-precision messages.

knowledge_statements.title: Bit-Communication Lower Bounds
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Transcript-counting lower bound for deterministic finite-bit protocols.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(I_1,\ldots,I_M\) be admissible instances whose required \(\varepsilon\)-valid decision outputs are pairwise disjoint. Consider a deterministic distributed protocol whose decision is a function of a binary communication transcript and which is correct on every \(I_j\). The transcripts produced by these instances must be pairwise distinct. If every transcript has length at most \(B\), at most \(2^{B+1}-1\) variable-length binary transcripts are available; therefore \[B\geq\left\lceil\log_2(M+1)\right\rceil-1.\] Under a fixed-length transcript convention the sharper bound is \(B\geq\lceil\log_2 M\rceil\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Distinguishing M instances with incompatible valid outputs requires enough communicated bits to encode at least M distinct transcripts.
assumptions_latex: The protocol is deterministic and correct on each \(I_j\).
The \(\varepsilon\)-valid decision-output sets of \(I_1,\ldots,I_M\) are pairwise disjoint.
Communication transcripts are binary strings of maximum length \(B\).

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The variable-length transcript counting calculation is internally consistent for deterministic binary transcripts, and the fixed-length specialization is correctly distinguished. However, no communication-complexity source is supplied, so the transcript model and lower bound lack required evidence.

children.title: Topology-Dependent Lower Bounds
children.top_down_role: Hardness indexed by graph diameter or spectral conditioning.

knowledge_statements.title: Topology-Dependent Lower Bounds
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Diameter-form information-propagation lower bound on a fixed communication graph.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(G=(V,E)\) contain nodes \(u,v\) at graph distance \(D\). Suppose two admissible instances differ only in data held at \(u\), while their \(\varepsilon\)-valid output sets at \(v\) are disjoint. In the synchronous neighbor-communication model, the state of \(v\) is identical on the two instances for every round \(R<D\), because information from \(u\) cannot yet reach \(v\). Thus no deterministic algorithm required to output correctly at \(v\) can terminate in fewer than \(D\) rounds on both instances, and its worst-case communication-round complexity satisfies \[R_A(\varepsilon;G)\geq D.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: When distant data changes the required output, information propagation forces at least the corresponding graph distance in communication rounds.
assumptions_latex: Each synchronous communication round moves information across at most one edge of \(G\).
The two instances differ only at node \(u\).
Their \(\varepsilon\)-valid output sets at node \(v\) are disjoint.

notation.meaning: Graph distance between the data node u and decision node v.
Worst-case communication rounds on graph G.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The diameter-form propagation argument is plausible for deterministic synchronous neighbor communication, but it has no cited source. It also covers only distance or diameter dependence, not the spectral-conditioning form named in the node role; that narrower scope is acceptable only if explicitly retained and supported by a formal topology-dependent lower-bound reference.

children.title: Accelerated Distributed Methods
children.top_down_role: Distributed methods using acceleration mechanisms for optimization or mixing.

assumptions_latex: \(W=W^\top\), \(W\mathbf 1=\mathbf 1\), and every nonconsensus eigenvalue of \(W\) lies in \([a,b]\subset(-1,1)\).
Agents can multiply a stacked vector by \(W\) in one communication round.

notation.meaning: Symmetric mixing matrix and consensus projector
Chebyshev polynomial of the first kind

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Chebyshev-accelerated communication primitive; coupling it to optimization requires a method-specific analysis.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Set \(c=(a+b)/2\), \(r=(b-a)/2\), and \[p_t(\lambda)=\frac{T_t((\lambda-c)/r)}{T_t((1-c)/r)}.\] Given \(X\), compute \(Y_t=p_t(W)X\) through the three-term Chebyshev recurrence, requiring \(t\) multiplications by \(W\), and output \(Y_t\). Since \(p_t(1)=1\), the average is preserved: \(JY_t=JX\). Spectral calculus gives \[\|Y_t-JX\|_F\le \max_{\lambda\in[a,b]}|p_t(\lambda)|\,\|X-JX\|_F.\] The minimax polynomial suppresses disagreement faster than unaccelerated powers of \(W\) when the nonconsensus spectrum approaches \(1\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Chebyshev filtering preserves the network average while reducing disagreement with a minimax degree-t polynomial, using t communication rounds.
knowledge_statements.title: Accelerated Distributed Methods

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The record describes a Chebyshev consensus-filtering primitive, not an accelerated distributed optimization method shown to belong to the enclosing lower-bound-matching algorithm family. It supplies neither an optimization coupling nor a matching complexity guarantee, and it has no citation.

children.title: Oracle–Network Tradeoffs

assumptions_latex: A distributed problem class, local-oracle model, communication model, and accuracy criterion are fixed.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\mathcal F_\varepsilon=\{(q,c):\exists A,\ (Q_{\rm or}(A),Q_{\rm com}(A))\preceq(q,c)\}\), with the tradeoff given by its Pareto-minimal boundary.

notation.meaning: Worst-case local-oracle and communication complexities of algorithm A

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Model-independent Pareto representation; numerical tradeoff curves require a specified function class and network oracle.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For each admissible algorithm \(A\), let \(Q_{\rm or}(A,\varepsilon)\) count local-oracle calls and let \(Q_{\rm com}(A,\varepsilon)\) count communication rounds needed to meet the prescribed accuracy. The attainable region is \[\mathcal F_\varepsilon=\bigl\{(q,c)\in\mathbb N^2:\exists A,\ Q_{\rm or}(A,\varepsilon)\le q,\ Q_{\rm com}(A,\varepsilon)\le c\bigr\}.\] It is upward closed. Its Pareto-minimal elements constitute the oracle-network tradeoff: improving one coordinate without worsening the other is impossible within the model. A lower-bound region \(\mathcal L_\varepsilon\) is matched when the attainable Pareto boundary agrees with its boundary up to the declared approximation factors.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Oracle-network tradeoffs are the Pareto boundary of attainable pairs of local-oracle calls and communication rounds at a fixed accuracy.

assumptions_latex: The parameter space \(\Theta\) is partitioned into regimes \(\Theta_1,\ldots,\Theta_K\).
Each regime has resource lower bounds \(L_{k,r}(\theta,\varepsilon)\) for resources \(r\) in a fixed finite set \(\mathcal R\).

notation.meaning: Parameter regimes, such as condition-number or network-gap ranges
Complexity and lower bound for resource r in regime k

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Formal uniformity condition for claims whose optimal algorithm or dominant resource changes across parameter ranges.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A family \(\{A_k\}_{k=1}^K\) is regime-specifically optimal for the partition \(\Theta=\bigcup_{k=1}^K\Theta_k\) if, for every counted resource \(r\in\mathcal R\), there are constants \(C_{k,r}>0\) and declared polylogarithmic factors \(\ell_{k,r}\) such that \[Q_{k,r}(\theta,\varepsilon)\le C_{k,r}L_{k,r}(\theta,\varepsilon)\ell_{k,r}(\theta,\varepsilon)\qquad\text{for all }\theta\in\Theta_k.\] The quantifier is uniform within each regime. Consequently, pointwise tuning at one parameter value, or matching only the dominant resource while violating another resource lower bound, is insufficient for regime-specific optimality.

The stepsize satisfies \(\eta>0\), the point satisfies \(x\in\operatorname{dom}r\), and the proximal map of \(r\) is exactly evaluable.
The stationarity tolerance satisfies \(\varepsilon\ge0\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Proximal-gradient residual certificate for unconstrained smooth-plus-convex composite optimization.

source_refs.locator: 3 Primal-dual splitting methods p. 69
source_refs.source_title: Large-Scale Convex Optimization: Algorithms & Analyses via Monotone Operators

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(F=f+r\) and \(\eta>0\), define \[G_\eta(x)=\frac1\eta\left(x-\operatorname{prox}_{\eta r}(x-\eta\nabla f(x))\right).\] A point \(x\in\operatorname{dom}r\), together with the evaluated gradient and proximal point, is an \(\varepsilon\)-composite-stationarity certificate if \[\|G_\eta(x)\|_2\le\varepsilon.\] The exact-zero relation is \[G_\eta(x)=0\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad0\in\nabla f(x)+\partial r(x).\] For a distributed finite sum, the gradient in the mapping must be the aggregated gradient evaluated at the reported common point.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A small proximal-gradient mapping certifies approximate composite stationarity, and a zero mapping is equivalent to the composite first-order condition.
knowledge_statements.title: Composite Stationarity Certificates

source_witnesses.locator: 3 Primal-dual splitting methods p. 69
source_witnesses.source_title: Large-Scale Convex Optimization: Algorithms & Analyses via Monotone Operators

children.title: Certificate-Mismatch Boundaries
children.top_down_role: Regimes where objective accuracy fails to represent stationarity quality.

assumptions_latex: Stationarity is measured only by \(|f'(x)|\).
No convexity, error bound, or Polyak–Łojasiewicz inequality is assumed.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Concrete boundary showing that smooth stationarity alone does not certify global objective accuracy.

source_refs.locator: 1.1 First-order methods in the modern era p. 1
source_refs.source_title: Large-Scale Convex Optimization: Algorithms & Analyses via Monotone Operators

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(f:\mathbb R\to\mathbb R\) be \(f(x)=\arctan x\), so \(f'(x)=1/(1+x^2)\) and \(f^*=\inf_x f(x)=-\pi/2\). For \(x_k=k\), \[|f'(x_k)|=\frac1{1+k^2}\longrightarrow0,\qquad f(x_k)-f^*=\arctan(k)+\frac\pi2\longrightarrow\pi.\] Thus arbitrarily accurate smooth-stationarity certificates can coexist with an objective gap bounded away from zero. Converting stationarity into objective accuracy therefore requires additional structure, such as convexity together with suitable growth information, an error bound, or a Polyak–Łojasiewicz inequality.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Without additional geometry, a vanishing gradient need not imply a small objective gap; arctangent supplies a concrete smooth counterexample.
knowledge_statements.title: Certificate-Mismatch Boundaries

source_witnesses.locator: 1.1 First-order methods in the modern era p. 1
source_witnesses.source_title: Large-Scale Convex Optimization: Algorithms & Analyses via Monotone Operators

children.title: Consensus-Residual Certificates
children.top_down_role: Residual measures for deviation from network agreement.

assumptions_latex: \(m,d\in\mathbb N\) are positive integers, and \(X=[x_1^\top;\ldots;x_m^\top]\in\mathbb R^{m\times d}\) stacks the agent states.
\(J=m^{-1}\mathbf1\mathbf1^\top\) is the orthogonal projector onto the consensus subspace.
The agreement tolerance satisfies \(\varepsilon\ge0\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Euclidean network-agreement certificate using orthogonal distance to the consensus subspace.

source_refs.locator: 11.2 Decentralized optimization with graph consensus p. 234

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For positive integers \(m,d\) and stacked states \(X=[x_1^\top;\ldots;x_m^\top]\in\mathbb R^{m\times d}\), define \[R_{\rm con}(X)=(I-J)X,\qquad J=\frac1m\mathbf1\mathbf1^\top.\] An \(\varepsilon\)-consensus-residual certificate satisfies \[\|R_{\rm con}(X)\|_F\le\varepsilon.\] The residual obeys \[\|R_{\rm con}(X)\|_F^2=\sum_{i=1}^m\|x_i-\bar x\|_2^2,\qquad R_{\rm con}(X)=0\Longleftrightarrow x_1=\cdots=x_m.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The distance of stacked agent states from the consensus subspace certifies aggregate disagreement and vanishes exactly at consensus.
knowledge_statements.title: Consensus-Residual Certificates

children.title: Disagreement-Energy Certificates
children.top_down_role: Aggregate measures of dispersion across agent states.

assumptions_latex: \(G=(V,E,w)\) is a connected undirected weighted graph with \(V=\{1,\ldots,m\}\), nonnegative symmetric weights \(w_{ij}=w_{ji}\), and Laplacian \(L\).
\(d\in\mathbb N\) is positive, and \(X=[x_1^\top;\ldots;x_m^\top]\in\mathbb R^{m\times d}\) stacks the vertex states.
The energy tolerance satisfies \(\varepsilon\ge0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\mathcal E_G(X)=\operatorname{tr}(X^\top L X)=\frac12\sum_{i,j=1}^m w_{ij}\|x_i-x_j\|_2^2\), with \(\mathcal E_G(X)=0\Longleftrightarrow x_1=\cdots=x_m\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Laplacian quadratic-form certificate for agreement over a connected undirected weighted network.

source_refs.locator: 11.2 Decentralized optimization with graph consensus p. 234
source_refs.source_title: Large-Scale Convex Optimization: Algorithms & Analyses via Monotone Operators

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a connected undirected weighted graph \(G=(V,E,w)\) with \(V=\{1,\ldots,m\}\), symmetric nonnegative weights \((w_{ij})\), Laplacian \(L\), and stacked states \(X=[x_1^\top;\ldots;x_m^\top]\), define \[\mathcal E_G(X)=\operatorname{tr}(X^\top L X)=\frac12\sum_{i=1}^m\sum_{j=1}^m w_{ij}\|x_i-x_j\|_2^2.\] An \(\varepsilon\)-disagreement-energy certificate satisfies \[\mathcal E_G(X)\le\varepsilon^2.\] For a connected graph, the exact-zero relation is \[\mathcal E_G(X)=0\Longleftrightarrow x_1=\cdots=x_m.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The Laplacian quadratic form equals weighted edge disagreement and, on a connected graph, vanishes exactly when every agent agrees.
knowledge_statements.title: Disagreement-Energy Certificates

source_witnesses.locator: 11.2 Decentralized optimization with graph consensus p. 234

children.title: Pairwise-Discrepancy Certificates
children.top_down_role: Agreement measures formed from neighboring or selected agent pairs.

assumptions_latex: \(G=(V,E)\) is a connected undirected graph with finite vertex set \(V\).
For a positive integer \(d\), every vertex \(i\in V\) holds a state \(x_i\in\mathbb R^d\), and every edge can report the norm of its endpoint-state difference.
The discrepancy tolerance satisfies \(\varepsilon\ge0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\delta_E(X)\le\varepsilon\Longrightarrow\|x_u-x_v\|_2\le d_G(u,v)\varepsilon\le D\varepsilon\) for all \(u,v\in V\), with \(\delta_E(X)=0\Longleftrightarrow x_u=x_v\) for all \(u,v\in V\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Edgewise maximum-norm agreement certificate on a finite connected undirected graph.

source_refs.locator: 11.2 Decentralized optimization with graph consensus p. 234
source_refs.source_title: Large-Scale Convex Optimization: Algorithms & Analyses via Monotone Operators

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a finite connected undirected graph \(G=(V,E)\) and states \(x_i\in\mathbb R^d\), define \[\delta_E(X)=\max_{\{i,j\}\in E}\|x_i-x_j\|_2.\] An \(\varepsilon\)-pairwise-discrepancy certificate satisfies \[\delta_E(X)\le\varepsilon.\] For all vertices \(u,v\in V\), it guarantees \[\|x_u-x_v\|_2\le d_G(u,v)\varepsilon\le D\varepsilon,\] where \(d_G\) is shortest-path distance and \(D\) is the graph diameter. Its exact-zero relation is \[\delta_E(X)=0\Longleftrightarrow x_u=x_v\quad\text{for all }u,v\in V.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: If every edge discrepancy is at most epsilon, every pairwise discrepancy is at most graph diameter times epsilon; zero edge discrepancy is global consensus on a connected graph.
knowledge_statements.title: Pairwise-Discrepancy Certificates

source_witnesses.locator: 11.2 Decentralized optimization with graph consensus p. 234
source_witnesses.source_title: Large-Scale Convex Optimization: Algorithms & Analyses via Monotone Operators

children.title: Local-to-Global Agreement Relations
children.top_down_role: Connections between locally observable discrepancies and global agreement.

assumptions_latex: \(G=(V,E,w)\) is a connected undirected weighted graph with \(V=\{1,\ldots,m\}\), Laplacian \(L\), and spectral gap \(\lambda_2(L)>0\).
\(d\in\mathbb N\) is positive, \(X=[x_1^\top;\ldots;x_m^\top]\in\mathbb R^{m\times d}\), and \(J=m^{-1}\mathbf1\mathbf1^\top\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Spectral and variance relations converting local graph disagreement into global consensus and all-pairs bounds.

source_refs.locator: 11.2 Decentralized optimization with graph consensus p. 234
source_refs.source_title: Large-Scale Convex Optimization: Algorithms & Analyses via Monotone Operators

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(G=(V,E,w)\) be a connected undirected weighted graph with \(V=\{1,\ldots,m\}\), Laplacian \(L\), and \(\lambda_2(L)>0\). For \(X=[x_1^\top;\ldots;x_m^\top]\in\mathbb R^{m\times d}\) and \(J=m^{-1}\mathbf1\mathbf1^\top\), the local-to-global agreement relations are \[\lambda_2(L)\|(I-J)X\|_F^2\le\operatorname{tr}(X^\top L X),\qquad \sum_{1\le i<j\le m}\|x_i-x_j\|_2^2=m\|(I-J)X\|_F^2.\] In particular, \[\operatorname{tr}(X^\top L X)\le\eta\Longrightarrow\|(I-J)X\|_F\le\sqrt{\eta/\lambda_2(L)}\] for every \(\eta\ge0\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The graph spectral gap converts disagreement energy into distance from consensus, while the variance identity converts consensus residual into total pairwise discrepancy.
knowledge_statements.title: Local-to-Global Agreement Relations

children.title: Coupling-Feasibility Certificates
children.top_down_role: Residual families for distributed constraint satisfaction.

assumptions_latex: \(X_i\subseteq\mathbb R^{d_i}\) is nonempty and closed for every \(i\).
\(A_i:\mathbb R^{d_i}\to\mathbb R^p\) is linear for every \(i\).
The distance and residual norm are evaluated using fixed norms on the relevant finite-dimensional spaces.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{dist}(x_i,X_i)\le\varepsilon_i\) for every \(i\) and \(\|\sum_{i=1}^mA_ix_i-b\|\le\varepsilon_c\) certify feasibility to the stated tolerances; zero tolerances certify exact feasibility.

notation.meaning: distance from a point to a set

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Residual certificate for affine coupling constraints in a separable distributed problem.

source_refs.locator: 11.1 Distributed optimization with centralized consensus p. 227
source_refs.source_title: Large-Scale Convex Optimization: Algorithms & Analyses via Monotone Operators

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(m\ge1\), let \(x_i\in\mathbb R^{d_i}\) be the vector reported by agent \(i\), and let the required local and coupling constraints be \(x_i\in X_i\) and \(\sum_{i=1}^mA_ix_i=b\), where \(b\in\mathbb R^p\). For tolerances \(\varepsilon_i\ge0\) and \(\varepsilon_c\ge0\), the tuple \((x_1,\ldots,x_m)\) has a coupling-feasibility certificate when
\[\operatorname{dist}(x_i,X_i)\le\varepsilon_i\quad(i=1,\ldots,m),\qquad \left\|\sum_{i=1}^mA_ix_i-b\right\|\le\varepsilon_c.\]
These residual inequalities certify exact feasibility when every tolerance is zero and feasibility to the displayed tolerances otherwise.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Local set-distance residuals and the aggregate affine-coupling residual certify how closely the reported distributed variables satisfy all local and coupling constraints.
knowledge_statements.title: Coupling-Feasibility Certificates

source_witnesses.locator: 11.1 Distributed optimization with centralized consensus p. 227
source_witnesses.source_title: Large-Scale Convex Optimization: Algorithms & Analyses via Monotone Operators

children.title: Primal-Dual Gap Certificates
children.top_down_role: Distributed duality and saddle-progress measures.

assumptions_latex: For every \(i\), \(X_i\subseteq\mathbb R^{d_i}\) is nonempty, closed, and convex, and \(f_i:\mathbb R^{d_i}\to\mathbb R\cup\{+\infty\}\) is proper and convex.
The primal optimal value \(P^\star\) is finite.
The reported \(x\) is primal feasible, and the selected \(y\) satisfies \(D(y)\in\mathbb R\).
The value \(D(y)\) is available to the certificate evaluator.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: If \(G(x,y)\le\varepsilon\), then \(0\le P(x)-P^\star\le G(x,y)\le\varepsilon\) and \(0\le P^\star-D(y)\le G(x,y)\le\varepsilon\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Weak-duality certificate for a convex distributed primal-dual pair.

source_refs.locator: 3 Primal-dual splitting methods p. 69
source_refs.source_title: Large-Scale Convex Optimization: Algorithms & Analyses via Monotone Operators

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(m\ge1\), let \(x=(x_1,ldots,x_m)\), and define \(P(x)=\sum_{i=1}^mf_i(x_i)\) subject to \(x_i\in X_i\) and \(Ax=\sum_{i=1}^mA_ix_i=b\), where \(A_i:\mathbb R^{d_i}\to\mathbb R^p\) is linear and \(b\in\mathbb R^p\). For \(y\in\mathbb R^p\), define
\[D(y)=\inf_{z_i\in X_i}\left\{\sum_{i=1}^mf_i(z_i)+\left\langle y,\sum_{i=1}^mA_iz_i-b\right\rangle\right\}.\]
For a primal-feasible \(x\) and a dual vector \(y\) for which \(D(y)\) is finite and available, the gap \(G(x,y)=P(x)-D(y)\) is nonnegative. For any \(\varepsilon\ge0\), the inequality \(G(x,y)\le\varepsilon\) certifies both \(P(x)-P^\star\le\varepsilon\) and \(P^\star-D(y)\le\varepsilon\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A feasible primal point and a dual point with a finite, evaluable dual value yield a nonnegative gap; a gap at most epsilon certifies both primal suboptimality and dual lower-bound error at most epsilon.
knowledge_statements.title: Primal-Dual Gap Certificates

source_witnesses.locator: 3 Primal-dual splitting methods p. 69
source_witnesses.source_title: Large-Scale Convex Optimization: Algorithms & Analyses via Monotone Operators

children.title: Locally Checkable Stopping Certificates
children.top_down_role: Termination evidence available without complete global state.

knowledge_statements.title: Locally Checkable Stopping Certificates
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Neighbor-local termination certificate for consensus and stationarity residuals.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(G=(V,E)\) be an undirected communication graph, and let agent \(i\) know \(x_i\), \(g_i\in\partial f_i(x_i)\), and its neighbors' iterates. A locally checkable stopping certificate at tolerances \((\varepsilon_c,\varepsilon_s)\) consists of local inequalities
\[\max_{j:\{i,j\}\in E}\|x_i-x_j\|\le\varepsilon_c,\qquad \left\|g_i+\sum_{j:\{i,j\}\in E}(\lambda_{ij}-\lambda_{ji})\right\|\le\varepsilon_s\]
for every agent, using exchanged edge multipliers \(\lambda_{ij}\). Acceptance by every agent certifies the displayed edge-consensus and local KKT-stationarity residual bounds without collecting the complete global state.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Each agent checks neighbor disagreement and its local KKT residual; unanimous acceptance certifies bounded global edge disagreement and componentwise stationarity.
assumptions_latex: \(G=(V,E)\) is connected and undirected.
Each \(f_i\) is proper and convex.
Adjacent agents can authenticate the iterates and edge multipliers used in their checks.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: All edge disagreements are at most \(\varepsilon_c\), and every local KKT-stationarity residual is at most \(\varepsilon_s\).

notation.meaning: directed copy of an edge multiplier

review_flags: A precise authoritative source for this particular locally checkable KKT certificate is required.
standard_field_rationale: neighbor-wise consensus and componentwise KKT residuals are standard distributed termination tests.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The certificate role fits the leaf, but no citation is supplied and the directed multiplier expression is not tied to a precisely oriented consensus constraint system or an edge-consistency condition. Those choices affect whether the displayed residual is a valid local KKT residual, so an authoritative source and exact formulation are required.

children.title: Cross-Device Federated Optimization
children.top_down_role: Large intermittent populations of resource-constrained clients.

knowledge_statements.title: Cross-Device Federated Optimization
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Federated objective with sampled participation from a large, intermittently available client population.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Cross-device federated optimization minimizes
\[F(w)=\sum_{i=1}^m p_iF_i(w),\qquad F_i(w)=\mathbb E_{\xi\sim P_i}[\ell(w;\xi)],\]
over a shared parameter \(w\in\mathbb R^d\), where the client population is large and each communication round accesses only an available subset \(S_t\subsetneq\{1,\ldots,m\}\). Client data remain local, participation may be intermittent, and the server update is computed from messages produced by clients in \(S_t\), rather than from simultaneous access to all local objectives or datasets.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A large population of intermittently available devices jointly minimizes a weighted objective through sampled client participation while retaining data locally.
assumptions_latex: All clients optimize a common parameter space \(\mathbb R^d\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The cross-device regime is characterized by the weighted federated objective and partial, availability-dependent client participation.
review_flags: No supplied locator directly supports the cross-device regime definition.
standard_field_rationale: sampled intermittent participation in a large client population is the conventional cross-device distinction.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The definition role fits the leaf, but no source with a locator supports the regime characterization. Requiring a strict subset in every round is stronger than the usual cross-device distinction and needs confirmation or correction from an authoritative federated-learning source.

knowledge_statements.title: Cross-Silo Federated Optimization
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Federated objective over a small set of persistent institutional clients.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Cross-silo federated optimization minimizes
\[F(w)=\sum_{i=1}^m p_iF_i(w),\qquad F_i(w)=\mathbb E_{\xi\sim P_i}[\ell(w;\xi)],\]
over a shared parameter \(w\in\mathbb R^d\), where the clients are a comparatively small, fixed collection of institutions. Each client maintains a local dataset and computational service, identities persist across rounds, and the protocol may schedule all clients or a known subset while exchanging model-derived messages instead of raw records.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A fixed, relatively small group of persistent institutions optimizes a weighted shared objective without pooling their raw datasets.
assumptions_latex: The institutional client set is fixed during the optimization horizon.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The cross-silo regime has persistent identified participants jointly optimizing \(F\) while retaining their local records.

notation.meaning: institution i's local population or empirical objective

children.title: Federation Alignment Taxonomy
children.top_down_role: Federation distinguished by sample, feature, and task alignment.

children.title: Horizontal Federation
children.top_down_role: Federation organized around aligned features with differing sample populations.

knowledge_statements.title: Horizontal Federation
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Federation aligned by feature schema but partitioned by observational units.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
A federation is horizontal when every client records the same feature-label schema \(\mathcal X\times\mathcal Y\), while clients hold distinct observational units. Formally, client \(i\) owns
\[D_i=\{(x_{ik},y_{ik}):k\in I_i\}\subseteq\mathcal X\times\mathcal Y,\]
with aligned coordinates across clients and typically disjoint identifier sets \(I_i\cap I_j=\varnothing\) for \(i\ne j\). Training minimizes an aggregate such as \(F(w)=\sum_i p_i|I_i|^{-1}\sum_{k\in I_i}\ell(w;x_{ik},y_{ik})\) without transferring the records in \(D_i\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Clients share the same feature and label schema but hold different observational units, so training aggregates objectives across row-partitioned data.
assumptions_latex: All clients use a common feature space \(\mathcal X\), label space \(\mathcal Y\), and model parameter \(w\).
Client record identifiers are aligned sufficiently to determine whether units overlap.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Horizontal federation represents a row-wise partition of a common-schema learning dataset.

notation.meaning: record identifiers held by client i

review_flags: No supplied locator supports the horizontal-federation taxonomy.
standard_field_rationale: common features with differing sample identities is the conventional horizontal partition.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The definition role fits this taxonomy leaf and the row-partition interpretation is standard, but no authoritative citation with a specific locator supports the exact definition, including the typical disjointness condition.

children.title: Vertical Federation
children.top_down_role: Federation organized around aligned entities with partitioned feature spaces.

knowledge_statements.title: Vertical Federation
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Federation aligned by entities but partitioned by feature coordinates.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
A federation is vertical when clients describe overlapping entities but hold different feature blocks. For a shared identifier set \(I\), client \(i\) holds \(x_k^{(i)}\in\mathcal X_i\) for entity \(k\in I\), and the complete covariate is
\[x_k=(x_k^{(1)},\ldots,x_k^{(m)})\in\mathcal X_1\times\cdots\times\mathcal X_m.\]
Labels may be held by one designated client. The parties jointly minimize a loss depending on the combined feature blocks while neither raw block nor entity-level records are centrally pooled.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Clients share entity identities but hold different feature columns, jointly evaluating a model whose loss depends on the combined feature blocks.
assumptions_latex: A privacy-preserving entity-alignment procedure identifies the common set \(I\).
Feature blocks have a specified common model and loss.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Vertical federation represents a column-wise feature partition over aligned entities.

notation.meaning: features of entity k held by client i

review_flags: No supplied locator supports the vertical-federation taxonomy.
standard_field_rationale: shared entities with differing feature blocks is the conventional vertical partition.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The definition role fits this taxonomy leaf and the feature-partition interpretation is standard, but no authoritative citation with a specific locator supports the stated entity-alignment and label-placement formulation.

children.title: Transfer Federation
children.top_down_role: Federation spanning limited alignment across samples, features, or tasks.

knowledge_statements.title: Transfer Federation
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Federation requiring transfer across mismatched sample and feature domains.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A federation is a transfer federation when participating clients have limited overlap in both observational units and feature spaces, so neither a common-schema horizontal partition nor an entity-aligned vertical partition applies. Client \(i\) has data from \(P_i\) on \(\mathcal X_i\times\mathcal Y_i\), and collaboration uses learned maps \(T_i:\mathcal X_i\to\mathcal Z\) or shared parameters to transfer information through a common representation space \(\mathcal Z\). The optimized objective couples client-specific prediction losses with an explicit cross-domain transfer or representation-alignment term.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Clients with mismatched samples and feature spaces collaborate through a shared representation or transfer term rather than direct row or column alignment.
assumptions_latex: At least two clients lack both complete entity alignment and a common feature schema.
A specified transfer map, shared representation, or cross-domain coupling relates their learning tasks.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Transfer federation couples otherwise nonaligned client domains through an explicit transferable representation or parameter relation.

notation.meaning: client-specific map into a shared representation

review_flags: Transfer-federation definitions vary, and no directly supporting locator was supplied.
The exact required transfer mechanism needs authoritative source confirmation.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The definition role fits the taxonomy leaf, but transfer-federation terminology is not uniform. No source supports the asserted requirement of learned maps, shared representations, or an explicit alignment term, so the mathematical scope cannot be validated reliably.

children.title: Decentralized Federated Optimization
children.top_down_role: Federated objectives optimized without a permanent central aggregator.

knowledge_statements.title: Decentralized Federated Optimization
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Consensus formulation of a federated objective without a permanent central server.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(G=(V,E)\) be a connected client communication graph. Decentralized federated optimization solves
\[\min_{w_1,\ldots,w_m}\ \sum_{i=1}^m p_iF_i(w_i)\quad\text{subject to}\quad w_i=w_j\ \text{for every }\{i,j\}\in E,\]
where client \(i\) evaluates \(F_i\) from its local data and exchanges model-derived messages only with graph neighbors. No permanent central aggregator computes the global update. Connectivity makes edge consensus equivalent to a common model \(w_1=\cdots=w_m\), recovering the weighted federated objective.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Clients optimize local objectives and enforce model consensus through peer-to-peer communication on a connected graph, without a permanent central aggregator.
assumptions_latex: \(G=(V,E)\) is connected and undirected.
\(p_i\ge0\) and \(\sum_i p_i=1\).
Each \(F_i\) is defined on a common parameter space.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Feasible points satisfy \(w_1=\cdots=w_m\), reducing the problem to \(\min_w\sum_i p_iF_i(w)\).

children.title: Statistical Heterogeneity
children.top_down_role: Differences among client data distributions and sampling populations.

knowledge_statements.title: Statistical Heterogeneity
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Client variability arising from unequal local data-generating distributions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let client \(i\) draw observations \(\xi\) from a probability distribution \(P_i\) on a common measurable sample space \((\Xi,\mathcal A)\). The federation has statistical heterogeneity when the family \(\{P_i\}_{i=1}^m\) is not constant, equivalently when there exist clients \(i\ne j\) and an event \(A\in\mathcal A\) such that \(P_i(A)\ne P_j(A)\). This may reflect differing covariate, label, conditional, or joint distributions, independently of unequal client sample counts.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Statistical heterogeneity occurs when at least two clients have different data-generating distributions, regardless of how many samples each client holds.
assumptions_latex: All \(P_i\) are probability measures on the same measurable space \((\Xi,\mathcal A)\).
review_flags: No supplied locator directly supports this federated statistical-heterogeneity definition.
standard_field_rationale: unequal client data distributions are the standard mathematical meaning.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The definition is precise and matches the statistical-heterogeneity leaf, but no citation with an inspectable locator is supplied. The standard-field rationale is not enough to establish the exact federated taxonomy statement for review acceptance.

children.title: Objective Heterogeneity
children.top_down_role: Differences among client risks, preferences, or local optimization targets.

knowledge_statements.title: Objective Heterogeneity
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Client variability measured by disagreement among local objective gradients.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let differentiable client objectives \(F_i:\mathbb R^d\to\mathbb R\) have weights \(p_i\ge0\), \(\sum_i p_i=1\), and let \(F(w)=\sum_i p_iF_i(w)\). Their objective heterogeneity at \(w\) is measured by
\[H(w)=\sum_{i=1}^m p_i\|\nabla F_i(w)-\nabla F(w)\|^2.\]
The objectives are heterogeneous on a domain \(W\subseteq\mathbb R^d\) when \(H(w)>0\) for some \(w\in W\); a uniform heterogeneity bound is \(H(w)\le B^2\) for every \(w\in W\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Objective heterogeneity is gradient disagreement between client objectives and their weighted aggregate; its weighted squared norm gives a pointwise quantitative measure.
assumptions_latex: Each \(F_i\) is differentiable on \(W\subseteq\mathbb R^d\).
\(p_i\ge0\) and \(\sum_i p_i=1\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(H(w)\ge0\), and \(H(w)=0\) exactly when every positive-weight client gradient equals \(\nabla F(w)\).
review_flags: Several inequivalent objective-heterogeneity measures exist, and no supporting locator was supplied.
The selected gradient-dissimilarity convention requires source confirmation.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The definition role fits the leaf, but objective heterogeneity has several inequivalent conventions. No source supports this particular weighted gradient-disagreement measure or the proposed uniform bound, so the selected mathematical version requires authoritative confirmation.

children.title: Client Sample-Weight Imbalance
children.top_down_role: Variation in client dataset sizes and their influence on the federated objective.

knowledge_statements.title: Client Sample-Weight Imbalance
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Unequal empirical-objective weights induced by unequal client sample sizes.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Suppose client \(i\) holds \(n_i\ge1\) observations and its empirical objective is \(F_i(w)=n_i^{-1}\sum_{k=1}^{n_i}\ell(w;\xi_{ik})\). Sample-proportional aggregation assigns
\[p_i=\frac{n_i}{N},\qquad N=\sum_{j=1}^m n_j,\qquad F(w)=\sum_{i=1}^m p_iF_i(w).\]
Client sample-weight imbalance occurs when the weights are nonuniform, equivalently when some \(n_i\ne n_j\). It may be summarized by \(R=n_{\max}/n_{\min}\ge1\), with exact balance precisely when \(R=1\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Unequal client sample counts create unequal sample-proportional objective weights; the largest-to-smallest count ratio quantifies the imbalance.
assumptions_latex: There are finitely many clients and every sample count satisfies \(n_i\ge1\).
The aggregate empirical risk weights every observation equally.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Sample-weight imbalance holds exactly when \((p_1,\ldots,p_m)\ne(1/m,\ldots,1/m)\), equivalently \(R>1\).

notation.meaning: number of observations at client i

review_flags: No supplied locator directly supports this client-weight convention.
standard_field_rationale: sample-proportional empirical-risk weighting is standard, but other federation objectives may choose different weights.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The definition role fits the leaf and the equivalences are correct under sample-proportional aggregation. Because federated objectives may use weights not induced by sample counts, an authoritative source with a specific locator is required to support this exact convention and scope.

children.title: Cross-Client Distribution Shift
children.top_down_role: Regimes where client populations exhibit systematic distributional separation.

assumptions_latex: Clients are indexed by \(i\in\{1,\ldots,n\}\), and client \(i\) draws data from a probability measure \(P_i\) on a common measurable space \((\mathcal Z,\mathcal A)\).
A common measurable loss \(\ell:X\times\mathcal Z\to\mathbb R\) induces \(F_i(x)=\mathbb E_{Z\sim P_i}[\ell(x;Z)]\) whenever the expectation exists.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Cross-client distribution shift holds exactly when \(P_i\ne P_j\) for some clients \(i,j\).

notation.meaning: Expected local objective induced by client i

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Distributional, rather than merely objective-value, heterogeneity on a shared sample space.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Cross-client distribution shift is the condition
\[
\exists i\ne j:\ P_i\ne P_j,
\]
equivalently, there exists \(A\in\mathcal A\) with \(P_i(A)\ne P_j(A)\). For a common loss, the induced objectives are \(F_i(x)=\int_{\mathcal Z}\ell(x;z)\,dP_i(z)\). Distribution shift need not imply \(F_i\ne F_j\), because distinct measures can yield identical expectations for the chosen loss class; conversely, the condition concerns the data-generating measures themselves.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Cross-client distribution shift occurs when at least two clients have different data distributions on the same measurable sample space.
knowledge_statements.title: Cross-Client Distribution Shift

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The distributional condition is mathematically standard and fits the leaf, but no inspectable citation supports this federated-learning usage. The parameter domain X is also not introduced as a set.

children.title: Systems Heterogeneity
children.top_down_role: Differences in compute, memory, energy, bandwidth, and availability.

assumptions_latex: At time \(t\), client \(i\) has a resource-and-availability profile \(r_i(t)\) in a common profile space \(\mathcal R\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Systems heterogeneity holds when \(r_i(t)\ne r_j(t)\) for some clients and relevant time.

notation.meaning: Compute, memory, energy, communication, and availability profile of client i

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Time-dependent device and communication variability, independent of statistical data differences.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let
\[
r_i(t)=(c_i(t),m_i(t),e_i(t),b_i(t),a_i(t))\in\mathcal R
\]
record client \(i\)'s compute capacity, memory, energy budget, bandwidth or latency characteristics, and availability at time \(t\). The federation has systems heterogeneity on a relevant time set \(T\) when
\[
\exists i\ne j,\ 
exists t\in T:\ r_i(t)\ne r_j(t).
\]
The definition permits deterministic, stochastic, and time-varying profiles and does not require the clients' data distributions or objectives to differ.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Systems heterogeneity means that clients differ over time in compute, memory, energy, communication capacity, latency, or availability.
knowledge_statements.title: Systems Heterogeneity

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The definition fits the systems-heterogeneity container, but it has no citation. In the displayed condition, the second existential appears as plain 'exists' rather than \exists and therefore does not express the intended quantified condition correctly.

children.title: Model Heterogeneity
children.top_down_role: Federation across distinct architectures or parameterizations.

assumptions_latex: Client \(i\) optimizes parameters \(\theta_i\in\Theta_i\) and produces outputs in a common prediction space \(\mathcal Y\).
Federated coordination is expressed through a common variable \(z\in Z\) and client-specific maps \(D_i:Z\to\Theta_i\), or through an equivalent shared prediction-level constraint.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Model heterogeneity holds when the local model classes or parameterizations are not all identical while a common coordination interface remains defined.

notation.meaning: Client-specific realization of a common coordination variable

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Architecture or parameter-space heterogeneity with an explicit common coordination interface.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
A federation is model-heterogeneous when its clients use local model classes \(\mathcal H_i=\{h_{i,\theta}:\theta\in\Theta_i\}\) for which
\[
\exists i\ne j:\ (\Theta_i,\mathcal H_i)\ne(
\Theta_j,\mathcal H_j),
\]
while a common coordination interface remains available. Such an interface may be a variable \(z\in Z\) with client realizations \(D_i(z)\in\Theta_i\), a shared representation, or comparable predictions in \(\mathcal Y\). Direct coordinatewise parameter averaging is defined only when compatible embeddings into a common vector space have been specified.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Model heterogeneity occurs when clients use distinct architectures or parameter spaces but retain a defined shared coordination or prediction interface.
knowledge_statements.title: Model Heterogeneity

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The definition fits the model-heterogeneity leaf, but the proposed coordination-interface formulation is not source-supported. The model classes h_{i,\theta} are also not assigned a common input domain.

children.title: Partial Client Participation
children.top_down_role: Optimization with sampled, unavailable, or delayed client subsets.

assumptions_latex: There are \(n\) clients with objective weights \(p_i>0\), \(\sum_i p_i=1\).
At round \(t\), a random available or selected subset \(S_t\subseteq\{1,\ldots,n\}\) is observed, with inclusion probability \(q_{i,t}=\mathbb P(i\in S_t)>0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Participation is partial when \(\mathbb P(S_t\ne\{1,\ldots,n\})>0\) for at least one round.

notation.meaning: Participating client subset at round t
Marginal inclusion probability of client i
Target objective weight of client i

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Random, unavailable, or delayed client subsets represented by roundwise inclusion events.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Partial client participation means
\[
\exists t:\ 
\mathbb P\!\left(S_t\ne\{1,\ldots,n\}\right)>0.
\]
For client quantities \(u_{i,t}\), the Horvitz--Thompson aggregate
\[
\widehat u_t=\sum_{i\in S_t}\frac{p_i}{q_{i,t}}u_{i,t}
\]
satisfies \(\mathbb E[\widehat u_t]=\sum_i p_i u_{i,t}\) when the quantities are fixed conditional on the sampling design. Without inclusion-probability correction, unequal participation can change the effective client weights.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Participation is partial when some communication round can omit clients because of sampling, unavailability, or delay.
knowledge_statements.title: Partial Client Participation

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The definition and inclusion-corrected aggregate are mathematically coherent and fit partial client participation, but no source is supplied for the federated formulation or its attached weighting property.

children.title: Participation-Fairness Distortion Boundary
children.top_down_role: Objective distortions caused by nonrepresentative participation.

children.title: Participation-Induced Objective Bias
children.top_down_role: Objective distortion arising from nonrepresentative client availability.

assumptions_latex: The target objective is \(F(x)=\sum_{i=1}^n p_iF_i(x)\), where \(p_i>0\) and \(\sum_i p_i=1\).
Client \(i\) has long-run positive participation probability \(q_i\), and aggregation does not correct unequal inclusion probabilities.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The effective objective is \(\widetilde F(x)=\sum_i\widetilde p_iF_i(x)\), with \(\widetilde p_i=p_iq_i/(\sum_jp_jq_j)\), rather than \(F\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Long-run exposure model for uncorrected unequal client participation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Under uncorrected participation, client \(i\)'s long-run exposure is proportional to \(p_iq_i\). Normalizing gives
\[
\widetilde p_i=\frac{p_iq_i}{\sum_{j=1}^np_jq_j},
\qquad
\widetilde F(x)=\sum_{i=1}^n\widetilde p_iF_i(x).
\]
Thus \(\widetilde F=F\) whenever all \(q_i\) are equal. If the \(q_i\) are unequal and
\[
\sum_i(\widetilde p_i-p_i)\nabla F_i(x)\ne0
\]
at some differentiability point \(x\), the effective and intended objective gradients differ there, exhibiting participation-induced objective bias.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Uncorrected unequal participation reweights client objectives by their participation probabilities and can move stationary points away from those of the intended objective.
knowledge_statements.title: Participation-Induced Objective Bias

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The weights p_iq_i arise only for a specified long-run aggregation/exposure model; merely saying that inclusion probabilities are uncorrected is insufficient because round-normalized aggregation can induce different weights. The plain statement additionally claims movement of stationary points, whereas the formula establishes only a gradient discrepancy at some point.

children.title: Client-Level Fairness
children.top_down_role: Equity of optimization outcomes across individual clients.

assumptions_latex: Each client has a finite real-valued loss \(F_i(x)\) at the evaluated model \(x\in X\).
A tolerance \(\varepsilon\ge0\) is fixed.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The model is \(\varepsilon\)-client-fair in loss parity exactly when \(\max_iF_i(x)-\min_iF_i(x)\le\varepsilon\).

notation.meaning: Loss or risk of client i at the common model

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Loss-parity version; other federated client-fairness notions require separate statements.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
In the client-loss-parity sense, define the disparity
\[
\Delta_{\mathrm{client}}(x)=
\max_{1\le i\le n}F_i(x)-
\min_{1\le i\le n}F_i(x).
\]
A model \(x\) is \(\varepsilon\)-client-fair when
\[
\Delta_{\mathrm{client}}(x)\le\varepsilon.
\]
The case \(\varepsilon=0\) requires equal loss for every client. This condition evaluates disparity across clients and is distinct from minimizing the weighted mean \(\sum_i p_iF_i(x)\), which alone imposes no bound on \(\Delta_{\mathrm{client}}(x)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Under loss parity, a model is client-fair when the largest difference between any clients' losses is at most the chosen tolerance.
knowledge_statements.title: Client-Level Fairness

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The loss-parity condition is precise and appropriately scoped, but client-level fairness has several inequivalent meanings and no citation establishes that this version is intended here.

children.title: Group Representation Fairness
children.top_down_role: Coverage and influence of client groups within participating populations.

assumptions_latex: Clients are partitioned into nonempty groups \(\mathcal G\), and client \(i\) receives normalized long-run exposure \(\rho_i\ge0\) with \(\sum_i\rho_i=1\).
Each group \(G\in\mathcal G\) has a target exposure \(\pi_G\ge0\), with \(\sum_G\pi_G=1\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Group representation is \(\varepsilon\)-fair exactly when \(\max_{G\in\mathcal G}|\sum_{i\in G}\rho_i-\pi_G|\le\varepsilon\).

notation.meaning: Partition of clients into protected or operational groups
Normalized exposure assigned to client i

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exposure-parity condition relative to explicitly supplied group targets.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The realized representation of group \(G\in\mathcal G\) is
\[
R_G=\sum_{i\in G}\rho_i.
\]
For prescribed target shares \(\pi_G\), group representation is \(\varepsilon\)-fair when
\[
\max_{G\in\mathcal G}|R_G-\pi_G|\le\varepsilon.
\]
Exact representation fairness corresponds to \(\varepsilon=0\). The targets may encode population shares, objective weights, or another declared policy, but they must be fixed independently of the realized participation whose fairness is being assessed.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Group representation fairness requires each group's long-run participation exposure to remain within a tolerance of its declared target share.
knowledge_statements.title: Group Representation Fairness

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The exposure-to-target condition is internally coherent and fits the leaf, but no source supports it as the intended group-representation fairness notion; the choice and interpretation of target shares are application dependent.

children.title: Fairness under Unequal Availability
children.top_down_role: Fairness boundaries created by persistent differences in client availability.

assumptions_latex: Client \(i\) is available with marginal probability \(q_i>0\), has target exposure \(p_i>0\), and \(\sum_i p_i=1\).
When available, client \(i\) is selected with conditional probability \(s_i\in[0,1]\), and the expected participation budget is \(m\in(0,\sum_iq_i]\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Exact target exposure with budget \(m\) is feasible exactly when \(mp_i\le q_i\) for every client, using \(s_i=mp_i/q_i\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Marginal-exposure feasibility under unequal availability and a fixed expected participation budget.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The unconditional exposure of client \(i\) is \(q_is_i\). Exact availability-adjusted fairness with target shares \(p_i\) and expected budget \(m\) requires
\[
q_is_i=mp_i\quad\text{for every }i.
\]
Consequently the unique marginal correction is
\[
s_i=\frac{mp_i}{q_i}.
\]
A valid policy with \(s_i\in[0,1]\) exists if and only if \(mp_i\le q_i\) for every \(i\). If this inequality fails, the target exposure is unattainable without reducing \(m\), relaxing the targets, or changing availability.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Inverse-availability selection realizes target client exposure only when no client's requested marginal exposure exceeds its availability probability.
knowledge_statements.title: Fairness under Unequal Availability

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The marginal feasibility calculation is correct for the stated per-client conditional-selection model without joint capacity constraints, but no citation supports this particular formulation of fairness under unequal availability.

children.title: Federated Local-Update Methods
children.top_down_role: Methods trading local computation against communication frequency.

children.title: Federated SGD
children.top_down_role: Federated aggregation after short local stochastic computations.

knowledge_statements.title: Federated SGD
knowledge_statements.scope_note: One-local-gradient, history-conditionally inclusion-corrected version of federated SGD.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Given \(x_0\in X\), stepsizes \(\eta_t>0\), weights \(p_i\), and a horizon \(T\), round \(t\) samples \(S_t\). Each \(i\in S_t\) draws \(\xi_{i,t}\) and returns \(g_i(x_t;\xi_{i,t})\). The server forms
\[
G_t=\sum_{i\in S_t}\frac{p_i}{q_{i,t}}g_i(x_t;\xi_{i,t}),
\qquad
x_{t+1}=x_t-\eta_tG_t.
\]
Under the stated history-conditional inclusion and oracle-unbiasedness assumptions,
\[
\mathbb E[G_t\mid\mathcal H_t]=\nabla F(x_t).
\]
Stop after \(T\) rounds and output \(x_T\), or a prespecified average of the iterates.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Federated SGD aggregates one stochastic gradient from each selected client and corrects by the client's history-conditional inclusion probability, yielding the intended objective gradient in conditional expectation.
assumptions_latex: The parameter domain \(X\) is a real vector space, \(p_i>0\), \(\sum_{i=1}^n p_i=1\), and the differentiable objective is \(F(x)=\sum_{i=1}^n p_iF_i(x)\).
Before sampling at round \(t\), the history \(\mathcal H_t\) contains \(x_t\), and \(q_{i,t}=\mathbb P(i\in S_t\mid\mathcal H_t)>0\).
For every client selected at round \(t\), \(\mathbb E[g_i(x_t;\xi_{i,t})\mid\mathcal H_t,\,i\in S_t]=\nabla F_i(x_t)\), and the displayed conditional expectations exist.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The returned iterate is generated by an inclusion-corrected stochastic-gradient update satisfying \(\mathbb E[G_t\mid\mathcal H_t]=\nabla F(x_t)\).

notation.meaning: Common server model at round t
Stochastic gradient computed by client i
History-conditional inclusion probability of client i at round t
Information available before round-t client sampling

children.title: Local-SGD Periodic-Averaging Calculus
children.top_down_role: Multiple local stochastic updates between global aggregations.

children.title: Local SGD Dynamics
children.top_down_role: Optimization behavior during multiple local stochastic-update epochs.

assumptions_latex: Client \(i\) has objective \(F_i\) and an unbiased stochastic-gradient oracle \(g_i\).
All participating clients start communication round \(t\) from the synchronized model \(x_t\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: After \(K_t\) local steps, client \(i\) supplies \(x_{i,t,K_t}\) for the next synchronization.

notation.meaning: Client i's local model after k steps in round t
Number of local updates in round t

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Synchronous local stochastic-gradient dynamics between communication events.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For every participating client \(i\in S_t\), initialize
\[
x_{i,t,0}=x_t.
\]
For \(k=0,\ldots,K_t-1\), independently sample local data \(\xi_{i,t,k}\) and update
\[
x_{i,t,k+1}=x_{i,t,k}-\eta_{t,k}g_i(x_{i,t,k};\xi_{i,t,k}).
\]
After completing \(K_t\) steps, client \(i\) transmits \(x_{i,t,K_t}\) or the equivalent displacement \(x_{i,t,K_t}-x_t\). The local phase itself performs no inter-client communication; synchronization is a separate aggregation operation.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Each selected client starts from the common model, takes a prescribed number of local stochastic-gradient steps, and returns its final model or displacement.
knowledge_statements.title: Local SGD Dynamics

children.title: Periodic Model Averaging
children.top_down_role: Global aggregation performed at recurring communication intervals.

assumptions_latex: At synchronization round \(t\), participating clients return local endpoints \(x_{i,t,K_t}\).
Aggregation weights \(a_{i,t}\ge0\) satisfy \(\sum_{i\in S_t}a_{i,t}=1\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The synchronization map averages the endpoints and resets every continuing client to the same model \(x_{t+1}\).

notation.meaning: Aggregation weight of participating client i

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Synchronous weighted averaging after each block of local updates.

source_refs.locator: 11.1 Distributed optimization with centralized consensus p. 227
source_refs.source_title: Large-Scale Convex Optimization: Algorithms & Analyses via Monotone Operators

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
After the local phase of round \(t\), the server computes
\[
x_{t+1}=
\sum_{i\in S_t}a_{i,t}x_{i,t,K_t},
\qquad

a_{i,t}\ge0,
\qquad
\sum_{i\in S_t}a_{i,t}=1.
\]
It then broadcasts \(x_{t+1}\), and each client participating in the next local phase is reset to that model. Repeating this operation after blocks of \(K_t\) local steps gives periodic model averaging. Stop after a prescribed number of synchronization rounds and output the final server model.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Periodic model averaging replaces selected clients' local endpoints by a weighted common model after every block of local updates.
knowledge_statements.title: Periodic Model Averaging
