children.title: Correlated Fault Regimes
children.top_down_role: Execution settings where multiple faults share a common cause or pattern.

knowledge_statements.title: Correlated Fault Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Dependence condition for distributed execution faults.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(Z_{i,k}\in\{0,1\}\) indicate a specified fault affecting component \(i\) at iteration \(k\). The execution is in a correlated fault regime when the joint law does not factor over component-time pairs:
\[\mathbb P\!\left(\bigcap_{(i,k)\in S}\{Z_{i,k}=z_{i,k}\}\right)\ne\prod_{(i,k)\in S}\mathbb P(Z_{i,k}=z_{i,k})\]
for some finite set \(S\) and assignment \((z_{i,k})\). Spatially common-cause faults and temporally persistent faults are included; independent Bernoulli failures are excluded.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Faults are correlated when their joint component-time distribution does not factor into independent marginal distributions.
assumptions_latex: \(Z_{i,k}\) are random variables on a common probability space.
\(S\) is finite.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The joint fault law fails to factor for some finite \(S\).

notation.meaning: Fault indicator for component i at iteration k.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The displayed nonfactorization correctly expresses failure of mutual independence for a binary component-time family, and condition fits the leaf. No citation supports adopting this broad probabilistic definition as the distributed fault regime represented by the container.

children.title: Federated Failure Boundaries
children.top_down_role: Breakdowns caused by heterogeneous objectives, participation, or local computation.

children.title: Client Drift
children.top_down_role: Local optimization moves that conflict with the aggregate objective.

knowledge_statements.title: Client Drift
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Drift of local federated steps relative to global descent.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(F(x)=\sum_{i=1}^n p_iF_i(x)\), where \(p_i>0\) and \(\sum_i p_i=1\). From common model \(x\), client \(i\) performs \(E\) local steps and returns displacement \(s_i=x_i^E-x\). Its client-drift vector relative to \(E\) global gradient steps of size \(\eta>0\) is
\[d_i(x)=s_i+\eta E\nabla F(x).\]
Nonzero \(d_i(x)\) measures local-global disagreement. The local move directly conflicts with aggregate descent when \(\langle s_i,\nabla F(x)\rangle>0\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Client drift is the discrepancy between a client's multi-step local displacement and the corresponding global-gradient displacement; positive gradient alignment indicates conflict.
assumptions_latex: \(F_i:\mathbb R^d\to\mathbb R\) are differentiable at \(x\).

notation.meaning: Client-drift vector relative to global descent.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: Client-drift conventions vary, and no source supports this one. The local update recursion and step sizes are unspecified, while E global gradient steps are represented by E times the gradient at the initial point. Moreover, nonzero discrepancy is broader than the container role of local moves conflicting with aggregate descent.

children.title: Federated Objective Inconsistency
children.top_down_role: Mismatch between implemented aggregation and intended population risk.

knowledge_statements.title: Federated Objective Inconsistency
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Mismatch between intended and effective federated objectives.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let the intended population objective be \(F(x)=\sum_{i=1}^n p_iF_i(x)\), with \(p_i\ge0\) and \(\sum_i p_i=1\). Suppose the implemented aggregation has expected normalized client weights \(q_i\ge0\), producing the effective objective \(\widetilde F(x)=\sum_iq_iF_i(x)\). Federated objective inconsistency is present when
\[
abla\widetilde F(x)
e
abla F(x)\]
for some common differentiability point \(x\). Weight mismatch alone is insufficient when it cancels because local objectives coincide.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Objective inconsistency occurs when implemented aggregation induces a gradient field different from that of the intended population-weighted objective.
assumptions_latex: \(F_i:\mathbb R^d\to\mathbb R\) are differentiable on a common domain.
\(p_i,q_i\ge0\), \(\sum_i p_i=\sum_i q_i=1\).

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The predicate is mathematically coherent and failure_boundary fits the container, but the effective weights depend on the participation and normalization protocol. A federated-optimization source is required to justify interpreting expected normalized weights as a fixed effective objective.

children.title: Participation-Selection Bias Taxonomy
children.top_down_role: Systematic exclusion or overrepresentation of client groups.

children.title: Participation Bias
children.top_down_role: Bias caused by systematic differences in client availability.

knowledge_statements.title: Participation Bias
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Bias induced by unequal client participation probabilities.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
At round \(k\), let \(I_i^k\in\{0,1\}\) indicate participation, with \(\pi_i^k=\mathbb P(I_i^k=1)>0\), and let \(g_i^k\in\mathbb R^d\) be client \(i\)'s target contribution. For deterministic aggregation weights \(a_i^k\), participation bias is present when
\[\mathbb E\!\left[\sum_{i=1}^n a_i^k I_i^k g_i^k\right]\ne\sum_{i=1}^n p_i g_i^k.\]
If participation is independent of the contributions, inverse-probability weights \(a_i^k=p_i/\pi_i^k\) remove this first-moment bias.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Participation bias occurs when the expected aggregate over participating clients differs from the intended population-weighted contribution.
assumptions_latex: \(g_i^k\in\mathbb R^d\) is integrable.
\(p_i\ge0\) and \(\sum_i p_i=1\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\mathbb E[\sum_i a_i^k I_i^k g_i^k]\ne\sum_i p_i g_i^k\).

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The first-moment bias predicate is coherent and condition fits the leaf. The inverse-probability correction depends on the precise stochastic relationship between participation and contributions, so the stated independence qualification and weighting claim require a targeted sampling source.

children.title: Client-Selection Bias
children.top_down_role: Bias caused by nonrepresentative client-selection policies.

knowledge_statements.title: Client-Selection Bias
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Bias from the server's conditional selection rule.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(A_k\) be the eligible clients at round \(k\), let \(S_k\subseteq A_k\) be the server-selected set, and let \(J_i^k=\mathbf1\{i\in S_k\}\). Given round information \(\mathcal H_k\), client-selection bias is present for contributions \(g_i^k\) when
\[\mathbb E\!\left[\sum_{i\in A_k}a_i^kJ_i^kg_i^k\mid\mathcal H_k\right]\ne\sum_{i=1}^n p_i g_i^k.\]
This isolates server selection after eligibility is determined; unequal availability belongs to participation bias.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Client-selection bias occurs when the server's conditional selection rule yields an expected aggregate different from the intended client-weighted contribution.
assumptions_latex: \(S_k\subseteq A_k\subseteq\{1,\ldots,n\}\).
\(g_i^k\) is conditionally integrable given \(\mathcal H_k\).
\(p_i\ge0\) and \(\sum_i p_i=1\).

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The intended distinction between eligibility and server selection is plausible, but no source supports it. The statement must specify which sets, weights, and contributions are measurable with respect to the round information and whether the full-population target on the right is conditional or deterministic.

children.title: Client-Group Underrepresentation
children.top_down_role: Persistent exclusion or insufficient influence of particular client groups.

knowledge_statements.title: Client-Group Underrepresentation
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Insufficient expected aggregation mass for a designated client group.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(G\subseteq\{1,\ldots,n\}\) be a designated client group with intended population mass \(P_G=\sum_{i\in G}p_i>0\). At round \(k\), let \(W_i^k\ge0\) be the random normalized aggregation weight assigned to client \(i\), with \(\sum_iW_i^k=1\). For tolerance \(\delta_G\in[0,1)\), group \(G\) is underrepresented when
\[\mathbb E\!\left[\sum_{i\in G}W_i^k\right]<(1-\delta_G)P_G.\]
The condition compares aggregation influence, not merely the number of selected clients.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A client group is underrepresented when its expected aggregation weight falls materially below its intended population weight.
assumptions_latex: \(G\ne\varnothing\) and \(P_G>0\).
\(W_i^k\ge0\) and \(\sum_iW_i^k=1\) almost surely.

notation.meaning: Intended population mass of the group.
Realized normalized aggregation weight of client i.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The condition is internally coherent and its kind fits the leaf, but no source supports aggregation weight as the chosen representation measure or the tolerance-based threshold. Targeted federated representation evidence is required.

children.title: Federated Objective Distortion
children.top_down_role: Deviation of the optimized objective from the intended client population objective.

assumptions_latex: There are \(m\ge 2\) clients with intended weights \(p_i\ge 0\), \(\sum_{i=1}^m p_i=1\).
Client participation induces effective weights \(q_i\ge 0\), \(\sum_{i=1}^m q_i=1\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Participation selection can change both the objective and its minimizers: \(F_q-F_p=\sum_i(q_i-p_i)f_i\), and generally \(\operatorname*{argmin}F_q\ne\operatorname*{argmin}F_p\).
review_flags: No supplied locator directly supports participation-induced objective distortion; a federated-learning source is required.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-client distortion caused solely by changing aggregation weights through nonrepresentative participation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(F_p(x)=\sum_{i=1}^m p_i f_i(x)\) be the intended objective and let \(F_q(x)=\sum_{i=1}^m q_i f_i(x)\) be the objective induced by participation. The distortion is \(D_q(x)=F_q(x)-F_p(x)=\sum_{i=1}^m(q_i-p_i)f_i(x)\). It need not preserve minimizers. For \(d=1\), \(f_1(x)=x^2\), \(f_2(x)=(x-2)^2\), \(p=(1/2,1/2)\), and \(q=(1,0)\), one has \(\operatorname*{argmin}F_p=\{1\}\) but \(\operatorname*{argmin}F_q=\{0\}\). Thus biased participation can optimize a different population objective even when every submitted update is exact.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Biased participation replaces intended client weights by effective weights and can move the optimizer, even when all participating clients compute exact updates.
knowledge_statements.title: Federated Objective Distortion

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The finite-client calculation and counterexample are internally correct and fit the failure-boundary container, but no citation supports interpreting participation frequencies as effective objective weights in the intended federated model.

children.title: Local Overtraining
children.top_down_role: Excessive local work amplifying heterogeneity and destabilizing aggregation.

assumptions_latex: Clients minimize differentiable objectives \(f_i:\mathbb R^d\to\mathbb R\) from a shared iterate.
Aggregation averages endpoints after \(K\) local descent steps.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: As \(K\) grows, averaged local endpoints can approach an optimizer different from the global minimizer, so additional exact local work need not improve federated progress.

notation.meaning: Number of local steps per round

review_flags: No supplied locator directly supports the local-overtraining failure mechanism; a federated-optimization convergence source is required.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Deterministic full-participation boundary for excessive local optimization under heterogeneous curvature.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Local overtraining occurs when increasing \(K\) drives each endpoint \(x_i^{(K)}\) toward a client-specific minimizer faster than aggregation tracks the minimizer of \(F=\sum_i p_i f_i\). For two equally weighted scalar clients, take \(f_1(x)=x^2/2\) and \(f_2(x)=a(x-1)^2/2\) with \(a>0\) and \(a\ne1\). If stable local descent is run to convergence, then \(x_1^{(K)}\to0\), \(x_2^{(K)}\to1\), and their average tends to \(1/2\), whereas \(\operatorname*{argmin}F=\{a/(1+a)\}\). Hence arbitrarily accurate local solutions can yield a persistently biased aggregate.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: With heterogeneous client curvature, many local steps can make averaged client solutions converge to a point different from the global optimizer.
knowledge_statements.title: Local Overtraining

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The quadratic example correctly shows that averaging converged local minimizers can differ from minimizing the weighted aggregate, and failure_boundary fits the node. A federated-optimization source is needed to substantiate this construction as the intended local-overtraining mechanism and delimit its algorithmic assumptions.

children.title: Adversarial Boundaries
children.top_down_role: Optimization-facing limits under malicious or strategically corrupted participation.

children.title: Byzantine Update Faults
children.top_down_role: Arbitrary or malicious optimization messages.

assumptions_latex: A server expects one update in \(\mathbb R^d\) from each selected client.
The Byzantine set \(B\) is not constrained by the prescribed local algorithm.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: For every \(i\in B\), the transmitted update may be any adaptive vector in \(\mathbb R^d\); guarantees must therefore quantify over all such choices.

notation.meaning: Message sent by client i in round t

review_flags: The supplied distributed-optimization locators do not address Byzantine fault models; a Byzantine-robust optimization source is required.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Message-level Byzantine fault model with adaptive, arbitrary client updates.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A Byzantine update fault is present when a client \(i\in B\) may transmit an arbitrary message \(u_i^t=\phi_i^t(\mathcal H_t,\xi_i^t)\in\mathbb R^d\) at round \(t\), where \(\phi_i^t\) is unrestricted, \(\mathcal H_t\) is the observable history, and \(\xi_i^t\) permits private randomness. The message need not equal a gradient, correspond to any dataset, or remain consistent across recipients or rounds. Honest clients \(i\notin B\) follow the specified update rule. A robustness statement under this model must hold uniformly over the Byzantine set and all admissible adaptive message strategies.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A Byzantine client may send any adaptive optimization vector, unrelated to data or the prescribed algorithm, while honest clients follow the protocol.
knowledge_statements.title: Byzantine Update Faults

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The definition broadly matches an adaptive Byzantine message model, but no Byzantine-robust optimization source is cited. The claim that messages may differ across recipients also exceeds the stated single-server, one-update assumption unless equivocation or multiple recipients are explicitly included.

children.title: Data-Objective Poisoning Interface
children.top_down_role: Optimization effects of corrupted local data or risks.

children.title: Data Poisoning Interface
children.top_down_role: Optimization effects arising from corrupted client training data.

assumptions_latex: Client \(i\) ordinarily forms an empirical objective from dataset \(D_i\).
An attacker may replace \(D_i\) by an admissible poisoned dataset \(D_i'\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The data-poisoning interface is the map \(D_i\mapsto D_i'\mapsto f_i'\mapsto u_i'\), with admissibility enforced at the dataset level.
review_flags: No supplied locator supports a formal federated data-poisoning interface or poisoning budget.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Dataset-level attack interface, distinguished from direct manipulation of objectives or transmitted updates.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given \(D_i=\{z_{ij}\}_{j=1}^{n_i}\), a data-poisoning interface permits an attacker to choose \(D_i'\in\mathcal A_i(D_i)\), where \(\mathcal A_i(D_i)\) is an explicitly declared admissible set, such as datasets obtained by replacing at most \(b_i\) examples. The client then forms \(f_i'(x)=|D_i'|^{-1}\sum_{z\in D_i'}\ell(x;z)\) and applies the prescribed optimizer to \(f_i'\). Thus the attack acts through \(D_i\mapsto D_i'\mapsto f_i'\mapsto u_i'\); it does not directly authorize an arbitrary objective or message beyond what some admissible \(D_i'\) induces.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Data poisoning changes an allowed number of client examples, then lets the normal training rule propagate that change into the objective and update.
knowledge_statements.title: Data Poisoning Interface

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The dataset-to-objective-to-update interface is coherent and definition is the correct kind, but the admissible poisoning model and example-replacement budget lack a supporting federated data-poisoning citation.

children.title: Objective Poisoning Interface
children.top_down_role: Optimization effects arising from manipulated local risks or preferences.

assumptions_latex: Client \(i\) has benign objective \(f_i:\mathbb R^d\to\mathbb R\).
The attack class specifies an admissible perturbation set \(\mathcal H_i\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Objective poisoning replaces \(f_i\) by \(f_i+h_i\) for \(h_i\in\mathcal H_i\), independently of whether the perturbed objective is realizable by poisoned data.
review_flags: No supplied locator establishes the intended objective-poisoning attack class or its relation to data realizability.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Function-level poisoning interface before execution of the prescribed local optimizer.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: An objective-poisoning interface permits an attacker controlling client \(i\) to replace \(f_i\) by \(\widetilde f_i=f_i+h_i\), where \(h_i\in\mathcal H_i\) and \(\mathcal H_i\) states all magnitude, smoothness, convexity, or support restrictions. The client update is then generated by the prescribed local algorithm applied to \(\widetilde f_i\). Unlike data poisoning, the interface does not require \(\widetilde f_i\) to equal an empirical risk derived from an admissible modified dataset. Unlike a Byzantine-message model, it still requires the transmitted update to be consistent with optimizing some allowed \(\widetilde f_i\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Objective poisoning directly perturbs a client loss within a declared function class, without requiring that the new loss arise from modified data.
knowledge_statements.title: Objective Poisoning Interface

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The function-level interface is mathematically explicit and distinguished from data and message poisoning, but its attack class and data-realizability distinction are not supported by a cited source.

children.title: Targeted Optimization Distortion
children.top_down_role: Adversarial influence directed toward selected outcomes or model behaviors.

assumptions_latex: The attacker controls objectives indexed by \(B\) and chooses admissible perturbations \(h_i\in\mathcal H_i\).
A target point \(x_{\mathrm{tar}}\in\mathbb R^d\) and tolerance \(\varepsilon\ge0\) are fixed.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A targeted distortion succeeds when \(x_{\mathrm{tar}}\) is \(\varepsilon\)-optimal for the poisoned aggregate while the declared admissibility and collateral constraints hold.
review_flags: No supplied source specifies a canonical success predicate for targeted federated optimization distortion.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Optimization-level success predicate for steering the aggregate toward a prescribed target.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\widetilde F(x)=\sum_{i\notin B}p_i f_i(x)+\sum_{i\in B}p_i(f_i(x)+h_i(x))\). A targeted optimization distortion toward \(x_{\mathrm{tar}}\) succeeds at tolerance \(\varepsilon\) when there exist \(h_i\in\mathcal H_i\) such that \(\widetilde F(x_{\mathrm{tar}})\le\inf_{x\in\mathbb R^d}\widetilde F(x)+\varepsilon\), together with every declared collateral constraint, such as \(C(h_1,\ldots,h_m)\le\rho\). The target is attacker-selected before evaluation. Without the target condition, merely increasing benign loss or preventing convergence constitutes untargeted disruption rather than targeted distortion.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A targeted attack succeeds when admissible poisoned objectives make a preselected point approximately optimal while satisfying the stated collateral constraints.
knowledge_statements.title: Targeted Optimization Distortion

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The epsilon-optimality predicate is precise and condition fits the terminal container, but no source establishes it as the intended success criterion for targeted optimization distortion or supports the chosen collateral-constraint formulation.

children.title: Poisoning Detectability Boundaries
children.top_down_role: Regimes where malicious local behavior is difficult to distinguish from heterogeneity.

assumptions_latex: A detector observes a transcript \(T\) and outputs either benign or poisoned.
Two admissible worlds induce transcript laws \(P_0\) and \(P_1\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: If \(P_0=P_1\), every detector \(\delta\) satisfies \(P_0(\delta(T)=1)+P_1(\delta(T)=0)=1\); uniform reliable detection is impossible.
review_flags: The indistinguishability argument is standard, but no supplied locator connects it to federated poisoning detectability.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Information-theoretic impossibility boundary based on observationally identical protocol transcripts.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(P_0\) be the law of the observable transcript \(T\) in an admissible benign world and \(P_1\) its law in an admissible poisoned world. If \(P_0=P_1\), then for every possibly randomized detector \(\delta(T)\in\{0,1\}\), with \(1\) denoting poisoning, \[P_0(\delta(T)=1)+P_1(\delta(T)=0)=1.\] Consequently at least one of its false-positive and false-negative probabilities is at least \(1/2\). Poisoning is therefore not uniformly detectable from \(T\) unless the model excludes observationally equivalent benign and poisoned worlds or supplies additional trusted information.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: When a benign world and a poisoned world produce identical observable transcripts, every detector has false-positive or false-negative probability at least one half.
knowledge_statements.title: Poisoning Detectability Boundaries

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The indistinguishability calculation is mathematically correct and failure_boundary is appropriate, but no inspectable citation connects this testing boundary to admissible benign and poisoned federated transcripts.

children.title: Collusion-Sybil Attack Interface
children.top_down_role: Optimization consequences of coordinated or duplicated malicious clients.

children.title: Colluding-Client Interface
children.top_down_role: Optimization consequences of coordinated malicious participants.

assumptions_latex: A controlled set \(B\) can communicate privately or share state.
Each controlled client submits one protocol-visible update per round.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Collusion allows the tuple \((u_i^t)_{i\in B}\) to follow an arbitrary joint strategy subject only to the declared per-client protocol constraints.

notation.meaning: Shared colluder state before round t
Update of client i at round t

review_flags: No supplied locator formalizes colluding clients in distributed or federated optimization.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Joint-strategy interface for multiple distinct controlled clients with shared information.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A colluding-client interface permits a controlled set \(B\) to choose its round-\(t\) messages jointly as \((u_i^t)_{i\in B}=\Phi_t(\mathcal H_t,S_t,\xi_t)\), where \(\mathcal H_t\) is the visible protocol history, \(S_t\) is shared private state, and \(\xi_t\) is joint randomness. Each component remains attached to a distinct registered client and must satisfy any declared per-client constraint. The defining feature is that the joint law need not factor across clients: \(P((u_i^t)_{i\in B}\mid\mathcal H_t)\ne\prod_{i\in B}P(u_i^t\mid\mathcal H_t)\) may hold.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Colluding clients coordinate their updates using shared state and randomness, so their joint behavior need not factor into independent client strategies.
knowledge_statements.title: Colluding-Client Interface

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The joint-strategy formulation fits a colluding-client interface and is internally consistent, but no source supports this particular information, shared-state, randomness, and per-client-constraint model.

children.title: Sybil-Client Interface
children.top_down_role: Optimization consequences of multiple malicious identities controlled by one actor.

assumptions_latex: One adversarial principal controls a set \(S\) of registered logical client identities.
The server treats identities as separate contributors unless an identity-control rule intervenes.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A Sybil interface permits one principal to submit the family \((u_s^t)_{s\in S}\) through multiple apparent clients and thereby acquire identity-dependent aggregation weight.
review_flags: No supplied locator supports a formal Sybil-client model for federated aggregation.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Identity-level attack interface in which one principal controls multiple apparent clients.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A Sybil-client interface exists when one adversarial principal controls \(k=|S|\ge2\) logical identities and may submit an update \(u_s^t\) under each \(s\in S\) during round \(t\). The server observes separate identities but does not observe their common controller. If aggregation assigns weights \(w_s^t\) by identity, the principal's direct aggregate contribution is \(\sum_{s\in S}w_s^t u_s^t\), rather than the contribution allowed to one physical principal. The interface must specify registration, participation, and weighting constraints; otherwise the effective adversarial weight is undefined.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A Sybil attacker uses multiple apparent client identities, allowing one controller to submit several updates and accumulate identity-based aggregation weight.
knowledge_statements.title: Sybil-Client Interface

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The definition clearly separates logical identities from their common controller and correctly notes dependence on registration and weighting rules, but it lacks a source for the federated Sybil threat model.

children.title: Coordinated Update Manipulation
children.top_down_role: Collective manipulation of submitted updates to amplify adversarial influence.

assumptions_latex: Colluding clients \(B\) submit vectors \(u_i\in\mathbb R^d\).
Each vector obeys a declared individual constraint \(u_i\in U_i\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A desired aggregate displacement \(b\) is coordinately realizable exactly when \(b\in\sum_{i\in B}w_iU_i\).

notation.meaning: Allowed update set for client i

review_flags: No supplied locator establishes this coordinated-update feasibility model in an adversarial aggregation setting.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: One-round feasibility condition for jointly producing a prescribed aggregate contribution.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For aggregation weights \(w_i\ge0\), coordinated update manipulation toward \(b\in\mathbb R^d\) is feasible when the colluders can choose \(u_i\in U_i\) jointly so that \(\sum_{i\in B}w_i u_i=b\). Equivalently, \[b\in\sum_{i\in B}w_iU_i:=\left\{\sum_{i\in B}w_i v_i:v_i\in U_i\right\}.\] This condition captures aggregate coordination even when every individual update satisfies its local admissibility test. If only approximate manipulation is required, feasibility becomes \(\operatorname{dist}(b,\sum_{i\in B}w_iU_i)\le\varepsilon\) for the declared norm and tolerance \(\varepsilon\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Colluders can realize a target aggregate shift precisely when that shift belongs to the weighted Minkowski sum of their individually allowed update sets.
knowledge_statements.title: Coordinated Update Manipulation

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The weighted Minkowski-sum equivalence follows from the declared one-round model, and condition is an appropriate content kind. A source is still required to establish that this feasibility model represents coordinated adversarial update manipulation in the target context.

children.title: Identity-Multiplicity Effects
children.top_down_role: Distortion of aggregation or selection caused by duplicated identities.

assumptions_latex: The server averages updates uniformly by registered identity.
There are \(n\ge1\) honest identities and \(k\ge1\) identical Sybil identities.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Duplicating one update \(v\) across \(k\) identities changes its aggregate coefficient from \(1/(n+1)\) to \(k/(n+k)\), approaching one as \(k\to\infty\).
review_flags: No supplied locator directly supports identity-multiplicity effects in federated aggregation.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact multiplicity effect under uniform identity-weighted mean aggregation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let honest updates be \(h_1,\ldots,h_n\) and suppose one adversarial principal repeats \(v\in\mathbb R^d\) through \(k\) identities. Uniform identity averaging returns \[A_k=\frac{\sum_{j=1}^n h_j+kv}{n+k}.\] Hence the principal's coefficient is \(k/(n+k)\), whereas a single identity would receive coefficient \(1/(n+1)\). Moreover \(A_k\to v\) as \(k\to\infty\). Thus an aggregator that weights identities rather than authenticated principals is not invariant under identity replication, even when all repeated update vectors are unchanged.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Under uniform identity averaging, duplicating one update across many identities increases its weight and can force the aggregate arbitrarily close to that update.
knowledge_statements.title: Identity-Multiplicity Effects

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The uniform-averaging formula and limiting multiplicity effect are correct, and property fits the node. No citation supports the identity-replication model or its relevance to Sybil behavior in federated aggregation.

children.title: Distributed Evaluation Boundaries
children.top_down_role: Comparability failures caused by incomplete cost models or unrealistic experiments.

children.title: Communication-Round-Only Evaluation
children.top_down_role: Efficiency evaluation omitting message size, latency, or local work.

assumptions_latex: Evaluation reports only the number \(R\) of synchronous communication rounds.
Message size, latency, local oracle calls, and local arithmetic are unreported.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Round count alone cannot order total communication, wall-clock time, or computation without additional per-round resource bounds.
review_flags: The supplied communication-aspects locator is relevant but does not specifically support the stated evaluation failure boundary.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Resource-accounting boundary for comparisons based exclusively on synchronous round count.

source_refs.locator: 1.3 Communication Aspects of Parallel and Distributed Systems p. 27
source_refs.source_title: Parallel and Distributed Computation: Numerical Methods

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For an execution with \(R\) rounds, total communicated bits are \(B=\sum_{r=1}^R b_r\) and total local work is \(C=\sum_{r=1}^R c_r\). Fixing \(R\) places no finite upper bound on either \(B\) or \(C\) when \(b_r\) and \(c_r\) are unrestricted. Two methods can therefore have the same round count while one transmits arbitrarily larger messages or performs arbitrarily more local oracle calls. Consequently a communication-round-only evaluation supports a resource comparison only after common bounds or measurements for message size, latency, participation, and local work are supplied.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Equal communication-round counts do not imply equal bandwidth, runtime, or local computation when per-round messages and work are unconstrained.
knowledge_statements.title: Communication-Round-Only Evaluation

children.title: Unrealistic Participation Evaluation
children.top_down_role: Experiments using availability patterns unlike the target deployment.

knowledge_statements.title: Unrealistic Participation Evaluation
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Distribution-shift boundary for client-availability patterns in finite-horizon distributed evaluations.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(Z_t\subseteq [m]\) be the clients participating at round \(t\), and let \(P\) and \(Q\) denote the deployment and experimental laws of \(Z_{1:T}\), respectively. For every measurable performance loss \(L(Z_{1:T})\in[0,1]\), \[\left|\mathbb E_P[L]-\mathbb E_Q[L]\right|\leq d_{\mathrm{TV}}(P,Q),\qquad \sup_{0\leq L\leq1}\left|\mathbb E_P[L]-\mathbb E_Q[L]\right|=d_{\mathrm{TV}}(P,Q).\] Hence an evaluation is participation-unrealistic beyond tolerance \(\varepsilon\) when \(d_{\mathrm{TV}}(P,Q)>\varepsilon\). In particular, if \(Q(Z_t=[m]\ \forall t)=1\) while \(P(Z_t=[m]\ \forall t)=0\), then \(d_{\mathrm{TV}}(P,Q)=1\), so experimental performance gives no distribution-free guarantee for deployment performance.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Evaluation under the wrong participation law can have maximal bias; full-participation experiments cannot certify deployment performance when full participation never occurs there.
assumptions_latex: \(m,T\in\mathbb N\) and \(Z_t\subseteq[m]\).
\(P\) and \(Q\) are probability laws on the same participation-sequence space.
\(L\) is measurable and takes values in \([0,1]\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(d_{\mathrm{TV}}(P,Q)>\varepsilon\) permits evaluation bias exceeding \(\varepsilon\), and mutually exclusive participation regimes permit bias \(1\).

notation.meaning: Set of clients participating at round t.
Total-variation distance, using the supremum-over-events convention.

children.title: Topology-Agnostic Comparison
children.top_down_role: Comparisons concealing differences in network conditioning.

assumptions_latex: \(W\in\mathbb R^{m\times m}\) is symmetric and doubly stochastic, and \(\lVert W-J\rVert_2<1\).
One communication round applies the mixing operator \(W\) once.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Communication rounds are topology-dependent resources because disagreement contracts by \(\rho(W)^k\), not by a topology-independent function of \(k\).

notation.meaning: Orthogonal averaging matrix onto the consensus subspace.
Spectral contraction factor on the disagreement subspace.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Failure of round-count comparisons that omit the contraction quality of network mixing.

source_refs.locator: 11.3 Decentralized optimization with mixing matrices p. 237
source_refs.source_title: Large-Scale Convex Optimization: Algorithms & Analyses via Monotone Operators

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\mathbf 1\in\mathbb R^m\) be the all-ones vector, let \(J=\mathbf 1\mathbf 1^{\mathsf T}/m\), and let \(I_m\) be the \(m\times m\) identity matrix. For a symmetric doubly stochastic matrix \(W\in\mathbb R^{m\times m}\), define \(\rho(W)=\lVert W-J\rVert_2<1\). For every \(k\in\mathbb N_0\), after \(k\) pure mixing rounds, disagreement satisfies \[\lVert W^k-J\rVert_2=\rho(W)^k.\] Thus equal communication-round counts across networks are not comparable unless \(W\), \(\rho(W)\), or an equivalent spectral-gap normalization is reported and controlled. For \(W_\alpha=(1-\alpha)I_m+\alpha J\) with \(0<\alpha<1\), \(\rho(W_\alpha)=1-\alpha\), whereas \(\rho(J)=0\). Consequently, one round gives exact averaging under \(J\) but leaves a fraction \(1-\alpha\) of worst-case disagreement under \(W_\alpha\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Equal round counts conceal unequal mixing: one topology may average exactly while another retains nearly all disagreement after the same communication.
knowledge_statements.title: Topology-Agnostic Comparison

children.title: Centralized-Baseline Budget Mismatch
children.top_down_role: Comparisons using inconsistent oracle, batch, or computation budgets.

knowledge_statements.title: Centralized-Baseline Budget Mismatch
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Resource-accounting boundary for centralized and distributed optimization comparisons.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For an execution through round \(K\), define total oracle cost \(C_{\mathrm{orc}}=\sum_{t=1}^K\sum_{i=1}^m q_{i,t}\) and total local computation \(C_{\mathrm{comp}}=\sum_{t=1}^K\sum_{i=1}^m c_{i,t}\), where inactive workers contribute zero. A centralized–distributed comparison is budget-mismatched if it reports performance at equal \(K\) while either \(C_{\mathrm{orc}}\) or \(C_{\mathrm{comp}}\) differs and the difference is not separately controlled. In particular, if each of \(m\) workers evaluates a batch of size \(b\) per round, the distributed method uses \(Kmb\) sample-oracle calls; a centralized baseline using one batch of size \(b\) uses only \(Kb\). Their equal-round comparison therefore differs by an oracle-budget factor of \(m\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Equal iteration counts are unfair when the distributed method receives more oracle calls, samples, or aggregate computation than the centralized baseline.
assumptions_latex: \(K,m,b\in\mathbb N\).
\(q_{i,t}\) and \(c_{i,t}\) count oracle calls and local computation for worker \(i\) at round \(t\).
Compared oracle calls have the same information content and unit cost.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Equal-round results do not isolate algorithmic performance when total oracle or computation budgets differ; the batch example has ratio \(Kmb/(Kb)=m\).

notation.meaning: Total number of sample-oracle calls across all workers.
Total local computation accumulated across workers.
